News.title: 'My son, 7, had six teeth removed after inhumane wait for treatment'
News.content:
'My son, 7, had six teeth removed after inhumane wait for treatment'

EXCLUSIVE: Children under 18, or under 19 and in full-time-education, can get free NHS dental appointments and treatment but there is a shortage of NHS practices

View 2 Images Hayley Bramhall, from Macclesfield, said it was "devastating" to see her son Philip in agony (Image: STEVE ALLEN)

A mum whose seven-year-old autistic son had six teeth removed due to a dental abscess has said it was "inhumane" he had to suffer a four-month wait in intense pain.

‌



Hayley Bramhall, from Macclesfield, said it was "devastating" to see her son Philip in agony. During the wait for "urgent" treatment, his abscess grew leading to the need for him to have teeth taken out.

‌



She said her non-verbal son has been holding his mouth and avoiding toothbrushing in a particular area since his surgery in July and she fears they might have to face another long and painful battle if he has another dental problem.

‌



Speaking about him having six teeth removed, Hayley said: "Eating's become more challenging because of that. He's a lot more irate and upset. As a family and for me, it's traumatic. It's frustrating. It makes you feel angry - angry at the lack of services.

Children waiting over a year in agony for tooth extractions READ MORE :

View 2 Images Nearly 10,000 children were admitted to hospital for rotting teeth last year, damning figures show. (Image: Getty Images)

"Frustrated at the fact that, for example, now I need to start the process again because I think he's got toothache. Although I don't know whether it's because he was in pain for four months, which is just inhumane in itself."

‌



Hayley has launched a petition on the Parliament website calling for a maximum 12-week wait for children with special educational needs requiring urgent dental care under sedation or general anaesthetic.

She said her son needs sedation and general anaesthetic just for check up, which can mean long waits that result in the problem getting worse.

"I think the pressure and the wait just for that is exceptional, never mind the wait for someone in extreme pain," she said. "It's devastating as a parent seeing him in pain all the time."

‌



Nearly 10,000 children admitted to hospital for rotting teeth last year, grim study shows

Nearly 10,000 children were admitted to hospital for rotting teeth last year, damning figures show.

In 2025, 8,930 under 18s were admitted for tooth decay, slightly up from 8,925 the year before, analysis by the Liberal Democrats shows.

Children under 18, or under 19 and in full-time-education, can get free NHS dental appointments and treatment but there is a shortage of NHS practices. Around 14 million people – or well over one in four of England’s adult population – were unable to access NHS dental care in 2025.

‌



The study found 470 dental practices have pulled out of the NHS and handed back their contracts since 2020 as ‘dental deserts’ spread across the country.

The research also found particular damage in rural areas, with higher numbers of dentists approaching retirement and a higher proportion leaving the profession.

Elsewhere, researchers found local Education Authorities have shelled out over £2.5million for school-aged pupils since 2020, including on toothbrush kits and on public health initiatives.

‌



Tooth decay remains the number one reason for hospital admissions among young children. The British Dental Association says some kids are waiting years to have teeth extracted because the surgery is competing with other operations on the NHS waiting list for operating theatre time.

Children usually require going under general anaesthetic for tooth extractions so this has to be done in hospital.

Lib Dem primary care spokeswoman Helen Maguire said: “Thousands of young children are being forced into hospital beds just to have their rotting teeth pulled out, millions are trapped in expanding 'dental deserts' unable to get an appointment, and local councils are being forced to shell out millions to patch up a broken system.”

‌



The Liberal Democrats have demanded a £750million Dental Rescue Package to revive access to local NHS appointments and guarantee regular checkups for children. It is also calling for emergency dental A&Es in every community across the country that provide walk-in urgent care seven days a week to ensure that nobody is left in agony.

The British Dental Association welcomed the commitment to new money and criticised a lack of new investment from the Labour Government. The Mirror has launched the Dentists for All campaign with the BDA calling for a return to universal access to NHS dentistry for everyone who needs it.

Eddie Crouch, BDA chair, said: “When millions of people have no options, it’s refreshing to see serious proposals to invest in expanding access to NHS dental care. The real threat to NHS dentistry has always been a poverty of ambition. Rearranging the deckchairs on the Titanic won’t help.”

‌



More than 40,000 people have signed a petition launched by 38 Degrees calling on Andy Burnham to make NHS Dentistry a priority, amid a crisis of people being forced to carry out DIY Dentistry and pull out their own teeth.

Veronica Hawking, Campaigns Director at 38 Degrees, said: "Nobody in modern Britain should be pulling out their own teeth because they can't get an NHS dentist.

"The Government has the public firmly on side - now it needs to properly fund NHS dentistry, so no one else is forced to take matters into their own hands."

Article continues below

A Department of Health and Social Care spokesperson said: "This government is fixing NHS dentistry after a decade of decline. We have improved access to urgent dental treatment by prioritising patients with the greatest need, and millions of additional courses of treatment have been delivered, including a significant amount for children.

“But there is still more to do - especially to increase the dentistry workforce - and that is why we’re rolling out more dentistry school training places in areas which need them, and cutting red tape to allow qualified dentists to practise.”

News.title: Major nuclear power station shut down by millions of invading jellyfish
News.content:
Major nuclear power station shut down by millions of invading jellyfish

The massive Gravelines nuclear power plant just 30 miles from Britain has been forced to close down in order to avoid disaster after a swarm of jellyfish got sucked into the cooling system on Monday

View 2 Images Jellyfish on the shore near the Gravelines nuclear power plant in Gravelines, northern France (file photo) (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Western Europe’s biggest nuclear power station has been shut down after it was invaded by millions of jellyfish.

‌



EDF’s Gravelines plant near Dunkirk, just 30 miles from Britain, was forced to shut down in order to avoid disaster on Monday as the sea creatures swarmed into the plant.

‌



EDF revealed how the jellyfish had been filter drums at the seawater pumping stations, used to cool the giant nuclear reactors at the heart of the plant.

‌



The company was forced to take emergency measures, with reactors two, three and four taken offline, while output from reactor one was halved.

“This situation has no impact on the safety of the facilities, the safety of our personnel, or the environment,” a statement from EDF said.

Only reactor six was operating at full power on Tuesday, with reactor five previously taken offline for scheduled works.

‌



View 2 Images A massive influx of jellyfish into seawater pumping stations has caused chaos at the Gravelines nuclear powe (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

The massive Gravelines plant has six reactors and pumps out 5,400 megawatts of juice, supplying around 70 per cent of the power in northern France’s Hauts-de-France region each year.

The jellyfish invasion comes exactly a year after another swarm of the creatures took the French nuclear site offline for two days.

‌



An invasive species of jellyfish, called the Asian Moon Jellyfish, have been making themselves at home in the English Channel and North Sea in 2020.

The species, usually native to the Pacific, is thought to have been brought here in the ballast tanks of supertankers and dumped into the seas around France and Britain.

Nuclear plants in China, Japan and India, which also rely of seawater for cooling, have previously been thrown into chaos by the slimy sea creatures. And last year power production at Gravelines came to a standstill after the jellies caused chaos.

Article continues below

The plant installed cameras monitoring the seawater intake and filters after last year’s fiasco and set up a warning system to give advanced notice of swarms heading their way.

The system saw fishing boats sent out of saturday with trawler nets in an attempt to thin the numbers of the invasive jellyfish. This helped to limit the latest invasion, the engineer said.

Meanwhile vacuum trucks are sucking out the jellyfish already trapped inside the plant. The engineer said that since no new jellies are arriving the plant will hopefully be back on line soon.

News.title: Mum reveals how son survived head-on motorway crash as car ‘drove wrong way’
News.content:
Mum reveals how son survived head-on motorway crash as car ‘drove wrong way’

Craig Fox, 22, miraculously walked away from a head-on collision on the M50 after he was hit by what is believed to be a stolen Toyota Yaris carrying eight underage teens as travelling 100mph.

View 2 Images The scene of the crash near junction 12 of the M50 (Image: © 2026 COLLINS PHOTO AGENCY)

A shocked mum has spoken of the moment she arrived at the scene of a crash involving her innocent son and a car allegedly carrying eight underage teenagers.

‌



The devastating collision took place as Sarah Jane Fox's son, Craig, 22, was driving on the M50 in Dublin when a reportedly stolen Toyota Yaris crashed into his Skoda Fabia head-on. The Toyota was travelling the wrong way down an off-ramp near junction 12 of the motorway at Firhouse around 5.30am on Sunday.

‌



It has been reported that eight teenagers, all under 16, were in the Toyota, including a 13-year-old boy who suffered critical, life-threatening injuries. Craig and the other seven teenagers were also taken to hospital, with the 22-year-old suffering internal bleeding.

‌



Still, he stepped out of his car to check on the teenagers in the other vehicle, with Ms Fox saying "there were guardian angels" watching over her son, who remains in shock in hospital after the crash.

"There were guardian angels with my child on Sunday morning," Ms Fox told the Neil Prendeville Show. "It's the only thing I can tell you how he walked out of that car."

She said Craig managed to get out of the wreckage before sitting down around 10 feet away. "But he walked out of that car and checked on the other kids. He was asking how they were."

‌



Ms Fox said Craig suffered internal bleeding following the crash but was able to avoid surgery. "Craig is doing well at the moment. He's stable," she said. "He had some internal bleeding yesterday, but it stopped without surgery, which was a relief.

"He's sitting up, talking, but he is sore all over, which is expected. He was hit head-on at 100 kilometres an hour so he's in shock as well."

View 2 Images Sarah Jane Fox believes 'guardian angels' were responsible for her son's survival (Image: Image: Mick O'Neill/Daily Mirror/Irish Daily Star.)

‌



Craig called his mother from a police officer's phone just after 5.30am to inform her of the incident. This was due to his own phone being thrown from the car during the crash, the Irish Mirror reports.

Ms Fox said: "Craig rang me at 5:32 from a police officer's phone. He couldn't find his phone. We realised then it had flown out of the car when it was spinning.

"He rang me from the police officer's phone, and I got into my car and was across the M50 as quickly as I could." Emergency services were on the scene within minutes, the mother said.

‌



"Craig said it was no more than two minutes before the police were jumping the barrier on the M50 because they came down the correct side of the road and came across to him," she said. The mother said she was particularly distressed after learning that those in the other vehicle were under 16.

"I'm not going to get into that part of it, but I have a feeling that another word isn't being used," she said. Asked about the ages, she confirmed: "Yeah, under 16."

Ms Fox said she had seen TikTok videos involving the young people and struggled with the circumstances surrounding the crash. "The TikTok videos show children in that car, and I keep saying the word children because that's all they are," she said.

‌



She said she had heard that the group had allegedly been in a stolen car for several hours before the collision, but stressed that this information was second-hand and that she could not confirm it. "Apparently, this is what I'm hearing, and again, it's I'm hearing it second-hand, so I can't confirm it," she said. "But they were out prior to hitting my child for a number of hours in a robbed car."

Despite her anger and heartbreak, Ms Fox repeatedly stressed that she was not looking to blame the children. "I don't blame the children for this. I'm not going to place blame on anyone," she said.

"It's after happening. My child is alive and he's lucky, but there has to be consequences for someone for what's happened."

‌



She added: "What they've done is wrong. I'm not taking or minimising what they've done is wrong. What I'm saying is, I'm not going to start placing hate and anger after the families. I hope they make it up for the justice system."

The crash has also left Craig without the car he relies on for his electrical apprenticeship. "My child has no car now. He's a third-year electrician, and he's no car for work now," Ms Fox said.

"And he's not going to have a car for a while." She said she was also worried about whether her son would be able to get behind the wheel again.

‌



"And the other thing is, is my child going to get back in a car after what's happened?" she said. Craig remembers the crash, according to his mother.

"Every bit of it,” she said when asked if he could recall what happened. "That's why, at the moment, he's still in shock. It's going to cause issues, I think."

Ms Fox described her son as a hard-working 22-year-old who secured his electrical apprenticeship himself and had been working since before he left school. "He's a good kid. He's a kind, caring, loving young fella that's gone out. He's been working since before he left school," she said.

‌



"He got his apprenticeship off his own back. He used his initiative. He got it all off his own back." She said Craig had been looking forward to finishing his apprenticeship and travelling.

"He goes to his gym. He has his girlfriend. He has his pals there - normal 22-year-old young fella," she said. "And his dream is that when he finishes electrical apprenticeship, that he goes travelling." For Ms Fox, however, the memory of the crash scene remains deeply distressing.

"Once I knew my child was okay, I could look at something else," she said. "But if you were at that crash site and you'd seen what I saw at that crash site - it was like a clown car with eight children coming out of it."

‌



She said emergency crews were treating those involved as the young people emerged from the vehicle. "Those kids that came out of it, were on the ground. Ambulance men everywhere," she said. "And that's, I think, why I have this reaction, because I saw the crash site."

For now, her focus is on Craig's recovery and the lasting impact the collision may have on his life. She is grateful her son survived, but believes what happened cannot simply be left without consequences.

"My child is alive and he’s lucky, but there has to be consequences for someone for what’s happened."

Article continues below

The State’s policing watchdog has launched an independent investigation into the incident. In a statement on Monday, Fiosrú, which investigates incidents involving contact with Gardaí where a member of the public has died or been seriously injured, confirmed it received a referral regarding the incident.

It said a team of investigators attended the scene and an independent investigation is ongoing.

"A referral does not necessarily mean a garda or gardaí have been accused of wrongdoing. Instead, it means that Fiosrú should independently investigate the incident to ascertain whether or not the act or omission of a garda or gardaí may have resulted in the death of, or serious harm to, a person," it said.

News.title: UK facing deadly 38C heat blast in just days as Brits urged to drink plenty and check on vulnerable family
News.content:
UK facing deadly 38C heat blast in just days as Brits urged to drink plenty and check on vulnerable family

The Met Office today said the UK is on course to record its hottest summer ever as Brits were warned of 38C temperatures and extreme weather warnings were issued

View 4 Images The record-breaking drought has driven rivers to record lows, with people seen on the cracked mud bed of Hollow Pond, east London (Image: Yui Mok/PA Wire)

Drought-hit Brits were today warned to brace themselves for a blistering 38C heatwave as health alerts kicked in and the UK looked set for its hottest summer on record.

‌



A spike in temperatures is anticipated as the Met Office issued an extreme heat warning, saying the "wider population is likely to experience some adverse health effects". The 15-hour amber warning covering all of England will begin at 9am on Thursday and was scheduled to last until midnight.

‌



Separately, UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) today activated amber heat health alerts for much of England, which will run until Friday, warning of a "rise in deaths". The Government has urged people to stay safe by drinking plenty of water, checking on vulnerable friends and family, and avoiding the sun at the hottest part of the day.

‌



View 4 Images The lost village of Nether Hambleton were exposed today because of the low water levels at Rutland Water reservoir (Image: Joe Giddens/PA Wire)

The scorching weather puts the UK on course for its hottest summer on record. Currently the mean average temperature stands at 16.48C between June 1 and August 10, which is 1.88C above the 1991-2020 average.

Met Office senior scientist Mike Kendon said: "Another record-breaking summer now looks increasingly likely for the UK, following the second-warmest June, and second-warmest July on record and yet another heatwave imminent."

‌



Pointing to repeated occasions in which the UK experienced temperatures of 35C or more, Kendon added: "These statistics are a clear reminder - if one were needed - of the stark changes that we are seeing in the UK's climate."

The record-breaking heatwave - the fifth of the year - has caused chaos across the UK, sparking raging wildfires, creating problems for farmers and driving rivers to record lows. The heat was so severe it exposed the remains of a lost village that was demolished and flooded to create a reservoir.

View 4 Images Scorched fields were seen near Jeremy Clarkson's Diddly Squat Farm as farmers faced more misery during the drought (Image: Jacob King/PA Wire)

‌



Stonework and the outlines of buildings in Nether Hambleton were seen today because of the low water levels at Rutland Water reservoir in the east Midlands. More than 3,000 acres of land were submerged in the 1970s to create what was then Europe's largest man-made lake, with residents rehoused in the surrounding areas. Among the lost buildings were 18th century homes and farmland growing barley to be sold to Germany for brewing lager and wheat which Hovis bought for breadmaking.

It came as the temperature are today thought to have topped 26C in London, 28C in Manchester and 28C in Cardiff, before the mercury is expected to soar in some areas to 34C tomorrow and 38C on Thursday. But meteorologists believe showers could move across the country on Sunday - bringing the first spattering of rain to southern areas in two months.

Searing temperatures have seen almost three quarters of England - affecting 45 million people - experience "flash droughts", with 27million people slapped with hosepipe bans. In Wales almost the entirety of the country was in drought, with hosepipe bans imposed by Wales Water for more than 33,000 people.

‌



View 4 Images The scorching weather has left the UK's grasslands - like those in Hampstead Heath - scorched and dry (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Met Office chief forecaster Chris Bulmer said: "While the peak heat will be more short-lived than recent heatwaves, temperatures widely into the mid-30Cs on Thursday bring the potential for impacts for some, which is why a Met Office warning has been issued.

"High pressure is now becoming dominant and temperatures will build day-by-day. Southerly and south-easterly winds will also tap into the hot conditions over Europe, which helps develop this further notable heat in what has been a hot and dry summer so far."

‌



Met Office Deputy Chief Forecaster David Oliver said: “While Thursday will be the peak of the heat this week, some warmth will remain in the south and south east on Friday, before easing more widely on Saturday as cooler air spreads south from the north west.”

Farmers are struggling to cope with the intense heat and experts warning it would drive up food and drink prices. The Food and Drink Federation (FDF) said "fruit, vegetable and grain supply" are being hit, with crop shortages set to feed into supermarket prices.

Images show dry fields at Jeremy Clarkson's Diddly Squat Farm in Chipping Norton, Oxfordshire. And people were seen walking on the exposed, cracked, and dried mud bed of Hollow Pond, near Wanstead, in east London.

‌



It came as firefighters continued to battle a series of fires across the UK, including one in the New Forest National Park, Hampshire. Emergency crews today began a third day of tackling tackling the blaze - that at one point covered an area equivalent to 140 football pitches - as they say they are "managing to contain" after working "tirelessly" through the night.

The area hit by the blaze, which started after a van caught fire on the nearby A31 near Ringwood on Sunday, is protected heathland and home to a number of rare species, according to the New Forest National Park Authority.

It came as the National Fire Chiefs Council said July was the busiest month on record for wildfires, with serbices responding to 966 wildfires this year, just shy of the 1,017 they attended during a record-breaking year in 2025. In July alone, firefighters attended 458 wildfires, whilst in the first 10 days of August crews have been called out to 185 wildfires.

‌



Phil Garrigan, chairman of the council, said: "The combination of drought conditions and another heatwave means the risk of fires remains high, and these incidents can place huge demands on firefighters and specialist resources. Many wildfires are preventable so we're asking people to be vigilant and take extra care outdoors while these conditions continue."

It came as the Fire Brigades Union said its members were under increased pressure as a result of an "unprecedented summer of dangerous and volatile wildfires". Steve Wright, the FBU general secretary, said the unpredictable environmental challenges the UK was now confronted with meant it was a "national priority" to have enough properly equipped firefighters to "face these threats".

He called for "increased funding, improved access to the best equipment and better national resilience" to combat rising demands. He said: "Our country is facing unpredictable environment.al challenges and it must be a national priority to ensure we have enough properly equipped firefighters to face these threats."

‌



Wright has previously said fire crews were stretched by staffing cuts - with 12,000 fewer firefighters in the UK than in 2010.

William Spencer, climate and first aid expert at the British Red Cross, said: "While periods of hot weather have become more familiar in recent years, they can still pose serious risks to health. In fact, after prolonged dry and warm conditions, it is more important than ever to follow heat safety advice.

"Simple steps such as wearing sunscreen, drinking plenty of fluids, seeking shade during the hottest parts of the day and taking regular breaks from the sun can help protect you and those around you. It's also important to look out for the signs of heat exhaustion and heatstroke, particularly among people who may be more vulnerable to the effects of extreme heat."

Article continues below

There are warnings older people are more at risk from the extreme heat, with Caroline Abrahams, Age UK's charity director, saying that as people age, their bodies find it harder to adapt to extremes of heat and cold.

She said: "Even younger and otherwise healthy people can feel the effects of very hot weather, but with temperatures forecast to reach up to 36C in some areas, the risks can be much greater for older people."

She urged people to check in on older neighbours, friends and relatives to see if they need support such as picking up the shopping or lending them a fan. She said: "The increasing frequency of heatwaves, alongside droughts, wildfires and hosepipe bans, shows how important it is that we do more to protect those most at risk as climate change continues to bring more extreme weather."

News.title: Trump will never secure deal and Iran will wait out warning, claims Tehran insider
News.content:
Trump will never secure deal and Iran will wait out warning, claims Tehran insider

AS President Donald Trump hurtles toward mid-term thrashing over war in Iran , Tehran appears to be preparing to wait it out, to outlast his presidency and ruin his legacy with humiliation

View 3 Images USS Carl Vinson steams towards Middle East bristling with F-35C warplanes (Image: SR Pablo Chavez/USS Carl Vinson / SWNS)

A Tehran political adviser has let slip his country will never do a deal with US President Donald Trump and will play for time until his presidency comes to an end.

‌



It comes as Trump claims since Iran is seeking compensation as part of any peace talks, he'll demand the same. It's part of a larger pivot by Trump, who's arguing that Iran is on the cusp of financially collapsing, but Tehran has hit back.

‌



Today Trump said the US Navy's blockade is preventing Iran from selling its oil on the international market, effectively choking the Iranian economy. "Yeah, they can make trouble," Trump said, "but they're broke."

‌



Iranian Parliamentary adviser Majid Skakeri declared: “Trump will not reach an agreement with us. We will accompany him until his term ends.” It is the closest an Iranian establishment figure has come to admitting its strategy of outwitting Trump through patiently controlling the Strait of Hormuz and being ambiguous.

Even though he does not represent the state his outburst offers a strong indication of the policy many Iranian nationalists are promoting. He said: “The path to victory is neither fighting nor a deal , it is managing the process of neither war nor peace, up to the point of victory. Publicly confirming negotiations with the US is sheer folly. The winning approach is denial, ambiguity and strategic patience.”

View 3 Images Iranian demonstrations across Tehran (Image: AP)

‌



Syria court sentences Bashar al-Assad to death for crimes against humanity READ MORE :

Shakeri is an adviser to Tehrans’s Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, and the policy means a stalemate for the Strait of Hormuz until January 2029.

The remarks represents one influential view within Iran's political establishment rather than a confirmed strategy formally adopted by Tehran. And current reporting indicates that Iranian officials are still pursuing diplomatic contacts under certain conditions.

Majed al-Ansari, Qatar’s Foreign Ministry spokesman, says negotiations between Oman and Iran on the future of shipping in the Strait of Hormuz have reached an advanced stage.

‌



That would indicate the US has been cut out of talks because of Trump’s threats and insults. Four people have been killed after Yemen’s Houthi rebels attacked an unidentified commercial ship in the Bab al-Mandeb Strait in the Red Sea.

View 3 Images Anti-government protests , Tehran (Image: UGC/AFP via Getty Images)

President Trump claimed the US controls the Strait of Hormuz and insisted Iran's economy is suffering due to the war. Trump also mirrored Tehran’s demands for compensation for damage caused by the conflict.

Article continues below

Despite the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps' determination to stand up to the US military there are still anti-government rallies taking place across Iran. In one incident in Tehran over the weekend flags were burned and demonstrators shouted slogans.

News.title: The Office star Lucy Davis reveals she's been diagnosed with terminal breast cancer aged 53
News.content:
The Office star Lucy Davis reveals she's been diagnosed with terminal breast cancer aged 53

The actress, famous for playing Dawn Tinsley, said: 'I’m not scared of whatever comes next. I’m at peace with it.'

The Office star Lucy Davis reveals she's been diagnosed with terminal breast cancer

The Office star Lucy Davis has revealed she's been diagnosed with "incurable" stage 4 breast cancer and said she "doesn't know how long she has left".

‌



Lucy, 53, shared the sad news with a video that showed her ringing the 'good luck' bell for cancer treatment bell having been told it was "too late" for chemotherapy. The actress told her followers: "I’m not scared of whatever comes next. I’m at peace with it."

‌



The actress, famous for playing Dawn Tinsley alongside Ricky Gervais and Martin Freeman in the BBC version of the Office and as Etta Candy in Wonder Woman, addressed fans in an Instagram post.

‌



She wrote: "A year and a half ago I was diagnosed with Stage 4 Breast Cancer, which has metastasized to my bones. Specifically to my spine, right hip, and my ribs. The cancer is incurable, and too late for chemo.

4 View 4 Images She told fans 'leaving my physical body just means going home' (Image: Getty Images) 4 View 4 Images Lucy Davis shared a video of her ringing the 'good luck bell' alongside her message (Image: Lucy Davis)

‌



"The initial lump that I felt, wasn’t a ‘lump’ as such; rather a kind of hard spot. Really tiny. I almost didn’t bother getting it checked. So I guess I’m saying don’t ignore anything - get everything checked out:)"

Lucy, is the daughter of British comic Jasper Carrott, 81, continued: "As of now, I’m trying to live out whatever might be left of my life in as fun a way as I possibly can.

"I always like to find the teachable moments in anything negative that happens. And cancer has not disappointed in that regard; there’s a lot I have learned from it, and I’m grateful for that.

‌



"As some of you will know, the pain can really be something else. Standing and walking for too long a time can be hard, and I need to use a wheelchair sometimes (so if you see me toddling around in one, feel free to give me a push!)

View 4 Images She appeared as Dawn Tinsley in the groundbreaking BBC sitcom The Office (Image: Lucy Davis/Instagram)

"The thing that has been most vital to me is humour. I asked my friends and family to make fun of me as much as possible (which they’re really good at), and most importantly of all to not treat me like a sick person. There’s nothing that will make you feel more unwell than being treated as if you’re unwell.

‌



"I’m not scared of whatever comes next. I’m at peace with it. I’ll see my Gracie [her dog, who died in 2024] sooner than expected, and for me, leaving my physical body just means going home. Any and all grieving is for my family; it’s far harder for them than for me."

She concluded: "I’m still going to keep up all my work for animal rights. It’s so important to me. And I still would like to keep working. I’m perfectly able to do so, and acting is one of the biggest joys in my life.

"For those of you on a similar journey to mine, I do wish you well. Cancer asks a lot from us, physically and mentally. And we all get to do it however we choose. Much love to you all."

‌



View 4 Images Lucy appearing as Hilda Spellman in The Chilling Adventures Of Sabrina

Her followers reacted in their thousands, with one writing: "Oh Lucy. I’m sending you so much love and wrapping you up so tightly. You will be in my prayers." Another wrote: "Sending all the love. Breaks my heart to see so many affected by cancer."

Earlier this year Lucy revealed that her mum had given her a kidney when she was in her mid-20s as part of a campaign called One's Enough.

Article continues below

She wrote: "My mum gave me a kidney over 28 years ago! Both my kidney, and her remaining one, are still going strong. Please consider donating if you can.

"It’s life changing and life saving. And I understand that the process is simpler than when we had our transplants. We were in hospital for 2 weeks back then, but I believe it’s a few days now."

News.title: Inside Gaza's tent city where hundreds of desperate families are living in overcrowded 50C camp
News.content:
Inside Gaza's tent city where hundreds of desperate families are living in overcrowded 50C camp

“People really suffer in this heat. Access to clean drinking water is still difficult. The results of having less clean water affect people when it comes to skin diseases and this is really spreading.”

View 5 Images Tents housing displaced Palestinians crowded along the Gaza City coastline (Image: Eldremle Rizek/ABACA/Shutterstock)

With a sea of tents stretching into the distance, it is an image laying bare war-torn Gaza’s hardship.

‌



Row-after-row of makeshift shelters line the coast, amid rubble and a battered building. These photos of Gaza City are a stark reality for Palestinians who have endured nearly three years of conflict.

‌



Charities have highlighted the difficulty of sweltering conditions for people surviving in tents. It comes after Israel rejected US President Donald Trump’s 15-point Gaza peace plan – saying it will not withdraw troops until Hamas is fully disarmed.

‌



View 5 Images Families sought refuge in temporary shelters after their homes were destroyed (Image: Eldremle Rizek/ABACA/Shutterstock)

Ed Miliband to tell Donald Trump's White House ending Iran war will bring down prices READ MORE :

Seba, 28, a translator for British charity UK-Med who lives in Gaza City, said: “People really suffer in this heat. I lived in a tent for two years and the hardest thing was during the summer time.

“Access to clean drinking water is still difficult. The results of having less clean water affect people when it comes to skin diseases and this is really spreading.”

‌



View 5 Images Locals are still struggling to get access to clean water (Image: Eldremle Rizek/ABACA/Shutterstock)

Meanwhile, Shurouq, 32, who works for Save the Children in the enclave, explained: “Across Gaza, people are enduring extreme heat with little protection or means to cool themselves.

“For those living in tents, conditions are even worse: tents can act like greenhouses, trapping heat with little ventilation. When temperatures outside feel like 37C, inside a tent they can feel like more than 50C.

‌



“The air is heavy because we are living by the sea, where the humidity is relentless. And overcrowding makes the situation much more difficult.”

View 5 Images People living in the tents may have already been displaced multiple times (Image: Eldremle Rizek/ABACA/Shutterstock)

Mum Shurouq, whose husband was killed in the early weeks of the war, has been displaced many times with her three-year-old daughter.

‌



She added: “We witness increasing cases of children suffering from heat-related illnesses such as heat exhaustion, sunstroke, severe dehydration, heat rash, skin infections resulting from sweating and poor hygiene, and worsening malnutrition and organ failure due to fluid loss and poor appetite."

View 5 Images The families are now living in difficult humanitarian conditions (Image: Eldremle Rizek/ABACA/Shutterstock)

The conflict was sparked by the Hamas-led October 7 attack on Israel in 2023 which killed about 1,200 people – with 251 hostages taken.

Article continues below

Israel’s military campaign in Gaza has left over 73,000 dead, according to the enclave’s health ministry.

News.title: Summer 2026 on course to be UK's hottest on record, says Met Office
News.content:
This summer is on course to be the UK's hottest since records began, according to the Met Office.

Only average conditions are needed for the remainder of August to surpass the record set just last year.

Provisional Met Office statistics show that the UK's mean temperature for meteorological summer so far (1 June to 10 August) currently stands at 16.48C (61.66F), which is 1.88C above the 1991-2020 average.

In summer 2025, the mean temperature across the country - which includes overnight lows as well as daytime highs - was 16.10C (60.98F).

It is in line with evidence that summers are getting hotter and are likely to become drier because of climate change.

News.title: Burnham 'confident' early release of PC Harper's killers can be halted
News.content:
Andy Burnham says he is "confident" PC Andrew Harper's killers can be excluded from the government's early release scheme, as outcry over the case grows.

The prime minister has now ordered the justice secretary to find a way to bar Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers, who were jailed for 13 years for manslaughter in 2020, from early release.

It marks a shift from last week, when he said there was "nothing more" he could do without risking the collapse of the prison system.

The move comes after days of pressure to exclude Harper's killers from the scheme, which is aiming to free about 5,000 offenders in England and Wales to make space in overcrowded jails.

Harper's mother, Debbie Adlam, told the BBC she was in "turmoil" following conflicting reports about whether two of her son's killers would be released from prison early, describing the handling of the situation as a "hash".

Conservative shadow home secretary Chris Philp accused Burnham and Labour of "re-traumatising victims and their families with their constant U-turns".

Burnham said a new plan to prevent more prisoners from being freed long before the end of their sentences would be presented to Parliament in September.

It comes after he initially announced some prisoners convicted of rape, serious child sex and other grooming offences would be barred from early release, after a review of the scheme he ordered after he became prime minister.

In an article published last week, external, Burnham said he had "wanted to go even further" but had "pushed to the very limits of what is possible to do".

He added: "I know I can look people in the eye and say to them there is nothing more I could have asked for without risking the prison system reaching capacity and collapsing within months."

But on Tuesday, Burnham insisted he had never accepted "there was nothing more that could be done" to prevent the early release of more offenders, including Harper's killers.

"I came into office and started pushing on this issue, and I have pushed every single day in office," he added.

Burnham said he would seek to hold talks with other political parties to build "consensus" on the approach to early releases.

News.title: Watch: Was Trump smuggled out of Air Force One in a catering truck?
News.content:
Donald Trump secretly switched planes when he was returning from a Nato meeting last month in order to avoid a threat to his life from Iran, US media has reported.

The president boarded Air Force One in Ankara, Turkey, on 8 July before being transported to another aircraft with the help of a catering truck, the Washington Post said.

He was then seen disembarking Air Force One in the UK, before boarding his newer, Qatari-gifted jet and returning to the US.

Trump spoke to journalists during his flight to the US but did not say whether he had been moved to a different plane.

The BBC's diplomatic correspondent Paul Adams explains.

News.title: Eclipse chasers scramble for glasses as stocks run low
News.content:
At a bakery in central London, stock has been flying off the shelves.

"I've sold, like, 100 this morning," a staff member tells the BBC. But it's not baked goods driving queues out of the door - customers are here to buy eclipse glasses.

They are among those hoping to catch a safe glimpse of Wednesday's solar eclipse - the UK's most significant since 1999 - but struggling to get their hands on the right gear.

Experts have urged eclipse enthusiasts not to look directly at the Sun - with even brief exposure causing lasting damage - and to seek out specialist glasses instead.

But online, pairs that meet safety specifications have all but sold out. Those still available either require a hefty next-day delivery fee or simply cannot arrive on time.

Even the Royal Museums Greenwich - recommended as a reputable retailer by UK health officials - has sold out, citing an "unprecedented volume" of orders.

Meanwhile, eclipse glasses have been turning up for sale in unexpected places as retailers try to capitalise on the demand.

"I Googled 'where can I get eclipse glasses but not through the post', because I realised I was too late," one customer waiting to buy three pairs at the bakery on Monday tells BBC Radio 4's PM programme.

"People have been struggling to find them all over," says another.

News.title: The Office actress Lucy Davis says she has 'incurable' cancer
News.content:
Lucy Davis, who played Dawn Tinsley in the original UK version of The Office, has revealed she has "incurable" breast cancer.

Davis, the daughter of comedian Jasper Carrott, starred as the office receptionist in the groundbreaking sitcom, which ran from 2001 to 2003.

A post from the 53-year-old actress on Instagram, external on Tuesday said: "I wanted to share something with you all that I've kept to myself for a while but for various reasons would like to share now.

"A year-and-a-half ago I was diagnosed with stage 4 breast cancer, which has metastasized [spread] to my bones. Specifically to my spine, right hip and my ribs. The cancer is incurable, and too late for chemo."

News.title: Councils to get more powers to stop vape and betting shops, PM announces
News.content:
New vape shops will require planning permission and councils will get more powers to block new betting shops, under government plans aimed at improving high streets.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said town centres had been "hollowed out" by decades of decline and for many people, the high streets they grew up with are "unrecognisable".

He said the plans were "shaped" by a series of BBC News investigations which exposed organised crime on high streets, revealing shops selling illegal cigarettes, vapes, cannabis and cocaine, enabling illegal working and suspected money-laundering.

The Conservatives and Reform said the proposals would lead to "more empty" shops, without tax relief for other small businesses.

Burnham said the measures will give councils more power to control what businesses open in town centres.

The proposals come as the prime minister embarks on a tour of the UK, with Downing Street saying he will be in "listening mode" during his visits as he works on a "10-year plan to bring back hope".

The plans announced by the government include:

Changes to planning law which would mean every new shop selling e-cigarettes, or vapes, would need to apply to their local council for permission to open (England only)

Tightening the definition of a vape shop to prevent businesses avoiding the rules by describing themselves as a general convenience store or retailer (England only)

Scrapping a rule known as "aim to permit", which currently restricts councils' ability to refuse new betting shops and 24-hour slot machine shops (Great Britain-wide)

Requiring planning permission for new adult gaming centres, which offer 24-hour access to gambling machines (England only)

New powers to extend closure orders for mini-marts and vape shops found to be selling illegal tobacco for up to twelve months, something previously proposed by former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer (England and Wales)

The National Crime Agency (NCA) estimates that at least Â£1bn of criminal cash is laundered through high street stores in the UK each year through businesses connected to the sale of fake goods, tax evasion, illegal working and illegal drug supply.

Burnham told the BBC that the changes would make it "easier for police to close a vape shop and have it closed for longer".

He said: "At the same time we're changing the planning regime... which should stop the proliferation of vape shops on our high streets."

The prime minister added that Operation Vulcan in Cheetham Hill, Greater Manchester, cleared the area of counterfeits and crime and "proved" what could be achieved.

"When I look at police reform across England, I will be asking for a similar approach to be taken," he said. "I want the strongest possible neighbourhood policing, with all agencies involved, to rip out criminal behaviour that is pulling places down."

Burnham said he did not accept the decline of the high street as "inevitable".

"I don't see why anywhere should have to accept they have empty shops, vape shops and the challenges that come with that."

Housing Secretary Angela Rayner told BBC Breakfast on Tuesday that many people were frustrated at vape and gambling outlets "popping up even near schools and some of them are linked to illegal activity and crime".

News.title: Criticism as thousands of seats empty at Europeans Athletics Championships
News.content:
Nearly 10,000 seats were empty at Birmingham's Alexander Stadium for the European Athletics Championships on Monday evening.

A crowd of 13,623 watched as Britain's 24-year-old sprinter Amy Hunt stormed to her first senior international title, in a stadium that has a capacity of 23,000.

Athletics supporters blamed ticket prices, with some describing them as "extortionate", while BBC commentator Steve Cram commented that spectator numbers were a "little disappointing".

But Birmingham 2026 organisers said they were "delighted" with ticket sales, which have "far surpassed" their targets with "Friday, Saturday and Sunday evening sessions approaching sell-out, with several other sessions close to capacity".

On Monday, Category A tickets for the home straight cost Â£150 with no concessions for juniors.

For the men's 100m final on Tuesday, those same seats cost Â£110, again with no concessions - while a similar ticket for the same final in Rome two years ago was 88 euros (Â£75).

It is Britain's first time hosting the championships in their 92-year history.

News.title: Perseid meteor shower reaches peak: When and where to catch a glimpse
News.content:
The best annual meteor shower has once again returned to our skies, and the Perseids dazzling display is set to peak on Wednesday night.

But skywatchers will be treated to not one, but two, impressive astronomical events within just a few hours of each other.

A deep partial solar eclipse will be also visible in the UK in the early evening before the Sun sets and the stars emerge. While the two events are unrelated, their timing makes for an exceptional night of stargazing.

Astronomer Dr Becky Smethurst said it was "the perfect cosmic coincidence of events".

Here is when to look up and where you will have the best views of the meteor shower.

News.title: How can Andy Burnham stop PC Harper's killers being released early?
News.content:
Just three weeks after becoming prime minister, Andy Burnham is already unpicking a key piece of legislation passed under his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer.

The Sentencing Act 2026 was designed to produce a semi-permanent solution to the prisons overcrowding crisis, by releasing large numbers of prisoners earlier than had been previously planned.

After ordering a review, Burnham announced that he would exclude most rapists, child sex offenders and members of grooming gangs from the legislation.

But that left many people convicted of manslaughter still eligible for early release, including two of the men convicted of the manslaughter of PC Andrew Harper - prompting outcry from his family and former colleagues.

Burnham now says he is "increasingly confident" of being able to prevent the early release of "other serious offenders" including PC Harper's killers.

But how might he do that and why have the options he is looking at been previously rejected?

News.title: England set to be one of the first countries to eliminate hepatitis C
News.content:
Hepatitis C is spread through contact with blood infected with the virus, such as by sharing needles with someone who has it.

Donor blood is already screened for it.

It is a silent disease, meaning people often have no symptoms until much later.

Untreated, it can cause serious and potentially life-threatening liver damage.

NHS England says that since 2015, more than 100,000 people have been diagnosed and treated for hepatitis C, meaning the country is already meeting that target.

Another goal - a 65% reduction in hepatitis C-related mortality compared with 2015 levels - has yet to be met, but might be before the 2030 target date.

Around 50,200 adults are living with hepatitis C, figures for England in 2024 suggest.

Estimates indicate 84.6% of those living with hepatitis C have been diagnosed - just short of the 90% target.

The Hepatitis C Trust says England is "on the cusp" of one of the most significant public health achievements in our country's history.

Prof Frankie Swords, NHS national medical director, added: "England is now leading the world in the mission to eliminate this disease and on course to beat the WHO's 2030 target, but we are determined to keep up the momentum and finish the job.

"We are committed to finding and treating everyone who needs support and would urge those at greater risk to come forward by ordering a free and confidential home-testing kit online."

Adults born in Ukraine, Romania, Estonia, Latvia, Poland, Albania, Lithuania, Bulgaria, Czechia or Slovakia are particularly urged to test, as some may have been infected through medical or dental procedures before 1991.

People can order a free, confidential NHS home self-testing kit, external without needing to speak to a GP.

News.title: London Heathrow no longer Europe's busiest airport
News.content:
Heathrow has lost its position as Europe's busiest airport to Istanbul, new figures show.

The west London airport said 7.86m passengers passed through its four terminals in July, whereas Istanbul Airport in Turkey's largest city recorded 8.15m passengers.

The US-Israel conflict with Iran has had an impact on Heathrow's passenger traffic with Middle East routes in July down 20.2% year-on-year.

Annual figures from trade body Airports Council International show Heathrow was Europe's busiest airport from 1996 to 2019. It lost that title in 2020 amid coronavirus travel restrictions before regaining it in 2023, holding it ever since.

Heathrow continues to operate its two runways at near-full capacity and is seeking government permission to build a third.

News.title: Fourth ex-police officer arrested over child abuse
News.content:
A fourth former South Yorkshire Police officer has been arrested on suspicion of non-recent child exploitation and abuse.

A total of 10 victims have now come forward to allege sexual abuse by former South Yorkshire Police officers in Rotherham.

The Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) earlier issued an update to the National Crime Agency's (NCA) investigation into alleged child sexual abuse by former officers of the force.

The BBC reported in July 2025 that five women who were exploited by grooming gangs as children said they were also abused by police officers in the town in the 1990s and early 2000s.

South Yorkshire Police initially investigated its own former officers before the NCA took over the inquiry.

Among the witness accounts reported by the BBC was the testimony of one woman who said she was raped from the age of 12 by a serving police officer in a marked police car.

She said he would threaten to "hand her back to the gang" if she did not comply.

A former South Yorkshire Police officer in his 60s was arrested in June by the NCA on suspicion of non-recent child sexual abuse offences.

He was taken into custody and later released on conditional bail pending further investigation.

Three other former officers have been arrested since December 2024 on suspicion of historical sexual offences - including attempted rape, indecent assault and misconduct in a public office.

The crimes are alleged to have taken place between 1995 and 2004 while the officers were on duty as constables. None has been charged.

At least 1,400 children were abused by men in Rotherham between 1997 and 2013, the landmark report from Prof Alexis Jay into the town's grooming gangs found in 2014.

News.title: Former army translator jailed for raping woman in private hire car
News.content:
A former translator for the British Army who raped a woman after becoming a private hire driver in Scotland has been jailed for seven years.

Abdul Nabizada attacked the 19-year-old after failing to take her home from a night out in Edinburgh in 2021.

The 36-year-old, who previously worked as an interpreter for the British, Danish and American militaries in Afghanistan, denied the charges and claimed to be suffering from post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) from an explosive device detonating near him.

Judge John Morris KC told Nabizada he had committed an "appalling betrayal of trust" during sentencing after he was found unanimously guilty at a High Court trial last month.

Nabizada, a father of four who lived in the Pilton area of Edinburgh, had applied for British citizenship after coming to the UK in 2016.

He had been a tailor in Afghanistan, but also worked with military personnel, translating his native Farsi alongside Dari, Pashto, Urdu and Arabic.

News.title: Antisemitism towards Jewish children 'shocking', government expert tells BBC
News.content:
Headteachers of some Jewish schools are spending more of their time dealing with security arrangements than on educational matters, a review into antisemitism in schools and colleges has found.

Sir David Bell, speaking for the first time about his ongoing government-commissioned independent review, told the BBC he had been struck by how many leaders of Jewish faith schools had told him security was their main concern - and that "sometimes education takes second place to that".

The extent of antisemitism directed at children and young people was "shocking" he said.

The report, due this autumn, examines experiences of Jewish pupils and staff in faith and secular schools and colleges in England.

Sir David said he found that pupils were "subject to regular harassment and abuse".

He said Jewish children and young people "are facing a pressure - and indeed one might say even a crisis - that is not the experience of other communities in this country".

The review is likely to recommend dedicated training for all teachers and improved education about antisemitism for pupils, the BBC has been told.

The BBC has spoken to several headteachers and staff at Jewish schools. All asked not to be named because of concerns over their security and that of their schools.

One headteacher said: "In recent years [security] has become an overwhelming priority and increased a significant amount. There have been weeks where approximately 90% of my time has been spent on security-related matters.

"Security concerns can become one of the many things that headteachers carry with them beyond the school day and, quite literally, can be among the things that keep me awake at night."

News.title: Girl, 6, dies and another child hurt in A12 crash
News.content:
A six-year-old girl was killed and another child was injured in a collision that shut part of the A12 on Monday, police have said.

The crash, involving a lorry and a car, happened at about 10:30 BST on the northbound carriageway near the Colchester United football stadium.

The road was shut in both directions and an air ambulance landed, while vehicles caught in the closure were turned around.

Det Insp Mark Fraser, of Essex Police, said the lorry driver had passed all road-side tests and was due to be interviewed in the coming days.

The injured child suffered a leg injury and was recovering in hospital, the force added.

The collision led to parts of Colchester being gridlocked throughout the day, while A12 queues stretched back to Marks Tey.

News.title: Golfer left shaking by 411-yard hole in one
News.content:
An amateur golfer was left "frozen" and "could not stop shaking" after hitting a hole in one from 411 yards (376 metres) - a one-in-six-million chance, according to one estimate.

Matthew Vigurs, from Droitwich in Worcestershire, narrowly missed out on claiming a Guinness World Record when he sank the shot during a league match at Great Barr Golf Club on 25 July in Sandwell near Birmingham.

The record sits with Robert Mitera, external who in 1965 at Miracle Hills Golf Course in Nebraska, USA,, external hit a hole in one from 447 yards (408 metres).

But despite being 36 yards (33 metres) short, 32-year-old Vigurs said: "I got married last year so obviously that's number one but this is definitely up there as a close second best moment of my life."

England Golf, external, the national governing body for amateur golf, believes Vigurs' achievement could be a national record, but that is yet to be confirmed.

But for any golfer a hole in one is a moment to remember and due to its rarity, Vigurs admitted he felt "stupid" even looking for his ball near the hole.

"We all hit good shots but I didn't expect it to go anywhere close to the green and I didn't know it had until we got up there," he said.

"We were looking for the balls but mine was missing.

"Everyone else was about 40 yards short of the green and we even had a look over the back of the green.

"I just double checked the hole and unbelievably I froze for about 10 seconds when I noticed the ball in the bottom.

"I rolled it over and saw my markings and we all went mad. It was surreal."

Stargazers will be treated to a dazzling sight as the annual Perseid meteor shower is set to follow a solar eclipse on Wednesday night.

The shower is usually one of the most spectacular of the year and will be visible across the UK if skies are clear, according to the Royal Astronomical Society.

The early hours of Thursday morning, between midnight and 5.30am, will be the ideal viewing time for Perseids, while the solar eclipse will be visible from the UK on Wednesday evening before sunset.

open image in gallery (PA Graphics) ( PA Graphics )

Some viewers should be able to see some meteors as soon as the sun sets, the society said.

Every summer, the Earth slams into a trail of debris from the Swift-Tuttle comet which causes the Perseids.

The meteoroids from the comet, mostly no bigger than a grain of sand, burn up as they hit the Earth’s atmosphere at 36 miles per second, to produce a shooting stream of light in the sky.

The shower meteors are named after the point in the sky where they appear to originate in the constellation of Perseus.

Those hoping to catch the shower have been advised to stay away from artificial light, avoid built-up areas if possible and try to find an unobstructed view of the sky.

Unlike many celestial events, meteor showers are easy to watch and no special equipment is needed, the society said.

Although the shower is set to peak overnight on 12 to 13 August, the shower will be active until 24 August.

Clear skies are forecast for much of the UK on Wednesday evening and into the early hours of Thursday, according to the Met Office.

For those wishing to view the solar eclipse, experts have warned that eclipse glasses are important for safe viewing and that sunglasses are insufficient.

The Office star Lucy Davis has “incurable” breast cancer, according to a post on her Instagram page.

The 53-year-old actress, who is the daughter of comedian Jasper Carrott, is best known for playing Dawn Tinsley in the BBC sitcom.

Davis said one of the most important things that has helped her through the cancer is humour, asking her friends and family to poke fun at the actress “as much as possible” and above all to not treat her like a “sick person”.

She also said said she will continue working for animal rights, adding that she would also like to keep working as an actress – a job which is one of the “biggest joys” of her life.

Lucy Davis shared the news on Instagram ( Instagram )

A post on Instagram said: “Hi friends:) I wanted to share something with you all that I’ve kept to myself for a while but for various reasons would like to share now..

“A year and a half ago I was diagnosed with Stage 4 Breast Cancer, which has metastasized to my bones. Specifically to my spine, right hip, and my ribs.

“The cancer is incurable, and too late for chemo..

“The initial lump that I felt, wasn’t a ‘lump’ as such; rather a kind of hard spot. Really tiny. I almost didn’t bother getting it checked. So I guess I’m saying don’t ignore anything - get everything checked out:).

“As of now, I’m trying to live out whatever might be left of my life in as fun a way as I possibly can. I always like to find the teachable moments in anything negative that happens. And cancer has not disappointed in that regard; there’s a lot I have learned from it, and I’m grateful for that..

“As some of you will know, the pain can really be something else. Standing and walking for too long a time can be hard, and I need to use a wheelchair sometimes (so if you see me toddling around in one, feel free to give me a push!).The thing that has been most vital to me is humour. I asked my friends and family to make fun of me as much as possible (which they’re really good at🙄), and most importantly of all to not treat me like a sick person. There’s nothing that will make you feel more unwell than being treated as if you’re unwell..I’m not scared of whatever comes next. I’m at peace with it. I’ll see my Gracie sooner than expected, and for me, leaving my physical body just means going home.

“Any and all grieving is for my family; it’s far harder for them than for me..

“I’m still going to keep up all my work for animal rights. It’s so important to me. And I still would like to keep working. I’m perfectly able to do so, and acting is one of the biggest joys in my life..For those of you on a similar journey to mine, I do wish you well. Cancer asks a lot from us, physically and mentally.

“And we all get to do it however we choose..Much love to you all”

Davis, who also appeared in Wonder Woman, shared her diagnosis alongside a video that showed her ringing ‘the cancer treatment bell’.

The actress shared a video of her ringing a bell and reading out a rhyme common in many cancer treatment centres to celebrate the end of treatment.

Reading out the poem, she said: “Ring this bell three times well. It’s a toll to clearly say my treatments are done, the course is run, and I am on my way.”

News.content:

Once every eight years, housing regulators in California issue local municipalities an obligatory task: construct a detailed proposal to build new residential properties.

The administration of Gov. Gavin Newsom sets specific goals for local governments across four separate tiers of affordability. Combined, these targets represent state officials' projections of how many homes are required to absorb projected population growth while addressing a multi-decade shortage of affordable places to live.

Because these quotas are distributed on a rolling schedule, a significant portion of California—including the whole of Southern California—passed its midway milestone this summer.

So how are these local jurisdictions faring when evaluated halfway through the process? The results for California are far from ideal. Evaluated on an academic grading scale, municipalities across the state would receive predominantly low marks.

open image in gallery The state’s total planning target adds up to nearly 2.5 million units over eight years, a reduction of the even more ambitious 3.5 million target Newsom set for his administration during his 2017 election ( Heather Diehl/Getty Images )

Data provided by local governments to the state housing department reveals that under a third of cities and counties are currently on pace to authorize enough "above moderate" units, the standard designation for market-rate housing.

The progress report for more affordable types of housing is even bleaker. Only 32 jurisdictions — less than 6% — are on track to hit their “very low” targets. That refers to housing within financial reach of anyone earning less than half the typical local income.

After years of nudging, political trolling and litigating, most cities and counties now have state-approved plans in place. But as the production numbers show, it’s one thing to plan and another to build. Almost nowhere in the state is actually seeing the new construction necessary “to meet the housing needs of all Californians,” as housing regulators have described these targets.

Only five jurisdictions in the entire state are permitting at a pace to hit all four income targets. Four are the lightly populated unincorporated bits of small, mostly rural counties: Plumas, Napa, Yolo and Mono. The fifth is Placerville, a town of roughly 11,000 people in the Sierra foothills east of Sacramento.

To be “on track,” a city or county needs to issue permits at a clip that, if sustained, would allow it to hit its state targets by the end of its planning cycle. State housing regulators told the city of Irvine in Orange County, for example, to plan for 8,671 market-rate units by 2030. Now halfway there, the city has issued more than 6,000, making it one of the minority of cities to be on pace to reach its target for above-moderate housing.

But for more affordable digs, Irvine, like most California cities, is far behind. The city has permitted just 9% of the very low-income housing needed to reach its target by the end of the decade. For the next most affordable category, which refers to units priced for those earning up to 80% of the regional median, it’s at a mere 3%.

What’s the housing hold up?

For anyone who has been monitoring the pace of new residential development in California over the last half century, the disconnect between housing planned and housing permitted won’t come as a surprise. The state’s total planning target adds up to nearly 2.5 million units over eight years, a reduction of the even more ambitious 3.5 million target Newsom set for his administration during his 2017 election. That 2.5 million figure works out to 312,500 new homes per year. Even during the state’s boomingest boom years in the early 1960s and mid-1980s, construction figures never reached such lofty heights.

This decade, despite a blizzard of state legislation and policy changes aimed at boosting the construction of new homes, the number of new homes built annually is still just north of 100,000.

Critics of the state’s planning process have long stressed that California’s targets are unrealistic and that local governments can only do so much.

“Cities cannot require developers to develop and cities don’t build housing,” said Jason Rhine, a lobbyist with the League of California Cities. You can lead a developer to a rezoned plot of land, in other words, but you can’t make them build.

open image in gallery Critics of the state’s planning process have long stressed that California’s targets are unrealistic and that local governments can only do so much ( Justin Sullivan/Getty Images )

Pro-development advocates counter that the uninspiring production numbers suggest that cities still aren’t doing enough to welcome more housing.

“Cities can argue that they don’t directly control production, but they do control fees, zoning and permitting,” said Laura Foote, executive director of YIMBY Action. The housing needs allocation process “is only as good as we have the political will to actually hold cities accountable.”

Foote directed some of the blame at state housing regulators for failing to compel cities to adopt more development-friendly policies.

In a written statement, housing department spokesperson Jennifer Hanson said regulators are “actively monitoring and enforcing” the commitments each jurisdiction has made in its housing plans. She also pointed to a couple of recent laws exempting many urban housing developments from environmental litigation and requiring local governments to allow for taller buildings near major public transportation stops. Both have already been used to “advance approved projects representing thousands of proposed homes,” she said.

There are many reasons that developers may or may not choose to build in a particular location. Some are in the power of local and state governments, like zoning and building codes, permitting timelines and fees. But many are not, said Hanson.

“Whether a project moves forward depends on interest rates, construction and land costs, access to capital, insurance and expected rents or sale prices,” she said.

Affordable housing construction faces an additional hurdle: A lack of public money. With very few exceptions, building homes that are affordable to those making below average incomes in California requires public subsidies, philanthropic capital or other lenders and investors willing to take a loss. Taxpayer support provided by the state has been in short supply after a voter-approved bond from 2018 that provided funding for California’s signature affordable development subsidy ran dry. That explains why the affordable production numbers are so much lower.

open image in gallery Affordable developers and other housing advocates are hoping voters will back an $11.25 billion state bond in November to replenish the coffers ( Frederic J. Brown / AFP via Getty Images )

Affordable developers and other housing advocates are hoping voters will back an $11.25 billion state bond in November to replenish the coffers.

Meanwhile, “moderate” income housing is especially tough to build, facing the financial worst of both worlds. It often doesn’t qualify for affordable subsidy programs that prioritize projects serving people further down the income ladder. But rents affordable to those earning median incomes are often too low for unsubsidized developers hoping to turn a profit.

An escape valve

The state may force local governments to lay the groundwork for new development — identifying potential sites, rezoning to allow for denser housing, changing local laws that make construction more economically feasible. But historically, local governments haven’t faced any consequences if nothing actually gets built.

That changed in 2017, when state lawmakers passed a landmark housing bill aimed at boosting new housing production where it was most needed. In jurisdictions that are halfway through their planning process but have yet to permit at least half their housing targets for above-moderate, low- and very low-income housing (housing affordable to a “moderate” income level isn’t included), the law requires local governments to fast track most apartment and condo projects. In exchange, developers have to set aside a certain number of affordable units and pay their workers more.

Of the 212 Southern California cities and counties that crossed the halfway point this year, all but four failed to hit those numbers and are now subject to the streamlining law.

But if history is any guide, that alone isn’t likely to trigger a building boom.

Private developers have insisted that the affordability requirements and higher wage standards written into the law make projects infeasible everywhere but in the highest rent neighborhoods. Since 2018, the law has been used to green light 27,961 units, according to the state’s housing department. That’s a significant sum, but it’s far from enough to close the gap.

Kansas City Chiefs wide receiver Rashee Rice described the 30 days he served in a Texas jail during the summer as a "learning experience" and a "reality check”, revealing that he navigated the stint by focusing on his rehabilitation from knee surgery and watching plenty of comedian Kevin Hart broadcasts on television to keep his spirits up.

The 26-year-old player was booked into a Dallas County jail on May 19 after violating the conditions of his probation stemming from his involvement in a car crash in Texas that injured several people.

Roughly a week prior to beginning his sentence, Rice underwent a surgical procedure to clean up joint debris in his right knee, which had caused persistent inflammation throughout much of the previous campaign.

Upon his release in June, Rice resumed his rehabilitation work alongside Chiefs quarterback Patrick Mahomes — who was working through his own recovery following surgery to repair torn knee ligaments — at the team's training facility in Kansas City prior to the launch of training camp.

"It was tough. It was mentally tough," Rice said of the jail stint on Tuesday, the first time the wide receiver has spoken publicly about his offseason. "They gave me ways to communicate with my teammates as well as my athletic trainer. Besides the hard times in there, just tried to keep positive — as much Kevin Hart as I could to laugh, and communicating with my teammates on the outside."

open image in gallery Rice kept himself entertained in jail by watching Kevin Hart ( Getty )

Rice has offered exceptional production for Kansas City whenever he has been available, securing 156 receptions for 1,797 yards and 14 touchdowns while contributing to the Chiefs' Super Bowl victory following the 2023 campaign. However, a suspension related to the highway collision alongside various physical setbacks forced him to miss significant action, restricting him to just 28 games played over his opening three years in the league.

The coming season is undoubtedly the most critical period of his professional career.

Beyond needing to answer a growing chorus of skeptics, Rice is entering the concluding year of his initial rookie contract. If he wants to earn a lucrative, long-term contract extension in Kansas City or elsewhere, he must prove his ability to remain on the field while consistently generating output for an offensive unit that desperately requires his playmaking presence.

"I mean, it's motivating," Rice said of impending free agency. "Honestly, just being back on the field with my brothers right now is motivating. That's in the future. And I'm just focusing on what's happening right now, and that's getting better for the team."

Kansas City is looking to rebound from a difficult 6-11 campaign during which Mahomes suffered a knee injury, several key starters went down with injuries, and an offensive unit previously regarded among the league's best struggled to produce as a shadow of itself well before those players were sidelined.

Chiefs general manager Brett Veach allocated the bulk of his draft stock toward defensive improvements, utilizing both first-round selections on that side of the ball. The primary addition intended to boost the offense was acquiring Super Bowl MVP Kenneth Walker III to serve as the team's primary running back.

Otherwise, Kansas City is depending on Rice and fellow wideouts Xavier Worthy and Tyquan Thornton to make substantial progress in their development, while counting on 36-year-old tight end Travis Kelce to remain a reliable target in the passing attack.

open image in gallery Rice is set for the most important season of his career ( AP )

"We're going to do some amazing things," Rice predicted, "not only because we're great receivers but we have a great coaching staff around us, and a great quarterback and foundation in general."

Mahomes has displayed his usual mobility throughout training camp, moving effectively on his repaired knee without noticeable limitations. That progress provides an encouraging sign for Rice, the overall aerial attack, and the Chiefs as they gear up for the upcoming campaign.

"He was my motivation every morning," Rice said.

When asked if he had a message for supporters disappointed by his legal issues or younger athletes who look up to him, Rice pointed back to Mahomes and the teammates who supported him throughout his recent difficulties.

"Find someone that you can lean on. Find someone you can talk to," Rice said, "and basically don't be scared to vocalize yourself, or say exactly what's on your mind, because someone is going through the same thing. There's too many people in the world for there not to be someone going through the same thing."

Rocky Flintoff made his first Lancashire century in a One-Day Cup thrashing of Somerset – and will now meet Ben Stokes and Durham in the quarter-finals.

The 18-year-old son of former England all-rounder Andrew brought up his maiden ton in 65 balls at Taunton as the visitors posted a new highest List A score of 443 for six.

Flintoff smashed eight fours and four sixes on his way to his milestone moment, with Somerset later subsiding to 269 all out in 39.2 overs.

Skipper George Balderson and Tom Aspinwall both took four wickets each as Lancashire coasted to a 174-run victory.

Lancashire will have home advantage in Friday’s quarter-final after Durham lost by 77 runs at Worcestershire and finished third in Group B.

Stokes suffered some heavy punishment as his nine overs went for 61 runs, with one wicket as reward, and the former England captain was dismissed for one as Durham were all out for 214.

open image in gallery Ben Stokes's Durham will face Lancashire in the last eight ( Getty )

No 7 batter Tom Taylor top scored with 86 from 74 balls for Worcestershire, but it was in vain for the Rapids who went out of the competition.

Yorkshire will host Nottinghamshire in the other quarter-final on Friday after finishing Group B runners-up.

Ben Coad (three for 22) and Dom Bess (three for 32) shone with the ball as Essex were dismissed cheaply for 151, and Will Bennison (60) and James Wharton (51 not out) helped Yorkshire complete a seven-wicket win.

Nottinghamshire qualified with a six-wicket win, overhauling a star-studded Surrey’s 298 with 13 balls to spare as George Munsey made 138 from 132 balls.

Leicestershire, who did not play on Tuesday, and Middlesex go straight into the semi-finals after topping their respective groups.

Middlesex wrapped up Group B with a comfortable 92-run win over Sussex. Joe Cracknell (128) and Nathan Fernandes (92) laid the platform for Middlesex’s 354 for eight with a third-wicket partnership of 202.

There were also wins for Derbyshire, Gloucestershire and Warwickshire.
