World.title: Liberia: Boakai Names Retired Army General to Head Anti-Drug Agency
World.content:
The Executive Mansion says Ziankahn's appointment reflects the President's confidence in his "leadership, integrity, and operational experience."

President Joseph Nyuma Boakai has made perhaps his most consequential national security appointment since assuming office, naming former Defense Minister, retired Major General Daniel Dee Ziankahn, as Director General of the Liberia Drug Enforcement Agency (LDEA) in a move that signals a fundamental shift in the government's strategy against transnational narcotics trafficking.

The appointment comes at a defining moment for Liberia's anti-drug campaign -- one marked by record cocaine seizures, allegations of institutional infiltration by organized crime, dismissals of senior security officials, and mounting international scrutiny over whether Liberia has become an emerging transit and storage hub for global narcotics syndicates.

Rather than selecting another career drug enforcement officer, President Boakai has entrusted the agency to one of the country's most experienced military minds, suggesting that the administration increasingly views narcotics trafficking not merely as a law enforcement problem but as a national security emergency.

Ziankahn's appointment follows months of extraordinary anti-narcotics operations that have transformed Liberia's security landscape.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The crisis reached international prominence after authorities intercepted approximately 237.6 kilograms of cocaine valued at about US$19 million at Roberts International Airport earlier this year. That operation exposed what investigators described as sophisticated trafficking methods involving airport operations and triggered an extensive criminal investigation.

Only weeks later, authorities executed an even more dramatic operation in Duazon, Margibi County, where investigators seized nearly 3.97 metric tons of suspected cocaine with an estimated international street value exceeding US$370 million -- one of the largest narcotics seizures ever recorded in Liberia and among the most significant in West Africa.

The scale of both seizures fundamentally altered perceptions of Liberia's role in international narcotics trafficking.

For years, security analysts had warned that West Africa was increasingly serving as a bridge between cocaine-producing regions in Latin America and lucrative consumer markets in Europe.

The Liberian seizures appeared to reinforce those concerns, suggesting that international trafficking organizations may have established increasingly sophisticated logistical networks within the country.

The investigations that followed produced consequences extending far beyond the drug seizures themselves.

As investigators traced the alleged trafficking operations, allegations emerged suggesting that elements within the security architecture may have been compromised.

President Boakai responded with an unprecedented series of administrative actions, dismissing, suspending and ordering investigations into officials from several security institutions, including the Liberia National Police (LNP), National Security Agency (NSA), Roberts International Airport (RIA), and the Liberia Drug Enforcement Agency itself.

Those measures reflected the administration's determination to demonstrate that no institution would be insulated from accountability if credible evidence of misconduct emerged.

The actions also exposed what many analysts consider the greatest institutional threat confronting the country's anti-drug campaign: the possibility that sophisticated international criminal organizations may seek to infiltrate state institutions responsible for combating them.

Such concerns are not unique to Liberia.

Across the world, transnational narcotics organizations have historically relied not only on logistical sophistication but also on corruption, insider facilitation and institutional compromise.

Why Ziankahn?

Against that backdrop, President Boakai's choice of Daniel Dee Ziankahn appears highly strategic.

Unlike many previous leaders of the LDEA, Ziankahn arrives with decades of experience in military command, institutional reform and national security planning.

During his tenure as Chief of Staff of the Armed Forces of Liberia (AFL), he became widely associated with efforts to professionalize Liberia's post-war military following years of civil conflict.

Working alongside international partners, including the United States, he helped oversee reforms aimed at transforming the AFL into a disciplined, professional institution operating under democratic civilian control.

His subsequent service as Minister of National Defense further expanded his experience managing complex security institutions and coordinating with regional and international partners.

More recently, Ziankahn has served as Military Adviser to President Boakai, providing strategic advice on national and regional security matters.

His appointment therefore brings together operational military leadership, institutional reform experience and direct presidential confidence.

Unlike a conventional law enforcement appointment, it places a seasoned strategic commander at the helm of the country's principal anti-narcotics agency.

The Executive Mansion emphasized that Ziankahn's appointment reflects the President's confidence in his "leadership, integrity, and operational experience," while assigning him direct responsibility for intensifying Liberia's campaign against illicit drugs and organized crime.

The President has also appointed to the LDEA Precious Rue as Deputy Director General for Operations and Prince Mulbah as Deputy Director General for Administration, pending Senate confirmation.

All three officials have been instructed to assume their responsibilities immediately in acting capacities.

The restructuring also returns Ernest Tarpeh to the National Security Agency, while former Officer-in-Charge Fitzgerald Biago has been indefinitely suspended from the Liberia National Police over ethical concerns pending further investigation.

Although the Ministry of Justice reportedly found no evidence directly linking Biago to narcotics trafficking, President Boakai concluded that ethical issues identified in the investigation warranted additional scrutiny.

That distinction reflects the administration's emerging message: legal innocence does not necessarily preclude administrative accountability where questions of institutional integrity arise.

Ziankahn's appointment inevitably raises broader questions about the evolving character of Liberia's anti-drug campaign.

Drug enforcement agencies traditionally operate as civilian law enforcement institutions emphasizing criminal investigations, prosecutions and intelligence gathering.

By selecting a retired four-star military officer to lead the LDEA, President Boakai appears to be elevating narcotics trafficking to the level of a national security threat.

That does not necessarily imply militarization of policing.

Rather, it suggests greater emphasis on intelligence coordination, operational discipline, inter-agency cooperation and strategic planning.

The President has directed the new leadership to work closely with the Ministry of Justice, Joint Security and international partners to dismantle trafficking networks, strengthen border controls and improve intelligence capabilities.

Such coordination will likely become increasingly important as investigations continue across multiple jurisdictions.

Liberia's response carries significance beyond its borders.

International partners -- including the United States, the European Union, the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC), ECOWAS and INTERPOL -- closely monitor countries serving as potential transit points for narcotics trafficking.

Major cocaine seizures often become tests of institutional credibility.

Foreign governments generally assess not only whether drugs are intercepted but also whether investigations reach the criminal networks responsible and whether compromised public officials are held accountable.

Close 

Boakai's successive dismissals, suspensions and institutional reforms therefore appear designed partly to reassure international partners that Liberia remains committed to confronting organized crime despite the scale of recent challenges.

Yet appointments alone cannot dismantle sophisticated international trafficking networks.

Experts note that sustainable success will depend on broader institutional reforms, including stronger financial investigations, improved border surveillance, enhanced intelligence-sharing, witness protection mechanisms, prosecutorial capacity and judicial efficiency.

Liberia must also continue strengthening airport security, maritime surveillance and anti-money laundering systems if it hopes to disrupt the financial infrastructure sustaining organized criminal enterprises.

Equally important will be restoring public confidence in institutions that recent investigations have exposed to allegations of misconduct.

Announcing the appointments, President Boakai reaffirmed that narcotics trafficking represents one of Liberia's gravest threats to national security, public health and national development.

"Our fight against drugs is a fight for the future of Liberia," the President declared. "We will continue to strengthen our institutions, hold public officials to the highest ethical standards, and pursue those who seek to poison our communities. There will be no safe haven for drug traffickers or those who aid and abet them."

Those remarks reinforce an earlier pledge made after the first major cocaine seizure that his administration would dismantle the criminal networks operating within Liberia rather than merely seize narcotics shipments.

The assignment, for Ziankahn, may become the most demanding chapter of a career spanning military leadership, defense policy and national security.

It also represents, for the President, a high-stakes bet that disciplined leadership, institutional credibility and strategic coordination can restore confidence in an agency whose reputation has been shaken by allegations of internal compromise.

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - August 11, 2026
World.content:
Zambia Election Set for Closely Fought Opposition Battle

Zambia's 13 August election has become a closely contested battle between the ruling United Party for National Development and the Tonse-Pamodzi opposition alliance, led by newcomer Brian Mundubile and backed by former Patriotic Front structures. The election is expected to test the opposition's strength and serve as a referendum on President Hakainde Hichilema's record. The government has made progress on debt restructuring, economic growth and inflation. But the high cost of living remains a big concern for voters. The poll is also taking place amid concerns over alleged state interference, restrictions on opposition activity and controversial legislative changes, making it a key test for Zambia's democracy.

WHO Warns DR Congo Ebola Response Falling Behind

More than 1,900 people have died in the Democratic Republic of Congo's Ebola outbreak. 60-70% of deaths occur in communities before patients reach treatment centres. The WHO said that the concentration of healthcare services in Bunia, Ituri province, is forcing patients to travel long distances and seek care too late. Poor transport systems may also increase transmission. The agency plans to expand treatment facilities closer to communities, add 400 Ebola beds and strengthen public awareness and early referrals. WHO is also looking to the town of Aru, where no new cases have been reported for two weeks after authorities expanded surveillance and response beyond individual patients to surrounding communities.



Nigeria Lassa Fever Cases Reach 1,000 in 2026

Nigeria has reported 1,000 confirmed cases of Lassa fever and 237 deaths in 2026, with cases reported in 23 states and 116 local government areas. Five states, Ondo, Bauchi, Taraba, Edo and Benue, account for 86% of confirmed cases. At least 53 healthcare workers have also been infected, prompting the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention to introduce a 30-day protection plan for frontline staff. The agency has said that late presentation, high treatment costs, poor sanitation and limited awareness are contributing to the outbreak and high fatality rate. Lassa fever is a viral haemorrhagic disease transmitted primarily through contact with food or household items contaminated by the urine or faeces of infected rodents.

Malawi Land Audit Flags Irregular Plot Allocations

Malawi's Ministry of Lands is set to release findings from a pilot land ownership audit in Lilongwe that reportedly uncovered irregularities in the allocation of plots in the affluent Area 3 and Area 10. The audit was launched in February 2026 to improve transparency and accountability in land administration. It is said to have identified politically exposed individuals, including current and former ministers, judges and MPs, among those allegedly linked to irregular land acquisitions. The findings could trigger political controversy, with questions remaining over whether those implicated will be publicly named or face legal or disciplinary action.

UN Somalia Auction Raises Security Concerns

The UN Support Office in Somalia (UNSOS) has opened a tender to auction vehicles, generators, IT equipment, medical supplies, construction machinery and other assets. This comes as Washington moves to end funding for the mission's logistical support by the end of 2026. UNSOS provides critical transport, fuel, food and other supplies to about 12,000 African troops and police serving under AUSSOM in the fight against al-Shabab. The auction has raised concerns among civil society groups over transparency and oversight. Regional leaders have warned that any premature reduction in international support could create a security vacuum as al-Shabab continues to operate in parts of Somalia.

Close 

Climate Change Shifts Africa's Malaria Risk

Climate change is reshaping malaria risk across Africa, with rising temperatures making parts of southern Africa and high-elevation areas of East Africa increasingly suitable for transmission, according to a new Nature study. Some parts of West and Central Africa may have become too hot for optimal malaria transmission. The region still bears about 95% of the global malaria burden. But experts warn that climate change is only part of the equation, with funding gaps, drug and insecticide resistance, and weak health systems still major threats. They are urging countries in emerging risk areas to step up malaria prevention and surveillance while maintaining elimination efforts in high-burden areas.

World.title: South Africa: Immigrant Traders See Their Livelihoods Destroyed By March and March
World.content:
Traders with documents and permits chased away, leaving Bellville bus terminus market almost empty

Dozens of immigrant traders who usually traded at the Golden Arrow terminus in Bellville are staying away because of anti-immigrant protests.

When we visited the once bustling site last week, it was quiet with only a handful of traders. Many stalls were deserted.

Some traders we spoke to said they had tried to set up shop in other areas but were stopped. They have not traded at the bus site since the March and March 30 June "deadline" demanding "illegal immigrants" leave South Africa.



"I need to pay rent, put food on the table, and pay the bills," a Zimbabwean man who asked to remain anonymous told GroundUp.

He said he has been selling clothes in Bellville for about five years. He left Zimbabwe in 2008 when its economy collapsed.

While he has not been directly threatened, he has witnessed others being harassed.

"They will take your stuff and throw it on the ground," he said.

"It hurts, but as much as it hurts, it's their country, and they're also marginalised people."

Another trader, who introduced herself as Meye, said she has had a permit to trade since 2010. She fled the DRC in 2003.

"We are legal; everything is correct. But they say we are foreigners and we need to go back to our country."

A single mother of three, she says she is now struggling to feed and school her children.

Another single mother, Safia, says she has been unable to trade despite having refugee status and a trading permit. She came from Somalia in 2010.

She said law enforcement needs to protect the traders better.

"I can't sleep at night because of what is happening. I can't even pay my rent. I can't support my children," she said.

Abdulhakim Husein, Western Cape director of the Somalia Association of South Africa, told GroundUp that he had been assisting traders since the start of July.

He said many asylum seekers and refugees are traders as they have to rely on being self-employed. They came from Somalia, DRC, Zimbabwe, Angola and Burundi.

He said that at a meeting on 13 July (which the City confirmed), it was agreed that traders with valid permits should be allowed to trade. But on 14 July, they received a message warning them about a March and March protest in the area.

Husein said they have approached a legal NGO for assistance.

City spokesperson Luthando Tyhalibongo said foreign nationals whose immigration status has been verified by Home Affairs are permitted to trade with a valid permit. These cost R78 per month.

Close 

"It is a concern whenever permitted traders, whether South African citizens or foreign nationals lawfully permitted to trade, are prevented from engaging in legal economic activity," he said.

He said intimidation and threats should be reported to SAPS.

World.title: South Africa: Gauteng Gets 500,000 Grade 1 and 8 Applications - South African News Briefs - August 11, 2026
World.content:
Gauteng Records Nearly 500,000 Grade 1 and 8 Applications

Almost half a million applications have been submitted for Grade 1 and Grade 8 places in Gauteng for the 2027 academic year since the online application system opened, reports EWN. The Gauteng Department of Education has said that improvements have been made to streamline the process. Education MEC Lebogang Maile has urged parents to apply early. The department also says learners awaiting specialised placement should receive interim support rather than remain on waiting lists, with officials focusing on successful placements and resolving outstanding cases.

Strong Winds Damage Homes in Free State

The South African Red Cross Society is assessing damage caused by strong winds and heavy rainfall in Koppies and other parts of the Free State, reports SABC News. Several homes have reportedly been damaged, including roofs blown off, as severe weather persists. Red Cross volunteers are working with disaster management authorities and municipalities. Assessments continue, with humanitarian assistance being provided to affected households.

Fadiel Adams Unlikely to Testify at Madlanga Commission

National Coloured Congress leader Fadiel Adams is unlikely to testify before the Madlanga Commission, reports EWN. This comes after the commission received his affidavit and supporting documents late. Adams was expected to testify about his involvement in an Investigating Directorate Against Corruption probe into alleged corruption within Crime Intelligence. In 2024, he asked IDAC to investigate claims that the Political Killings Task Team had misused secret service funds for luxury accommodation and vehicles.

World.title: Trump cheers Alito staying for another Supreme Court term: 'One of the greatest of all time'
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

In a late-night social media post, President Donald Trump celebrated Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito's decision to remain on the bench for another term.

Trump’s celebration of the 76-year-old conservative stalwart’s decision to put off retirement comes as the midterms raise the stakes over how long Republicans will retain the Senate majority needed to confirm any eventual successor.

"Great news for our Country! Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito has announced that he is staying for another Term," Trump wrote Monday night on Truth Social. "He is one of the Greatest of All Time. We are all lucky!"

Alito confirmed last week that he plans to remain on the nation's highest court for its coming term, batting down months of speculation that he could retire while Trump is in the White House and Republicans still control the Senate.

ALITO NOT EXPECTED TO RETIRE THIS TERM, COOLING SUPREME COURT VACANCY SPECULATION: SOURCES

"Obviously, I'm here for another term," Alito said in an interview published by The Wall Street Journal.

The Supreme Court’s next term begins in October and typically concludes with its final opinions in late June or early July. The justices are currently on their summer recess.

Alito and fellow conservative Justice Clarence Thomas, 78, have faced some calls from conservatives to step down, which would give Trump one potential last chance to appoint a fourth Supreme Court justice to the lifetime post.

Trump appointed three others during his first term in office – Neil Gorsuch, Brett Kavanaugh and Amy Coney Barrett – giving the court a 6-3 conservative majority that has issued a series of major rulings since 2020.

"It's not pleasant, in the sense that it's a reminder of mortality," Alito told the Journal about the calls to retire. "It's like, what are those vultures doing up there? They are flying around. But it goes with life tenure."

TRUMP REVEALS HE HAS MULTI-PICK SCOTUS PLAN READY AS RETIREMENT SPECULATION HEATS UP

The window to replace one of the court's oldest conservative justices with a younger jurist who could potentially remain on the bench for decades might narrow considerably after November.

Republicans currently hold a 53-47 Senate advantage, counting the two independents who caucus with Democrats on the Democratic side. Because Supreme Court nominees require Senate confirmation, a Democratic takeover in the 2026 midterms could effectively prevent Trump from replacing Alito — or any other justice — with a nominee opposed by a unified Democratic majority.

Democrats would need a net gain of four seats to reach 51 and take outright control, with Republican Vice President JD Vance otherwise positioned to break a 50-50 tie.

That reality places unusual weight on Alito's decision to remain.

Alito was born April 1, 1950, making him 76, and has served on the Supreme Court since January 2006 after being nominated by President George W. Bush. He is one of the court's most consistently conservative members.

The court has disclosed relatively little about Alito's health over the years, signaling he remains in good health. Alito did have a minor incident while attending a Federalist Society event in Philadelphia on March 20, being treated for dehydration after his security detail urged him to see a doctor rather than make the roughly three-hour drive home.

He was released that night, was subsequently examined by his physician and returned to work the following Monday.

NPR RETRACTS FALSE REPORT CLAIMING JUSTICE SAMUEL ALITO IS RETIRING FROM THE SUPREME COURT

Questions about Alito’s longevity on the bench and decision to stay introduces another potential inflection point: the 2028 presidential election.

If the White House changes parties in 2028, Alito remaining beyond Trump’s term carries the risk for conservatives that a future Democratic president could nominate his successor the following January.

That outcome is far from predetermined, and subject to whatever party controls the Senate, but the modern political era has repeatedly seen the White House swing between parties.

In six of the seven elections since 1988 that produced a new president, control of the presidency also changed parties — the lone exception being Republican George H.W. Bush's victory after Ronald Reagan in 1988. That run includes the succession from Bush to Bill Clinton, George W. Bush, Barack Obama, Trump, Joe Biden and back to Trump.

For Trump, the stakes surrounding an aging Supreme Court justice are hardly theoretical.

He confronted perhaps the most consequential Supreme Court vacancy of his first presidency on Sept. 18, 2020, when reporters informed him on an airport tarmac after a campaign rally in Bemidji, Minnesota, that liberal Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg had died.

TRUMP PRAISES LINDSEY GRAHAM AS SENATOR WHOSE KAVANAUGH FIGHT CHANGED SUPREME COURT HISTORY

"She just died? Wow. I didn't know that," Trump said before praising Ginsburg as an "amazing woman" who had led an "amazing life."

The timing immediately transformed the final weeks of the 2020 presidential campaign.

Trump moved quickly to select then-Judge Amy Coney Barrett to replace Ginsburg – just eight days after her death – and the Republican-controlled Senate confirmed Barrett on Oct. 26, 2020, by a 52-48 vote, just 27 days after her nomination, eight days before Election Day.

Landing three new justices during a single four-year presidential term was a historically rare achievement. Not since Richard Nixon's first term had a president placed at least three new members on the Supreme Court in one term. Nixon ultimately placed four — Warren Burger, Harry Blackmun, Lewis Powell and William Rehnquist — on the court before beginning his second term.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Trump's three appointments have continued to shape some of the most consequential rulings of his second administration, making the future of Alito's seat particularly significant for both parties.

For now, Alito has made his choice to stay active, with Trump is cheering him on.

Reuters contributed to this report.

World.title: Francesca Hong asked about lack of AOC endorsement and the House Dem's remark about the 'Woke 1' era
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Wisconsin Democratic socialist gubernatorial primary candidate Francesca Hong fielded questions on Monday pertaining to progressive U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., who did not endorse Hong in Tuesday's primary contest.

Asked why she thinks the congresswoman — who is often referred to simply by her initials AOC — and U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., did not back her, Hong said, "I have so much respect for the senator and the congresswoman, and they are working tirelessly to make sure that we can flip Congress and the Senate and get Democrats wins in the midterms. I look forward to conversations with them about that too."

Pressed on whether she believes the two lawmakers not endorsing her signals they don't believe she can win the state, Hong said that a gubernatorial contest "is different from federal elections."

WISCONSIN PROGRESSIVE HONG'S SUPPORTERS ARE CONFIDENT SHE'S THE ANSWER TO AFFORDABILITY AHEAD OF PRIMARY

During a Sunday interview on ABC's "This Week," Jonathan Karl asked Ocasio-Cortez whether she would endorse Hong.

"No, I haven't endorsed in that race. My focus has been in winning back the Congress, winning back the House and positioning ourselves to have the best, ah, chance possible to, to win the Senate," she said.

SOCIALIST FRONTRUNNER IN THE HOT SEAT AFTER 'CANCEL THANKSGIVING' POST EMERGES ONLINE

Karl asked the congresswoman about controversial comments Hong has made in the past.

Ocasio-Cortez indicated that her "understanding is that... Francesca Hong has made clear her present stances to her electorate" and "moved away from" prior comments.

"And I have a local city councilman that has this... saying, 'Woke 1 was crazy,'" she said, laughing. "And I think that what's important is that we have to assess what a candidate is saying now."

When asked on Monday about Ocasio-Cortez's wokeness-related comment, Hong, a Democratic Socialists of America member, suggested that individuals "are opening their eyes to an economy that is deeply rigged against working class people" and that she will speak about how to "deliver for working class people by taxing the ultra rich, ensure that we have a moratorium on data centers, that we're raising wages, fighting for universal childcare and that we fully fund our public schools."

AOC TRIES TO LAUGH OFF 'CRAZY' WOKE ERA AS THING OF THE PAST, BUT CONSERVATIVES AREN'T AMUSED

World.title: Buffalo Bills in damage control mode over their $2.2 billion stadium that is getting crushed online by fans
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

First, the Buffalo Bills put out a statement on Monday, defending the honor of their new $2.2 billion stadium that was getting absolutely crushed on social media – with photo evidence, no less – for how poorly architects laid out some of the place's sightlines.

Then the club put its chief operating officer and its vice president of stadium development on a conference call with reporters to explain how the fans, some of whom are taxpayers footing $850 million of the cost for the building, didn't have the whole story when they posted those cringe photos of obstructed views and videos of poor rain coverage during the Bills' Saturday practice.

So, yes, the Buffalo Bills are in full crisis management mode right now and the damage control isn't about an injury to a valuable player or a questionable coaching decision.

NY GOVERNOR KATHY HOCHUL TRIES TO GET BILLS CHANT GOING AT NEW STADIUM, COMPLETELY FAILS

It's all about a multi-billion-dollar project that, so far, is not quite living up to some of the billing it presented to fans, including personal seat license holders.

"So far, we’ve heard from less than one percent of our PSL holders about anything sightline related," Bills COO Pete Guelli told Western New York area reporters on the conference call Monday. "Relative to that specific issue, we feel very confident what was represented via the virtual venue is accurate to what people saw when they sat in their seats.

"If anybody feels otherwise, we’re taking this on a case-by-case basis, and we’ll address any concerns that they have."

The concerns were all over social media. And they turned what was supposed to be a triumphant moment for a proud franchise into something more closely resembling the season's first loss.

Because, apparently, clear sightlines throughout the facility is beyond the scope of what is possible for a $2.2 billion stadium in 2026.

"Any building you would walk into, there would be some obstructed seating," Guelli explained. "There are seats where we could create a different design, put in a blank area, or they give you the option to put in a seat that might be obstructed for football, but can be used for any other event like a concert. There’s always partial-view or limited-view seats, and we think those were pretty clearly depicted in our virtual venue."

The sight-lines weren't the only problem. Of course not.

Some fans complained their views were blocked by vendors or other fans walking about as the Bills practiced.

JOSH ALLEN DELIVERS FULL-THROATED UNSOLICITED DEFENSE OF BUFFALO BILLS' HIDEOUS NEW UNIFORMS

The club is responding by pointing out that at actual games, fans and vendors will be instructed to wait for the whistle before being allowed to move about. So, yes, the raucous, rowdy Bills crowds that sometimes stood the entire game at the old Highmark Stadium might be going away.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

Games will now be coordinated something like tennis matches.

There were also complaints about new Highmark Stadium's video boards because of their uninspiring size and scope.

The Rochester Democrat & Chronicle reported that was done on purpose because club owner Terry Pegula wanted fans focused on the field and not the scoreboards. The speaker system, the paper reported, was more of a priority investment for Pegula.

So, team ownership apparently forgot that video killed the radio star about 50 years ago.

"We’re learning a lot about the building, and that includes game presentation," vice president of stadium development John Polka told reporters. "We’ll look at how much of the scoreboard we’re using for video versus using for content. We also have things in this building that we didn’t have before.

"We have a nine-foot ribbon board right below that scoreboard that we may want to use differently. But with the raw size of the scoreboards, we’re comfortable and confident that those are the way we intended and designed them."

World.title: Shake Shack customer hits 'no tip' at kiosk, then watches prices jump in viral video
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

The Utah man behind a viral video appearing to show prices increase at a Shake Shack kiosk after his wife declined to leave a tip says he initially didn't believe her when she told him what had happened.

Brian Powell, 45, told Fox News Digital that he and his wife were waiting to catch a flight out of Salt Lake City when she purchased three milkshakes from the airport's Shake Shack location.

"My wife came to me after buying some shakes and said, 'They charged me more after I didn't tip,'" Powell told Fox News Digital during a Zoom interview from London, where he was vacationing with his wife. "And I thought it was a little interesting."

NO TIPS, WORSE SERVICE? RESTAURANT OWNERS WARN TREND IS 'DEGRADING' DINING EXPERIENCE

Powell said he had visited the location several times before and had never noticed anything similar. Admitting that he was "a bit skeptical," Powell said he returned to the kiosk with his wife and recreated the order while recording the process on his phone.

"We basically went up and duplicated our order, and the same thing happened," Powell said.

The video shows two of the three shakes initially listed at $5.99 each. After "no tip" is selected, the kiosk displays a notice saying there has been a pricing update before the shakes appear at $6.49 each — an increase of 50 cents per drink.

Shake Shack told Fox News Digital the price change was caused by a technology error and that charging customers more for declining to tip is not company policy.

CLICK HERE TO 

"It is not Shake Shack policy, nor that of our licensees, to increase the price of menu items when no tip is added," a spokesperson for the company said.

The airport location is owned and operated by HMSHost, a Shake Shack licensee.

HMSHost investigated and "determined it was an error within their kiosk technology that they have informed us has since been resolved," according to Shake Shack.

"We'll continue working with all our licensed partners to make sure every guest is taken care of at Shake Shack," the spokesperson added.

Powell said that when he recorded the video, he didn't know whether the price change was deliberate or simply a glitch.

"Because I had been to that Shake Shack before, it felt fishy to me, but honestly, I did not know," Powell said. "I mean, the reality is, I've even tipped at that Shake Shack before. … I just thought it was peculiar that, all of a sudden, we were being charged when we pressed 'no tip.'"

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

Powell said he never expected the video to attract so much attention. He edited and posted it while waiting for a delayed flight and watched its audience surge after taking off.

"The video has been overwhelming," Powell said, adding that the number of comments flooding his social media inbox made it "impossible" to read through all of them.

Powell's video shines a light on many Americans' larger frustration with tipping prompts at self-service businesses.

"I think my own personal opinion is maybe tipping culture's a little bit out of hand, based on this experience," Powell said.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"The entire video was kind of generated by my frustration that, you know, here I was being charged for something I didn't necessarily feel like I should have been charged for."

Powell said he may revisit the kiosk when he returns to Salt Lake City to see if, in fact, the issue has been resolved.

World.title: An ultra-rare Cooper Flagg trading card has been found, and the Mavericks are prepared to give a lot for it
World.content:

A 1-of-1 Cooper Flagg rookie card from Topps with the 2025 first pick's NBA Debut patch from his first game has been the holy grail of sports cards as of late, so much so that the Dallas Mavericks put out a "bounty" for it.

World.title: Arizona Gov. Katie Hobbs chooses former Republican as running mate in re-election bid
World.content:
Democratic Arizona Gov. Katie Hobbs has chosen a former Republican as her running mate for her re-election bid this November.

On Tuesday, Hobbs named John Giles, who served as a GOP mayor of Mesa, Arizona, from 2014 to 2025, as her pick for lieutenant governor.

In a joint video announcement with Giles, Hobbs said she has fought for Arizonans as governor by cutting taxes, securing the border and supporting public safety.

“Now, for the first time in our state’s history, we are electing a governor and lieutenant governor on the same ticket. And the first thing I looked for in a running mate was someone who shares that value of putting Arizonans ahead of partisan politics,” Hobbs said.

Giles said, “I was a lifelong Republican before becoming an independent because extremists shouldn’t stand in the way of getting things done.”

Giles changed his party affiliation to independent in May and voted in the Democratic primary last month, Hobbs’ communications director Michael Beyer confirmed to NBC News.

Voters will elect a lieutenant governor for the first time this fall after a ballot measure creating the position was approved in the 2022 election.

The New York Times was first to report on Hobbs’ plans.

Hobbs faces a competitive race against Rep. Andy Biggs, R-Ariz., who previously chaired the conservative House Freedom Caucus and has served in Congress since 2017. Biggs has selected former state lawmaker Sine Kerr as his running mate. Biggs won the Republican primary last month, beating fellow Rep. David Schweikert and businessmen Scott Neely and Ken Miceli.

While mayor of Mesa, Giles endorsed then-Vice President Kamala Harris for president in the 2024 election and spoke at the Democratic National Convention in Chicago that year about his disappointment with the Republican Party.

“I’m a lifelong Republican, so I feel a little out of place tonight. But I feel more at home here than in today’s Republican Party,” Giles said in his remarks. “The Grand Old Party has been kidnapped by extremists and devolved into a cult — the cult of Donald Trump.”

He added: “I have an urgent message for the majority of Americans who, like me, are in the political middle. John McCain’s Republican Party is gone, and we don’t owe a damn thing to what’s been left behind.”

The nonpartisan Cook Political Report rated the governor’s race as leaning Democratic in the battleground state, which President Donald Trump carried in 2016 and 2024 and Joe Biden won in 2020.

In 2022, Hobbs defeated Republican Kari Lake in the gubernatorial election by less than 1 percentage point. Before serving as governor, Hobbs was Arizona’s secretary of state. She also has been the minority leader in the state Senate and a member of the state House.

Hobbs recently formed a coalition of former and current Republican and independent leaders who support her re-election, which included Giles and more than 50 other business leaders and officials.

The Democratic incumbent has touted her record of working across the aisle, including signing more than 900 pieces of bipartisan legislation into law, according to her campaign. She has also highlighted her efforts to expand affordable housing and secure the border and her repeal of the state’s 1864 near-total abortion ban.

Biggs, meanwhile, has promoted his relationship with Trump and has run on a campaign touting his support for lowering taxes and border security.

World.title: Former Marine held in Russia for more than 4 years has been released
World.content:
A former U.S. Marine who spent more than four years in a Russian prison and is believed to be seriously ill has been released and was on his way back to the United States on Tuesday.

President Donald Trump announced the release on Truth Social, saying Robert Gilman, 32, was freed after he discussed the case with Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Trump said Gilman, a teacher, was released “very much on a Humanitarian Basis,” with no exchange of prisoners having taken place. He is expected to land at Andrews Air Force Base in Washington, D.C.

The president added in his post that he had spoken to Gilman “and he had one request — A GREAT cheeseburger when he lands. I will take care of that!”

The Russian government has not commented on the release.

Robert Gilman during a hearing in Voronezh, Russia in September 2024. Andrey Arhipov / Sputnik via AP

About 50 days ago, Gilman was diagnosed with a “dissociative stupor — a condition where he is non-responsive and unable to interact or eat,” Sen. Ed Markey, D-Mass., said in a statement following the man’s release.

“He was essentially catatonic and also suffered a severe case of pneumonia,” added Markey, who has been campaigning for Gilman’s release. “We don’t yet know the full details of his current condition or the long-term impact on his recovery.”

Gilman’s sister Lexie Hudson thanked Trump in a statement issued by Global Reach, an advocacy group representing his family.

“There is no other reason that Robert is alive today other than that President Trump heard about the case and took action,” she said.

“I am looking forward to seeing Robert. I haven’t been able to speak with him once since this all began,” she added. “We will make sure that he gets the treatment and support that he needs.”

Before his release, Hudson said in a statement on Sunday that she was worried that he would die if he wasn’t freed. “I’m more afraid for my brother than I have been since this horrible nightmare started,” she said in the statement issued by Global Reach.

Her comments on Sunday came around a month after Russia’s Kommersant newspaper reported that Gilman had been ​admitted to a hospital. Quoting his lawyer Irina Brazhnikova, the business daily reported that he was receiving treatment but it was too early to talk about a diagnosis.

Gilman, who served in the Marines from August 2019 until August 2020, had been detained in 2022. He was initially handed a 3 ½— year sentence for beating a police officer after being taken off a train for causing a disturbance.

While serving his sentence, in October 2024 Gilman was accused of attacking a prison inspector during a cell check, beating an investigator and assaulting a guard; he was sentenced to eight years and one month.

Last year, his sentence was extended again to 10 years after he was found guilty of assaulting prison guards.

Gilman’s American supporters contend he was ill when he was first arrested and also that he was provoked while in prison into actions that led to further charges.

According to Markey, Gilman was “subjected to physical torture, forced medication, and provocations by Russian authorities,” throughout his detention.

“There is no doubt that his treatment by Russian authorities is the reason Robert is in this precarious state today,” he added.

Gilman was one of at least 10 Americans known to be imprisoned in Russia.

World.title: Watch Live: Second psychiatric nurse practitioner testifies at Lindsay Clancy trial
World.content:
Lindsay Clancy's murder trial in Massachusetts resumed Tuesday with testimony from Rebecca Jollotta, a second psychiatric nurse practitioner who treated Clancy in 2022.

You can watch the trial live on CBS News Boston in the embedded video or on YouTube when court is in session. Court is currently in the lunch recess until 2 p.m.

Clancy, who turned 36 on Tuesday, has pleaded not guilty to first-degree murder in the deaths of her three children, 5-year-old Cora, 3-year-old Dawson and 8-month-old Callan, in their home in Duxbury on Jan. 24, 2023.

Prosecutors, led by assistant district attorney Jennifer Sprague, say she planned the murders. Clancy's attorney Kevin Reddington says she admits killing her children, but she shouldn't be held criminally responsible because she was suffering from postpartum psychosis and bipolar disorder.

Rebecca Jollotta, who works at South Shore Health in Weymouth and treated Clancy starting in November 2022, has spent much of Tuesday on the stand.

Prosecutor finishes questioning psychiatric nurse practitioner

On Dec. 15, 2022, Lindsay and her husband at the time, Patrick Clancy, called Jollotta to say it had been "the worst day" for Lindsay.

Jollotta testified that Clancy was having persistent thoughts of suicide and they were ready to get her assessed for a higher level of care.

According to Jollotta, she told the couple to go to Mass General Hospital, which has a psychiatric unit. Jollotta said she recommended inpatient care for Clancy.

The next day, Jollotta learned that Clancy had gone to the ER, but decided to remain outpatient. She began to attend a program at Women and Infants Hospital of Rhode Island.

After less than a week, Clancy was discharged from the program in Rhode Island. Jollotta said she told Clancy she was concerned that she'd been discharged.

Jollotta said her last contact with Clancy was Dec. 21, 2022. On Dec. 30, 2022, Patrick Clancy called South Shore Health to say his wife was safe but wanted to go to McLean Hospital in Belmont, Massachusetts.

Sprague completed her questioning just before 1 p.m. by confirming with Jollotta that Clancy never told her she had a plan to harm herself and kill her children.

Psychiatric nurse practitioner eyed bipolar disorder

Jollotta said that after mostly speaking virtually with Clancy, she later met with her and her ex-husband Patrick in person on Dec. 6, 2022. Lindsay and Patrick Clancy were married at the time of their children's deaths, but have since divorced and Patrick has remarried.

According to Jollotta, Clancy did not mention anything about hearing voices, hallucinations, or suicidal intent during the in-person meeting.

"I discussed to her and her husband the possibility of an underlying bipolar disorder," Jollotta said.

Jollotta said she recalls Patrick Clancy saying, "My wife is not bipolar."

The next day, Clancy messaged Jollotta to say that she had not slept well, took Ativan and then "got desperate" and took Benadryl.

"I'm desperate and really need help," Jollotta testified that Clancy told her.

Clancy asked for different medications, and Jollotta again suggested that she was concerned about a potential underlying mood and bipolar disorder.

On Dec. 12, 2022, Jollotta said she told Clancy she "strongly, strongly recommend" a partial hospitalization program.

Clancy had an in-person appointment scheduled for the next day, but she called to make it a virtual meeting.

"I feel like I'm going to die and I don't care"

Clancy was prescribed medications to help with her mental health struggles. According to Jollotta, after four days Clancy said the medication was not working. Jollotta said she encouraged Clancy to give it more time.

Rebecca Jollotta testifies at Lindsay Clancy's trial on Aug. 11, 2026 at Plymouth Superior Court. CBS Boston

Jollotta said it was common practice to pair a low dosage of medications together to manage a person's symptoms.

"I thought it would help with depression, anxiety and sleep," Jollotta said.

Jollotta testified that Clancy did not report feeling suicidal, but said she "can't keep going on like this."

On Dec. 1, 2022, Clancy messaged Jollotta through the MyChart app.

"Sorry for all the messages, this is just a scary time for me," Clancy wrote, adding that she was scared of starting medications. In another message, Clancy wrote "I'm willing to try anything."

Clancy said she was concerned that she felt addicted to one of the medications, Ativan.

"I feel concerningly numb right now ... like I have no emotion whatsoever," Clancy wrote to Jollotta that same day. "I feel like I'm going to die and I don't care. What do I do about this?"

Jollotta provided resources to Clancy for crisis intervention in case the symptoms got worse. She testified that she did not tell Clancy to go to the emergency room right away. She thought it seemed like anhedonia, which is a symptom of depression that can make people lose the ability to feel pleasure.

"My concern about that statement was that I wanted her to have access to the resources if it worsened," Jollotta said.

Defense wants to call TikTok user

Before testimony began for the day, attorneys argued before Judge William Sullivan about potential testimony from Emily Thorndike, who posted a TikTok video about her experience working at McLean Hospital in Belmont, Massachusetts.

Thorndike took issue with the positive description of McLean during Sprague's questioning of Lindsay Clancy's ex-husband Patrick.

Prosecutors say the testimony should not be allowed because Thorndike was not working at the facility when Clancy was admitted for treatment in 2022.

Judge Sullivan took arguments under advisement but did not make a ruling.

Lindsay Clancy trial

Julie Paul, the 61st witness in the trial, was on the stand briefly to start the day Tuesday. She testified for the prosecution Monday afternoon, telling the court she prescribed some psychiatric drugs to Clancy and that Clancy never mentioned having thoughts of killing herself or her children.

Paul was set for cross-examination on Tuesday, but it only lasted about a minute and she stepped down.

If convicted of first-degree murder, Lindsay Clancy faces life in prison without parole. If the jury of 12 women and six men finds that she was not criminally responsible for the deaths of her children, she will be sent to a state psychiatric hospital in Massachusetts.

If you or someone you know is in emotional distress or a suicidal crisis, you can reach the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline by calling or texting 988. You can also chat with the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline here.

For more information about mental health care resources and support, The National Alliance on Mental Illness HelpLine can be reached Monday through Friday, 10 a.m.–10 p.m. ET, at 1-800-950-NAMI (6264) or email info@nami.org.

World.title: Maine lifeguard "started swimming like hell" when shark pulled him underwater
World.content:
A lifeguard in Maine said he "started swimming like hell" when a shark grabbed onto his buoy and pulled him underwater off the coast of Scarborough Beach on Saturday.

Greg Wilfert said he initially thought he was caught in the propeller of a boat.

"'Cause that's the only thing I could think of until I realized there was no boat," he said.

Wilfert said he was pulled about 5 feet underwater before he was able to get free and emerge on shore unharmed.

"It was frightening," he said. "I'm not going to deny that."

More shark sightings

Officials along the East Coast say there are more sharks closer to shore in areas where they don't usually go.

Since last week, at least a dozen sharks have been spotted close to popular beaches in the area of Wilfert's encounter, according to Scarborough's marine resources officer Daryen Granata.

"Usually we'll see one or two here and there. This is a large volume, larger than I've seen, and I've worked this area for 30-plus years," Granata said.

The trend is happening as conservation efforts have led to an increase in marine life populations in recent years, experts say.

"We're gonna see more of everything, including more sharks," OCEARCH founder Chris Fischer explained.

His nonprofit studies sharks by catching, tagging and collecting data before releasing them back into the ocean.

"It means just try to be a little bit more aware of what's going on in the environment around you. You see a lot of life, steer clear of that," he warned.

Still, shark encounters remain rare. Last year, the International Shark Attack File reported 25 unprovoked bites.

Six states are holding primaries on Tuesday, with the unpredictable Democratic primaries in Wisconsin and Minnesota coming to a close as South Carolina Republicans choose a successor for the late Sen. Lindsey Graham's seat.

In Wisconsin, the democratic socialist Francesca Hong and the more moderate David Crowley are duking it out for the Democratic nomination in the governor's race after two other candidates dropped out of the race. President Trump's ally, Rep. Tom Tiffany, is all but certain to win the GOP nomination.

With Minnesota Democratic Sen. Tina Smith not running for reelection, Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan and Rep. Angie Craig are fighting for the Democratic nomination for Senate in another proxy battle between two different factions of the party. Sen. Amy Klobuchar is opting to run for governor, and faces no significant primary opposition in the race to replace Gov. Tim Walz, who is not running for reelection.

On the ballot for the Republican nomination for the Minnesota Senate seat, Michele Tafoya, a former sportscaster, is considered the frontrunner against Adam Schwarze, a retired Navy SEAL, and Royce White, a former professional basketball player who was the 2024 GOP candidate. In the governor's race, MyPillow CEO Mike Lindell, Minnesota House Speaker Lisa Demuth and businessman Kendall Qualls are the major contenders for the GOP nomination.

And in South Carolina, the sprint to Tuesday's special primary election to replace Graham on the ticket comes to a head. Graham's sister, Sen. Darline Graham, has been appointed to fill out the remainder of his term and is facing off against nine primary challengers for a spot on the ballot in November.

Here are the major races to watch today:

South Carolina

Ten Republicans are facing off in South Carolina Tuesday in a special primary election to represent the party on the ballot in November, after Graham's sudden death last month.

Graham, a four-term senator, had secured the GOP nomination in June in his bid for six more years representing South Carolina. After his death, his sister, Darline Graham, was appointed to serve until January. And days after she was sworn into office, she announced that she was running for a full term representing the Palmetto State — with Mr. Trump's encouragement.

But the president's endorsement of Graham didn't prevent a slew of Republicans from jumping into the race. Reps. Russell Fry and Ralph Norman are also seeking the nomination, along with former South Carolina Gov. Mark Sanford and businessman Mark Lynch, who lost the June primary to the late senator.

If no candidate secures a majority of the vote in Tuesday's primary, the contest could head to a runoff later this month to determine who takes on Democrat Annie Andrews in November.

Wisconsin governor's race

Mr. Trump won perennial swing state Wisconsin in 2024 by less than a point, and the state is one of only two in the country with one Republican senator and one Democratic senator. (In Maine, independent Sen. Angus King caucuses with Democrats, while the state's other senator is GOP Sen. Susan Collins.)

Two-term Democratic Gov. Tony Evers is not running for reelection, opening up the Democratic nomination for governor. Former Lt. Gov. Mandela Barnes, who lost the 2022 Senate race against Sen. Ron Johnson by one point, had thrown his hat in the ring, along with Lt. Gov. Sara Rodriguez, Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley and Francesca Hong, a state lawmaker and former chef.

The race started to take a completely different shape in July, when Crowley dropped his bid and threw his support behind Rodriguez, who was considered more of an establishment candidate. But Rodriguez dropped out days later after discovering her campaign had less money in the bank than previously believed.

Although Barnes had pulled out a surprise victory in the 2022 Senate primary as a progressive candidate and won statewide as the state's first Black lieutenant governor in 2018, Hong had risen to be the frontrunner.

With Wisconsin voters facing those hard-left choices on the ballot, Crowley then announced he would return to the campaign trail as a centrist Democrat. Crowley said in a debate last month that he initially made the decision to drop out based on data, but "we were going off false data," prompting him to return to the race.

Barnes then announced on July 30 — less than two weeks before the primary — that he would be dropping his bid, saying, "it's becoming very clear who the Democratic nominee is going to be," pointing to Hong. Barnes' announcement came as the Milwaukee Journal Sentinel was investigating allegations that he was taking advantage of his role in the party to have sexual encounters with young adult women. Barnes has not addressed the allegations and has not been accused of any crimes.

The two frontrunners in the Democratic primary are now Hong and Crowley, who has since gotten Evers' backing, setting up a battle between the party's moderate and progressive factions. Barnes' and Rodriguez's names remain on the ballot due to their late withdrawals from the race.

The rise of Hong, who had the backing of the Wisconsin chapters of the Democratic Socialists of America, comes a year after progressive Zohran Mamdani won the New York City mayor's race and several other DSA members and those aligned with the organization have notched victories in primaries this year.

But some of Hong's social media comments from 2019 to 2021 have also come to light: She called for defunding the police and abolishing ICE and the U.S. Senate, disparaged that there were "too many old white people who didn't think we spoke English" at a rural location of the Wisconsin favorite Culver's and called to "cancel Thanksgiving." Hong has disavowed some of these comments, and told Politico last week that Thanksgiving is her favorite holiday.

If Hong wins on Tuesday night, her campaign staff is planning a staff overhaul that would bring in more experienced campaign operatives — particularly in the areas of communications and rapid response — following a turbulent close to her primary campaign, two Democratic sources with knowledge of the planning told CBS News.

Tiffany, the GOP candidate, does not face any significant primary challengers. Tiffany is a member of the hard-right House Freedom Caucus, and has been one of Mr. Trump's allies in denying the outcome of the 2020 election.

Wisconsin House races

Wisconsin has eight congressional districts, with two Democrats and six Republicans representing the state in the House. Democrats have been focused on flipping two of those GOP-held seats.

Wisconsin's 3rd District, located in a rural part of the state heavily affected by Mr. Trump's agriculture and tariff policies, is represented by Rep. Derrick Van Orden, an ally of Mr. Trump's. Van Orden defeated Democrat Rebecca Cooke by 11,000 votes in 2024. The district is considered a toss-up by Sabato's Crystal Ball at the University of Virginia's Center for Politics, and the Democrats' House campaign arm has prioritized the district in its Red to Blue program.

Cooke is running again for the Democratic nomination, and this time has the backing of the Democrats' House campaign arm. Cooke, who has worked as a political consultant, faces Eau Claire City Council member Emily Berge.

Democrats are also targeting Wisconsin's 1st District, the district once represented by former House Speaker Paul Ryan and represented by Rep. Bryan Steil since 2018, although the district is considered Likely Republican by Sabato's Crystal Ball and would likely be a reach for any Democrat. Three Democrats — Mitchell Berman, Lorenzo Santos and Miguel Aranda — are running to take on Steil, who won reelection by nine points in 2024 and has $6 million cash on hand.

With Tiffany running for governor, his seat in the 7th District, a safe Republican seat, is now open. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy's son-in-law Michael Alfonso is considered the frontrunner for the seat and has the backing of Mr. Trump and House Speaker Mike Johnson. He faces four GOP challengers.

Minnesota Senate race

Minnesota was ground zero for the Trump administration's immigration policies earlier this year, drawing national scrutiny after the fatal shootings of two American citizens by federal agents in Minneapolis. And the issue is front and center in this year's primaries as candidates eye the Democratic and Republican nomination for an open Senate seat.

On the Democratic side, a dynamic familiar to the 2026 midterms is playing out between Rep. Angie Craig, a centrist candidate backed by a slew of national Democrats, and Minnesota Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, a progressive endorsed by the likes of Sens. Bernie Sanders and Elizabeth Warren.

Amid the debate over immigration enforcement, Craig has faced criticism over her previous stances, including her vote last year for the Laken Riley Act immigration enforcement bill, while Flanagan has been unequivocal in her opposition to the administration's immigration policies. But Craig's supporters have argued that the four-term congresswoman is the more electable candidate, especially as Flanagan has been tied to the Minnesota governor's handling of the multimillion-dollar fraud schemes in the state.

On the GOP side, among those vying to be the Republican nominee are Michele Tafoya, a former sports broadcaster, former basketball player Royce White and Adam Schwarze, a retired Navy SEAL. And although Minnesota hasn't elected a Republican to the Senate since 2002, the GOP is hoping to make inroads as it seeks to hold on to control of the chamber next year, seeing some opportunity in a state that former Vice President Kamala Harris won by just four points in 2024.

Minnesota House races

Rep. Ilhan Omar occupies a safe Democratic district in Minneapolis, where the winner is favored to win in November. Omar was first elected in 2018 in an open election, but she has faced centrist opposition in primaries since then.

In this year's contest, she faces four primary challengers, but she is expected to win the nomination again.

Alabama House races

After the Supreme Court ruling in May that narrowed Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, which required majority Black districts in some states, Alabama postponed its House primaries until Aug. 11 so state lawmakers could redraw the districts.

Alabama is currently represented by two Democrats and five Republicans, and Republicans redrew their maps to make the 2nd District friendlier to Republicans, endangering Democratic Rep. Shomari Figures, who won the seat in 2024. Sabato's Crystal Ball now considers the seat likely Republican.

Rhett Marques is the frontrunner in the GOP primary for that seat, with the backing of Mr. Trump, Alabama Sen. Katie Britt and House GOP leadership. Marques is facing five challengers on Tuesday.

Connecticut

Democratic Connecticut Gov. Ned Lamont is running for reelection, and is facing a primary challenger — the first time in 50 years that an incumbent governor in Connecticut has been challenged in the primary, according to CBS Hartford affiliate WFSB.

According to a poll from Sacred Heart University and CT Insider, Lamont is leading Democratic state Rep. Josh Elliott by 35 points.

Republican Ryan Fazio is not facing any challengers on Tuesday. The same poll found Lamont leading Fazio by 20 points in a general election, and Elliott had a nearly 20-point lead over Fazio as well.

Rep. John Larson of the 1st District is also facing primary challengers for the first time since he was elected in 1998. Larson and his three challengers — former Hartford Mayor Luke Bronin, West Hartford state Rep. Jillian Gilchrest and Hartford Board of Education member Ruth Fortune — agree on key policy issues, but the race has focused on generational change. Bronin, Larson's most well-known and best-funded opponent, has zeroed in on Larson's age — 78 — and long tenure in Congress.

Vermont

Two Democrats are vying to take on Vermont's Republican Gov. Phil Scott in November: Amanda Janoo and Aly Richards. Scott is running for a sixth term, but a University of New Hampshire poll from July found that he has his lowest approval rating since April 2022. Neither Janoo nor Richards has held elected office before, making a November challenge difficult.

In Vermont's at-large congressional district, Republicans Gerald Malloy and Mark Coeste are vying to take on incumbent Democratic Rep. Becca Balint. But the same July UNH poll found that both would trail her in a general election matchup.

World.title: What is Medicare Extra Help and who qualifies for it now?
World.content:
We may receive commissions from some links to products on this page. Promotions are subject to availability and retailer terms.

If you're struggling with prescription drug costs on Medicare, it's worth knowing what Extra Help offers. Mohd Izzuan/Getty Images

Prescription drug costs have changed considerably for Medicare beneficiaries over the last few years. Case in point? The introduction of a federal cap on annual out-of-pocket Medicare Part D spending has provided an important new layer of protection, with the limit rising from $2,000 in 2025 to $2,100 in 2026. But even with that safeguard in place, paying for medications can still put significant pressure on retirees and others living on limited incomes.

After all, the out-of-pocket Part D cap doesn't eliminate the other expenses that can come with Medicare drug coverage. Depending on the plan and the prescriptions someone takes, there are premiums, deductibles and pharmacy costs that can still add up — and can put more strain on retirees' budgets and compete with the cost of housing, groceries and other necessities for a spot in a tight monthly budget.

That's where programs designed to reduce Medicare expenses can become especially valuable. One of those programs, known as Medicare Extra Help, specifically targets prescription drug costs. What exactly is this program, though, and who qualifies to take advantage of it? That's what we'll outline below.

Find out more about your Medicare Supplemental coverage options here.

What is Medicare Extra Help and who qualifies for it now?

Medicare Extra Help, formally known as the Part D Low-Income Subsidy (LIS), is a program that's intended to substantially reduce what eligible Medicare beneficiaries pay for prescription drug coverage. But how you qualify depends on your financial situation and the other benefits you receive. Here's what to know:

What is Medicare Extra Help?

Medicare Extra Help is a federal program for people with Medicare who have limited incomes and financial resources. The assistance applies specifically to Medicare Part D prescription drug coverage rather than the broader medical costs associated with Medicare Parts A and B.

For example, Extra Help can reduce the Part D plan premium and deductible to $0 for those who qualify in 2026. It also limits what beneficiaries pay for prescriptions at participating pharmacies, capping generic drug prices at $5.10 and $12.65 for brand-name drugs in most cases. And, some beneficiaries may pay even less based on their Medicaid status and income.

Medicare Extra Help recipients don't have to pay a Part D late enrollment penalty while receiving the assistance, either. And once their total drug costs reach the $2,100 Part D out-of-pocket threshold, they pay nothing for covered Part D prescriptions for the remainder of the year.

Compare your Medigap options and find the right policy today.

Who qualifies for Medicare Extra Help?

Some Medicare beneficiaries automatically qualify for Extra Help. That includes people who receive full Medicaid benefits, get assistance from a Medicare Savings Program to pay their Part B premiums or receive Supplemental Security Income (SSI) benefits. Those beneficiaries generally don't need to submit a separate Extra Help application to take advantage of what the program offers.

Others may qualify based on their income and financial resources. The annual income limit is $23,940 for individuals or $32,460 for married couples for 2026, and the resource limit is $18,090 for individuals and $36,100 for married couples. Those with incomes under those thresholds may qualify. Note, though, that different income limits apply in Alaska and Hawaii.

Resources considered when determining eligibility typically include the money held in checking and savings accounts, stocks, bonds, mutual funds and retirement accounts. Your home, one vehicle, household items, personal possessions and certain other assets generally aren't counted.

How Medicare Extra Help and Medigap can work together

Extra Help can significantly reduce prescription drug expenses for those who qualify, but it doesn't address every out-of-pocket cost Medicare beneficiaries may encounter. Original Medicare can still leave you responsible for deductibles, copayments and coinsurance, and there's no annual out-of-pocket maximum for covered Part A and Part B services.

Medicare supplemental insurance, also known as Medigap, is one option for addressing some of those expenses. Private insurers sell Medigap policies to help cover certain costs that Original Medicare doesn't pay. Depending on the plan, that can include some or all of your Part A and Part B coinsurance, certain deductibles and other eligible expenses.

Medigap and Extra Help aren't interchangeable, though. Extra Help is designed specifically to reduce Medicare Part D prescription drug costs for retirees who meet the program's financial requirements. Medigap primarily helps with certain out-of-pocket costs left behind by Original Medicare, and Medigap policies sold today generally don't include prescription drug coverage. Beneficiaries who want drug coverage typically need a separate Part D plan.

As a result, qualifying for Extra Help doesn't necessarily eliminate the potential value of Medigap. Someone who qualifies for Extra Help could use the program to lower eligible Part D expenses while carrying a Medigap policy to reduce certain costs associated with Original Medicare. However, Medigap comes with its own premiums, so it's important to weigh the cost of a policy against the coverage it provides and the medical expenses you're likely to face.

The bottom line

Medicare's prescription drug benefit offers more protection against large medication bills than it did just a few years ago, but Part D costs can still be difficult to absorb on a limited budget. Extra Help can reduce several of those expenses for beneficiaries who meet the program's requirements, so it may be worth checking your eligibility even if your income or resources are close to the limits.

But prescription drugs are only one piece of the Medicare cost equation. If you use Original Medicare, it may also be worth considering whether a Medigap policy makes sense for the deductibles, coinsurance and other eligible expenses Extra Help doesn't address. Evaluating the two separately can help you determine where your biggest coverage gaps are — and which forms of assistance or supplemental coverage could make those costs more predictable.

World.title: DOJ office says Trump's outside advisers can be shielded by executive privilege
World.content:
President Trump's outside advisers — individuals who are not employed by the federal government — may now be protected from future congressional and legal investigations, according to a new opinion from the Justice Department's Office of Legal Counsel.

In a 21-page opinion published Monday evening, the Office of Legal Counsel told the White House that the president can move to extend executive privilege, the right of the president to contain confidential communications within the executive branch, to advisers who do not work for the White House, but who provide him with direct advice.

The new opinion says that executive privilege can apply to private advisers of the president if the communications "relate to official presidential decisionmaking," are confidential, and involve conversations between the president and his direct team of advisers.

The opinion, which is not binding, comes months before a contentious midterm election that could result in Democrats winning one or both houses in Congress. If that were to happen, a barrage of investigations could follow and may expand the number of individuals potentially protected from future testimony or investigation.

Executive privilege is often asserted by the president in conversations with executive branch staff, like lawyers who work for the White House, but the new step could protect Mr. Trump's outside legal counsel and other advisers from divulging information in future congressional investigations or legal proceedings.

"At bottom, the purpose of executive privilege is to protect the government's decisionmaking processes," the opinion said. It was signed by Assistant Attorney General T. Elliot Gaiser, who leads the Office of Legal Counsel.

"The need for presidential confidentiality applies to communications with private advisers just as it does with government officials. A President might determine that a private adviser has unique insight or experience, and that full knowledge about a contemplated decision cannot be obtained through consultation with only government employees," the opinion continued.

This is not the first OLC opinion by Mr. Trump's Justice Department that has broken with historical precedent.

In April, Gaiser authored an opinion that said the federal law enacted in the wake of the Watergate scandal that requires the president to preserve certain documents and turn them over to the National Archives at the end of his administration is unconstitutional, and that Mr. Trump does not need to comply with it.

Weeks after the opinion was published, a federal judge in Washington, D.C. ordered White House staff and President Trump's top advisers to comply with the law after a government oversight group and the American Historical Association sued to invalidate the opinion.

The opinion could also shield outside Trump adviser and lawyer Boris Epshteyn, who was recently subpoenaed by the American Bar Association in a lawsuit filed last year related to the White House's alleged "intimidation policy" against major law firms that resulted in executive orders targeting four firms and deals made with several others.

The American Bar Association is seeking communications between Epshteyn and the White House, and the DOJ has moved to quash the subpoena, arguing Epshteyn "provided the President with privileged and confidential advice in connection with the Executive Orders at issue."
