He also stressed “the significant role of Trump’s personal efforts” in establishing peace.

“The two leaders welcomed the fact that the Washington Peace Summit had led to real peace between Armenia and Azerbaijan, which people in both countries can see and feel. […] Prime Minister Pashinyan and President Trump reaffirmed their determination to begin work on the construction of TRIPP in the near future. They also discussed other issues on the bilateral Armenian-US and international agendas,” the Armenian prime minister’s office said.

Talks with Aliyev

According to the prime minister’s office, Pashinyan and Aliyev discussed progress in normalising relations over the past year. They also focused on the development of trade and economic ties between the two countries.

“In this context, the sides highlighted Azerbaijan’s exports of petroleum products to Armenia, as well as the transit of goods through Azerbaijan to Armenia and from Armenia to other destinations. They also exchanged views on the implementation of the TRIPP project in line with the agreements reached in Washington. They stressed the importance of continuing efforts to advance the peace process and ensure long-term peace, stability, connectivity and economic cooperation in the region.”

Comment

Political analyst Tigran Grigoryan says:

“The main result of the Washington summit is that it brought a period of relative stability to the region. For a year now, we have not had to discuss possible escalations or security risks coming from Azerbaijan.

The second positive factor is that the atmosphere has changed to some extent and shifted towards cooperation. “As for Azerbaijan, it continues to promote certain aggressive strategies, such as its ‘Western Azerbaijan’ narrative. But it is also taking steps aimed at establishing peace. Opening its territory for transit is one example, along with other similar measures.

Naturally, it is better for Azerbaijan to open its territory, establish contacts and start trade than for the region to face the risk of escalation.

But, as we have repeatedly pointed out, we will only be able to assess the final results of this process not when the TRIPP project becomes operational, but after we see what else follows TRIPP. Our assessment in the coming years will depend on these developments.

If TRIPP is implemented, and Armenia also gains access to Iran and Russia through Azerbaijani territory, and if the Armenian-Turkish border opens, then we will certainly be able to consider the process a success. If none of this happens, or only some of it is achieved, the assessment could be different.

But once again, the stability that came to the region as a result of the Washington summit is extremely important for Armenia. From 2020 to 2025, security threats dominated our lives. Progress on security, without a doubt, also gives us an opportunity to focus on other issues.”

Washington peace summit: one year on

World.title: Eight Turkish parliamentary parties call for ending Abkhazia’s isolation
World.content:
Eight parliamentary parties in Turkey have called for an end to Abkhazia‘s isolation. The initiative primarily calls for Turkey to recognise the Abkhaz passport as a valid document for crossing the Turkish border, as well as for direct sea and air links between Turkey and Abkhazia to open.

Representatives of opposition factions announced the initiative at a joint press conference in the Turkish parliament. The initiative forms part of the “End Abkhazia’s Isolation” public campaign, which the local diaspora launched in early July 2026. The diaspora organised the campaign.

“Just imagine: hundreds of thousands of people of Abkhaz origin and their relatives live in Turkey, yet the Abkhaz passport is not valid here. Abkhaz people cannot travel to Turkey to attend the funerals of their relatives, while young people cannot enrol in universities.

These are the realities of international relations. Sometimes states are prepared to turn a blind eye to tragedies and anti-democratic practices that affect their own citizens’ relatives.

We are saying openly: Abkhaz passports must be recognised as valid documents at our border crossings. This disgrace must come to an end,” said Tuncer Bakırhan, an MP from the Democratic Party.

The eight parliamentary parties calling for an end to Abkhazia’s isolation represent a broad range of political forces, from the far right to the far left. What unites them is that they are all in opposition. The largest of them is the Yeni Parti (“New Party”), which has 91 MPs in the current parliament. Together, the eight parties hold 166 of the 600 seats in parliament.

The support from the opposition parties was not welcomed by the leadership of the Federation of Abkhaz Cultural Centres in the Republic of Turkey. More precisely, the Federation’s leadership appears to have objected not to the MPs themselves, but to the organisers of the “End Abkhazia’s Isolation” campaign.

The Federation does not dispute the campaign’s demands: recognition of Abkhaz passports and the opening of transport links between Abkhazia and Turkey. Its objections concern the “right to represent” and the “right to initiate” such efforts.

In Abkhazia, the Federation’s reaction was met with strong criticism from both politicians and civil society representatives.

“If any Abkhaz person in Turkey or elsewhere makes progress on our common cause, we should all support them and, if possible, join them, rather than argue over who is authorised to do what.

If our representatives in Turkey focus solely on preserving the language and culture, they should not interfere with those working to advance the political cause. If they consider such advocacy part of their remit, they should join them. That is how it looks from Abkhazia,” said Duat Khutaba, head of the Abkhaz parliament’s Committee on Legislation.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

Campaign to end Abkhazia’s isolation

World.title: Ex-US marine Robert Gilman freed from Russian jail on 'humanitarian basis'
World.content:
Russia has freed a former US marine who had been jailed since 2022 after President Vladimir Putin approved his release on humanitarian grounds, Donald Trump has said.

The White House and the State Department had been urging Moscow to release Robert Gilman, 32, so he could receive medical treatment in the US.

"After my discussions with President Vladimir Putin, Russia has agreed to release him, very much on a Humanitarian Basis," the US president said in a post on Truth Social.

" We appreciate this decision, and the fact that Russia asked for no one in return — No exchange took place. "

Mr Gilman was expected to arrive in Washington DC in the coming hours, Mr Trump added.

The former marine was being held in a prison in Voronezh, about 550 kilometres south of Moscow. The exact circumstances of his health are unclear.

But an advocacy group representing Mr Gilman's family last week said he had been relocated in late June after a medical assessment. He was moved from a prison hospital to the psychiatric ward of a civilian emergency hospital in a catatonic-like state assessed as a "dissociative stupor", Eric Lebson from the Global Reach group said.

US officials said Mr Gilman was on a State Department plane on Tuesday, US time, travelling from Russia to Washington Dulles Airport.

Kremlin rejects European assessment Navalny died of poisoning The Kremlin has rejected accusations from five European countries that the Russian state had killed late Kremlin critic Alexei Navalny two years ago using toxin from poison dart frogs.

A US official who spoke to Mr Gilman said he was walking and talking.

"All things considered he seems to be in good shape," the official said.

Mr Gilman will be evaluated on the flight by four doctors, said the US officials, who spoke on condition of anonymity. His mother, Nina, was also on board.

When he arrives in Washington, Mr Gilman will be greeted by US envoy Steve Witkoff and deputy national security adviser Sebastian Gorka, the US officials said. Both men had sought Mr Gilman's release along with Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Trump son-in-law Jared Kushner, US special envoy for hostage response Adam Boehler and other officials.

After that, Mr Gilman is likely to be flown to a rehabilitation centre in San Antonio, Texas, for medical treatment, the officials said.

Arrested over police officer incident

Mr Gilman, who served in the US Marines from August 2019 until August 2020, was travelling by train when he was arrested in January 2022 in Voronezh, Mr Lebson said.

He was detained for allegedly kicking a police officer while drunk, according to Russian state media.

However, his father, Vladimir Gilman, who emigrated to Massachusetts from Russia, wrote in an October 2024 Boston Globe op-ed that the charges were false.

His son, he said, had fallen ill when the incident occurred and accidentally kicked the officer. The officer was uninjured, dropped the charges, and did not present evidence at the trial, he wrote.

Mr Gilman was sentenced to four and a half years in jail. He was one of at least 10 Americans known to be imprisoned in Russia.

The US officials said a Russian senior official, Yuri Ushakov, informed Trump aides last week that Mr Putin had agreed to sign a decree pardoning Mr Gilman for humanitarian purposes, given Mr Putin's friendship with the president.

The release resulted from intense negotiations over the weekend by US and Russian officials. The US did not exchange any Russian prisoners in order to gain Mr Gilman's release and no concessions were made, the officials said.

"It's a goodwill gesture," one official said.

A State Department spokesperson said Mr Gilman had been recently designated as wrongfully detained and that it was hoped that another American with the same designation, Stephen Hubbard, would now be released along with other Americans "unjustly held in Russia".

Mr Hubbard, a retired schoolteacher, was sentenced in October 2024 to almost seven years in a penal colony after a court found him guilty of serving in a Ukrainian territorial defence unit against Russian forces, tasked with manning a checkpoint.

Mr Hubbard denied the charge.

Reuters

World.title: Four killed in Houthi attack on Red Sea cargo ship, sources say
World.content:
Four crew members have been killed in a suspected attack by Iran-backed Houthis on a small cargo vessel in the Bab el-Mandeb strait on Tuesday while a container ship was hit by a missile off Pakistan in a suspected US attack, sources said.

The fatalities aboard the Egyptian-owned Tihamah, if confirmed, would be the first deaths in a Houthi strike on shipping since the Iran war began on February 28. The Houthis have not claimed the attack.

Two Pakistanis and one Indonesian person were killed as the ship sailed from Salalah in Oman via Djibouti, the Yemeni sources said. After the attack, the crew lost control of the vessel and were approached by Yemeni coastguard, they added.

Iran war has spread beyond one strait The Middle East conflict isn't just widening, it's highlighting more vulnerabilities in the region.

The Houthis declared a maritime embargo against Saudi Arabia in the Red Sea on July 20 in response to what they described as a Saudi siege. Riyadh denies that Yemen is under siege.

The ship was hit by an unknown projectile, according to a report received by the British navy affiliated agency UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO).

The incident occurred while the ship was at anchor north-east of Perim Island, Yemen, British maritime security group Ambrey said.

Attack off Pakistan

The Panama-flagged container ship Vela Nova was struck by a missile in an attack off Pakistan while sailing into the Gulf of Oman, maritime security sources told Reuters.

The Wall Street Journal reported the vessel was attacked by a US helicopter which fired a Hellfire missile at the ship's rudder after it tried to evade a US blockade of Iran-linked shipping in the region.

What can help clear sea mine threats in Strait of Hormuz Clearing the Strait of Hormuz of Iranian sea mine threats will be a painstaking and challenging process.

There was no immediate comment from US Central Command.

If confirmed, it would be the 12th vessel attacked by US forces since its blockade was announced in April and the third since the blockade was reimposed on July 14.

The ship was believed to have been hit some 71 nautical miles off Pakistan's coast, UK maritime risk management group Vanguard and a maritime security source said.

The UKMTO also said it had received a report of an incident involving a container ship and military forces.

Shipping traffic

Shipping through the Bab el-Mandeb strait and Red Sea has fallen by more than 50 per cent since an earlier wave of Houthi attacks on shipping in 2023-25.

They have fallen further since the Houthis announced their blockade last month — with an average of 32 ships per day passing through the strait last week, according to Kpler data, down from an average of 50 before the blockade.

Ambrey noted that the cargo ship, which sources said was the Tihamah, was not Saudi-owned or operated and that it had departed the Yemeni government-held port of al-Mokha on Saturday.

LSEG data lists Egyptian companies as owners and managers of the ship. Neither responded to Reuters emails and phone calls seeking immediate comment.

Traffic is even more disrupted in the Strait of Hormuz with just six passing through on Monday, down from a 10-day average of about 11 and prewar levels of some 130 to 140.

Reuters

World.title: Colombia quake death toll reaches 224 with more than 2,700 missing
World.content:
The death toll from this week's earthquake in Colombia has risen to 224, local authorities say, as rescue crews continue to scour the rubble of collapsed buildings for survivors.

The 7.4-magnitude quake rattled western parts of the South American country, with the worst effects being felt in the cities of Cali, Quibdo and Pereira.

Roughly 1,600 buildings were reported damaged or collapsed in the aftermath, and more than 2,700 people have been reported missing.

Online, families were taking to citizen-run websites to post information about missing loved ones.

Among the worst hit areas is Choco, which is one of the poorest and most neglected regions of Colombia, and little is known about the extent of damage there.

Search and rescue workers have worked through the night to find those trapped under collapsed buildings. (AP: Santiago Saldarriaga)

In Quibdo, the capital of Colombia's Choco department, local official Jenny Rivas said public services and communications "have been virtually shut down."

Venezuelan President Abelardo de la Espriella travelled to Quibdo on Monday night, local time, to assess the damage, where he announced he was mobilising "the entire military and police apparatus" to respond, deploying engineers, rescue workers and search dogs.

He announced rental subsidies for those whose homes were damaged while they undergo repairs.

The US State Department announced it would provide $US15.5 million ($21 million) for emergency shelter, food and other aid. Governments across Latin America also lined up to help.

'The city fell down around us'

The earthquake came after two back-to-back quakes in June caused widespread devastation and claimed the lives of more than 6,300 people in neighbouring Venezuela.

Many Colombians were only beginning to grapple with the disaster's longer-term consequences.

Mónica Sánchez owns a small company that makes work uniforms. Her home city, Pereira, was one of the worst hit, and a wall inside the factory collapsed.

At least 1,600 buildings have been damaged or destroyed in the quake. (AP: Juan Diaz)

Ms Sánchez and her 12 workers were able to get outside just in time.

"It was shocking — the city fell down around us," she said.

Another resident of the city, tattoo artist Andres Hernandez, told AFP he was worried about falling asleep because of the risk posed by more buildings that were "on the verge of collapsing".

He described the moment the earthquake struck, forcing him from his home and out onto the street for safety.

"It was a movie scene, because I saw the poles, the cables, everything moving. I'm worried about my family, my friends," he said.

AFP/AP/Reuters

World.title: Syria sentences former leader Bashar al-Assad to death in absentia
World.content:
A Syrian court has sentenced ousted leader Bashar al-Assad to death after a trial in absentia, convicting him of a range of crimes including killings, torture, and arbitrary arrest during the country's nearly 14-year war.

It was the first conviction against Assad, who was ousted in a rebel offensive in December 2024.

His exit ended decades of his family's iron-fisted rule over Syria, and a brutal war that killed hundreds of thousands of Syrians.

Assad, now 60 years old, fled the capital Damascus as rebel fighters approached nearly two years ago, and is currently in Moscow.

Russian President Vladimir Putin (right) granted Bashar al-Assad a safe haven in Moscow on "humanitarian grounds". (Reuters: Sputnik/Mikhail Klimentyev)

In a trial of former government officials on Tuesday, a judge handed down a death sentence to Assad.

They were over the crimes of "premeditated and intentional murder of more than one person and of children, torture, arbitrary arrest and crimes against humanity".

It remains uncertain whether Syria's new authorities will be able to persuade Moscow to extradite Assad.

Atef Najib, a security official under Assad, was also sentenced to death.

Atef Najib, seen here in April, was physically present in the Damascus court where he received a death sentence. (Reuters: Khalil Ashawi)

Najib is Assad's cousin and the former head of political security in Deraa province in southern Syria's Deraa.

After the fall of a dictator, Syria dares to hope From Bashar al-Assad's abandoned palace to the site of one of the country's most horrific massacres, the ABC spent three days in Syria, uncovering the fallen dictator's secrets.

In the courtroom, he appeared inside a cage as the judge delivered his sentence.

Assad, who was born in 1965, became president in 2000 after his father Hafez died.

He maintained the family's rule and the dominance of their Alawite sect in the Sunni Muslim-majority country and Syria's status as an Iranian ally hostile to Israel and the US.

Shaped in its early years by the Iraq war and crisis in Lebanon, Assad's rule was defined by civil war.

It spiralled out of the 2011 Arab Spring, when Syrians demanding democracy took to the streets, to be met with deadly force.

Wires/ABC

World.title: 'Incredible disconnection': What Sussan Ley saw in the US shocked her
World.content:
After 276 days as the first female leader of the Coalition, Sussan Ley was axed as Opposition leader. It led to a life-changing and eye-opening experience as she found solitude, her voice and an empathy for the downtrodden of middle America while on its 'road to nowhere'.

Here, on a series of Greyhound buses, Ms Ley saw the United States. She saw a dispassionate and divided nation but one that cannot be compared to Australia.

"I think we make a mistake if we try to draw parallels," Ms Ley told 7.30 in her first interview since exiting politics.

"And if you go to the US and feel that there are immediate parallels, well, the first thing that hits you is that there actually are not."

While Ms Ley was away and out of the spotlight, the rise of One Nation has continued.

The party has soared in opinion polls and its leader Pauline Hanson has captured plenty of attention and coverage.

Senator Hanson's meeting with convicted criminal and far-right activist Tommy Robinson courted controversy but it has been her comments about wanting to make Australia a monocultural society that have drawn much discussion.

One Nation and its leader Pauline Hanson have enjoyed a rise in the polls. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

Ms Ley said her visit to the US only strengthened her view of the success of multiculturalism in Australia.

"I am a huge supporter of the Australian multicultural project for the simple reason that we have been able to achieve multicultural Australia not by erasing people's differences but by giving them space to belong," Ms Ley told 7.30.

"I think this is something we should all be incredibly proud of.

"I'm not a political commentator for the US, but I didn't see communities melting together like I see here.

"In fact, I saw different communities from different backgrounds sitting very uncomfortably alongside each other."

Prisoners, nuns and homeless travel companions

Asked if that meant that One Nation had got it wrong Ms Ley was noncommittal but said what she also saw in the US was a clear disconnect between the elite political class and those she travelled with.

Sussan Ley was on a journey to find her own voice after her political career ended. (Supplied: Sussan Ley)

As she travelled on those Greyhound buses — with "a lot of sketchy and strange characters" — on a journey she had dreamt up more than two decades ago, Ms Ley said she found the true US.

It was a surprising reckoning.

"I always felt that to the views of America that tourists had, that the media had, that we hear so much in the Zeitgeist, the view from Disneyland, the Statue of Liberty, Yosemite, Vegas, were just not the real America.

" I wanted to see that ... and I did. And what I saw was incredible and surprising. "

While the trip Ms Ley undertook was hardly the glitz and glamour of driving Pacific Coast Highway or Route 66 it removed some of the romanticism that usually surrounds the notion of the great American road trip.

The Greyhound bus has long been a cheaper option for the masses but what Ms Ley saw and heard revealed more about modern day USA.

Travelling through the middle of America on a Greyhound bus had been a bucket list item for Sussan Ley. (Supplied: Sussan Ley)

"In some states, you get a ticket to get on the Greyhound if you're homeless and the state wants you to leave," Ms Ley said.

"There were some returning prisoners, there were some nuns, there were veterans, there were many assistance dogs.

"I saw very, very few children.

"There were people whose lives were in transition and disarray, and that's what struck me from the moment I got on the first bus.

"There's several buses to get from the top of North Dakota to the bottom of Texas but it's hard to describe the expression on someone's face that comes from a lifetime of being overlooked.

"When I sat next to people and saw them in their most unguarded moments, the gap between what they hopefully looked into a future with and the reality that gradually settled on them was apparent.

"And what I mean by that is that I was often in awe of the dignity and the humanity of so many people that I travelled with."

America's 'incredible disconnection'

Asked what she learned about those "overlooked" Americans, Ms Ley said it was their disconnect from the political class that confronted her.

Donald Trump promised to make the United States better. (Supplied: Sussan Ley)

"The disconnection really was quite confronting," she told 7.30.

"I expected as I travelled to still see that clenched fist sense of pride in the US, in the flag, in the identity of the country.

"I've got to be honest, I didn't see that.

"It doesn't mean it didn't exist in people's hearts, but I didn't see it expressed, what I saw was incredible disconnection.

"I saw disconnection as a human condition rather than a political constituency. And people were simply not interested in the institutions and the organisations that ostensibly are there to represent them, to look after them and to be there for them.

"If you look back over history, you see the public in America and obviously around the world engaged, active, angry. What I saw was just an incredible stepping back and disinterest."

Ms Ley says what she saw was a people disconnected with their politicians. (Reuters: Kylie Cooper)

Asked to reconcile her understanding of the downtrodden, Ms Ley said it had been a constant.

"It was always there," she said.

" But remember that when you speak as a politician, you speak as a politician. You don't always speak with your own voice. "

Ms Ley said now that she has returned she will not be back in politics. That chapter is closed and she has no regrets.

"If I think about my time in politics, I'm proud of what I achieved," she said.

"I don't dwell on it because I'm very much focused on the next chapter of my life."

What that is Ms Ley says she is still unsure of but hopes it leads to a better Australia.

"I want to contribute to public life for the benefit of my grandchildren and their future in this country and to make it a better place," she said.

"How that happens, I'm not yet sure, but I am committed to that mission."

Watch 7.30, Mondays to Thursdays 7:30pm on ABC iview and ABC TV

World.title: Cats confirm Kolodjashnij unavailable to play amid concussion waiver saga
World.content:
The player at the centre of a concussion waiver controversy, Geelong's Jake Kolodjashnij, will not play this weekend as the club prepares to find out whether it will face sanctions.

It emerged last Thursday that the Cats struck a secret agreement with a player, who had had a history of concussions.

Kolodjashnij went public confirming he was the player involved.

The waiver has since been removed from his contract.

"Geelong Cats defender Jake Kolodjashnij will be unavailable for selection at AFL or VFL level this weekend," the club said a statement late on Tuesday.

"The care and wellbeing of Jake remains the club's priority, and the club will continue to support him and his family through this period."

The Cats had until the end of Tuesday to respond to the "please explain" from the AFL over the concussion waiver that Kolodjashnij signed but which was never seen by the AFL or the AFLPA.

Geelong Cats board holds crisis meeting over concussion deal Geelong is about to reply to the AFL's please explain as the Cats brace for a potential massive penalty over the secret concussion deal with Jake Kolodjashnij.

Amid speculation over the futures of Geelong chief executive Steve Hocking and AFL chairman Craig Drummond, the club board had held a crisis meeting on Monday to work out its response to the league.

Hocking was Cats chief executive and Drummond was the club president when the deal was struck two years ago with Koladjashnij.

The Geelong defender signed a waiver that meant he effectively took on legal responsibility for future brain trauma in a bid to indemnify the club and its medical staff from potential court action.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

Media reports on Tuesday said that the AFL Commission had hired independent legal counsel to help determine whether the Cats should face sanctions over the issue.

The 31-year-old Kolodjashnij was drafted by the club in 2013 and he has played 209 games for Geelong.

He last played at AFL level for the Cats against GWS a month ago.

His twin brother Kade, who played for Gold Coast and Melbourne, was forced to retire in 2020 due to concussion issues.

World.title: Sydney fugitive arrested in Lebanon accused of running crime syndicate
World.content:
For years, fugitive George Dib had been a mystery.

The son of a respected service station entrepreneur, Mr Dib first appeared on the radar of law enforcement in 2013, then he vanished.

But Australian authorities had been watching.

Mr Dib, arrested last week in Lebanon, is now facing the possibility of spending decades in a Middle Eastern jail over claims he directed a global organised crime syndicate while on the run.

"He is suspected of brokering and organising multiple drug shipments to Australia on behalf of a wide range of criminal syndicates from around the world during the past 11 years," the Australian Federal Police (AFP) said after his capture in Lebanon last week.

His father is not accused of any wrongdoing.

Fugitives join forces overseas

For more than a decade, George Dib has been the source of underworld and police intrigue.

Though never convicted of a crime, Mr Dib was suspected to be part of the "Aussie Cartel", before it was systematically dismantled in Türkiye in 2023.

But according to an intelligence file from the NSW Crime Commission obtained by the ABC, Mr Dib is accused of being a main player in another offshore drug conglomerate.

A NSW Police mugshot of Rafat Alameddine, who has since fled to Lebanon. (Supplied: NSW Police)

The report names Mr Dib alongside fellow Lebanese fugitives Bilal Haouchar and Alameddine crime family boss Rafat Alameddine among other alleged Sydney criminals who joined forces.

Alameddine is wanted by NSW Police accused of two murders at the height of the Alameddines' gang war with the Hamzy family in 2021.

Haouchar himself was sentenced to eight years in jail by a Beirut court in May 2025 for a raft of drug crimes he committed while on the run from Australia.

Haouchar remains locked up in a Lebanese jail after AFP intelligence helped to jail him there. (Supplied: NSW Police)

Mr Dib, Alameddine and Haouchar are accused of sending threatening messages dubbed 'AUS weekly market updates' to Sydney's criminal milieu "in an attempt to set the distribution price of cocaine at $225,000 per kilogram".

Fall of 'The Commission'

It is alleged Mr Dib's coalition of criminals' rise came as another toppled.

The "AUS weekly market updates" landed in the inboxes of gangsters across Sydney in June 2023.

Just days earlier, the final domino of rival drug cartel "The Commission" fell when Alen Moradian was shot dead inside a Bondi car park.

Crime boss Alen Moradian. (Supplied: Nine Entertainment)

The Commission operated under a similar rule of law, spreading similar threatening message throughout the underworld through 2022 to 2023.

"To the drop kick wannabe gangsters who just called out the Commission. "You shouldn't try to claim things you did not know. "We have been dominating Sydney for the past 3 years now and like puppy dogs you have all submitted each time. "We are well aware who is responsible, writing up that message to throw the scene off won't work. "And you/they/them pop your head out of hiding you can bet your dollar we will be there to chop it off. "The weak dog who wrote that message has most likely paid us before and now feeling tough, nevertheless no stone will unturned. No friend will be loyal. "Watch this and you will know what we are about."

Though its authors were not clarified in the NSW Crime Commission intelligence, the following message was spread the day after Moradian was killed.

"To every one trying to call the shots that are hiding in different countries and playing with NSW prices. "We regret to inform your commission we control the prices in NSW from now on. "This is not just a warning but a threat to everyone who thinks they can run the streets here. "All NSW crews have come together to end your so called commission. Please remember the bullets dont rust here especially when you guys want to threaten familys we will also not toelerate this and will respond with kidnapping knee capping and if we hear any of your crews are trying to control prices under your guidelines we will come after anyone from your commission. "You guys will now follow our rules and respect us prices will be dropping at anyones will … "Thank you."

World.title: Alleged 2007 murder at Adelaide party involved 'payback', court told
World.content:
A man standing trial for murder over a fatal birthday party stabbing almost 20 years ago was allegedly among a group of men who stormed the celebrations seeking "payback", a court has heard.

Kimlong Rim, 38, is standing trial in South Australia's Supreme Court after pleading not guilty to the murder of Thea Kheav, 21, outside a party at Parafield Gardens, in Adelaide's north, in December 2007.

Opening the trial on Tuesday, prosecutor Kos Lesses told the jury that while Mr Rim did not inflict the fatal stab wound, he was among a group of four men accused of murdering Mr Kheav.

He said Mr Kheav was a guest at the 18th birthday party, which he had attended with his brothers.

"An argument broke out with one of the Kheav brothers and one of the men from the accused's group," Mr Lesses said.

He told the jury that that man had left the party "in an angry state" but later returned in a convoy of cars with "a large group of men", including Mr Rim and three others allegedly involved in the murder.

"[They] armed themselves with bottles and planks of wood, along with a machete-type knife," Mr Lesses said.

"They arrived at that party as a group and it's alleged they disrupted the party as a group. It's alleged they were working as a team, or a group.

"As a result of that group attack, Thea Kheav was fatally stabbed and died at the scene of this birthday party."

Kimlong Rim (left) is standing trial after pleading not guilty to the 2007 murder of Thea Kheav. (ABC News)

Mr Lesses told the jury the altercation took part in two stages, beginning when Mr Kheav was first struck with a bottle while standing next to a woman.

The jury was also told the second stage involved Mr Kheav's attempt to flee into the backyard of the house.

Mr Lesses said Mr Kheav had tried to climb over gates, but he was pulled to the ground where he was "kicked and punched, along with being stabbed in the chest with a long-bladed knife".

Crime about 'payback', court told

Mr Lesses said that despite the efforts of paramedics, Mr Kheav was unable to be resuscitated.

His cause of death was later determined to be a single stab wound to his chest, but he also had other injuries on his body, including a cut to his face.

Mr Lesses said the alleged crime was "borne out of a retaliation".

"It's about an armed group of men who retaliated by attending as a group to disrupt the party and effect payback on one of the Kheav brothers," Mr Lesses said.

Police attended the scene after a party was held at a Parafield Gardens house. (ABC News: ABC News)

Mr Lesses told the jury the alleged murder weapon was never recovered but had been described as "looking like a machete".

Mr Rim's defence barrister, Ryan Williams SC, told the jury it was not disputed his client was at the party and had "engaged in deplorable behaviour", but he said Mr Rim was not a murderer.

"What is in dispute is this idea that he is a murderer," he said.

" Put simply, ladies and gentlemen, the issues in dispute do not concern whether or not he, together with others, acted generally angrily, violently or whatever … but whether what he did, what he actually had in his mind, make him a murderer. "

Justice Rachael Gray, who is presiding over the trial, urged the 14-person jury to keep an open mind until it retires to consider a verdict.

The trial is expected to continue for three weeks.

World.title: Why a five-hour, 10.35am weekday game with no parking is the hottest ticket in town
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCity life Why a five-hour, 10.35am weekday game with no parking is the hottest ticket in town Cara Waters August 12, 2026 — 12:05am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

If Melbourne employers note an increase in sickies on a Friday morning in September, American football might well be to blame. The MCG will host Australia’s first in-season NFL game on September 11, and demand for a piece of the action is high, with tickets for the game selling out in the first half hour of release. Former NFL star Todd Gurley at Marriott Bonvoy’s W Hotel. Gurley played for the Los Angeles Rams, who will take on the San Francisco 49ers at the MCG in September. Jason South Pubs and hotels across Melbourne are preparing for an influx of NFL fans from overseas and interstate to watch the Los Angeles Rams and the San Francisco 49ers. Todd Gurley, a former Rams player, is in Melbourne as a Marriott Bonvoy ambassador ahead of the event, which is expected to attract a crowd of 100,000.



“I’ve talked to a lot of people; they’re just super-excited about it,” he said from the penthouse suite of the W Hotel. “I mean playing at the G is just legendary ... I know everybody’s pumped.” Related Article Exclusive

City life The art of the deal: Victoria to pay millions more than host cities overseas to bring NFL to Melbourne Gurley said the game was “a little bit early”, starting at 10.35am, a time aimed squarely at a US television audience, but said fans could expect a good contest in what would be the first NFL game of the season. “The NFL did think highly of Melbourne to give them two good teams instead of sending two trash teams over here,” he said. “I would say that they got two winners.” Gurley said Australian fans watching the game should be prepared for a long game that would last a minimum of four hours.



“It will be a lot of TV timeouts,” he said. “There will be hydration breaks out there, we call it, but it will give the fans more time to go grab a beverage.” Gurley and fellow Marriott ambassador Dylan Alcott said they expected Australians to get into the spirit early, inspired by the tailgate parties at NFL games in the United States out of cars and trucks parked around the ground. Fans tailgate in the car park before a Dallas Cowboys game in Arlington, Texas. Getty Images “I can safely say Australians and Melburnians don’t mind tailgating at 6am,” Alcott said. “They will find a way.” There will be no public parking, and therefore no tailgating at the MCG car parks, but an NFL Kickoff Festival will be held at Melbourne Park with NFL exhibits, flag football clinics, watch parties and an American food village. The Glasshouse in Olympic Park will host Australia’s Best Tailgate.



Marmont restaurant at Crown will be a base for the Los Angeles Rams during the event, and owner Grant Smillie said the venue would show the game and then host an after-party for Rams fans. Related Article Updated

American Football Tickets to Australia’s first NFL game went on sale. 26 minutes later, they were nearly all gone “With the novelty of an early morning start, by 2pm there will be a lot of people looking for sustenance after having breakfast beers,” Smillie said. “I think it is going to be an unofficial public holiday.” Over at the Waterside Hotel, manager Tommy Ellison said the pub was serving a special American-inspired menu of Buffalo chicken wings with blue cheese ranch, mozzarella sticks, spicy fried chicken burgers, glazed barbecue pork ribs and buckets of Budweiser beer. “It used to be a bit of a niche sport for Australians to follow,” he said. “But people are really getting into it.”



This masthead revealed that the multi-year contract secured by the Victorian government is likely to cost taxpayers between $10 million and $15 million per game, but Ellison said he thought the price was worth it. “The timing’s a bit weird,” he said. “It is very early on a Friday, so that does mean that people aren’t going to drink as they would on a Friday or Saturday night. From what we’re seeing here at least, I do believe it will be a really, really big weekend for Melbourne and for the economy.” Todd Gurley in his playing days for the Los Angeles Rams. Getty Images Data released by the state government shows fans from more than 35 countries have already bought tickets to the game, and almost 50 per cent of spectators at the MCG are expected to be from interstate or overseas. Hotel occupancy in the Melbourne CBD is up 39 per cent for the night of the game compared to the same day last year.



Minister for Major Events Anthony Carbines said events such as the NFL game were “economic powerhouses”, filling hotels, supporting jobs and putting Victoria on the world stage. The game will be screened as a standalone Thursday night football fixture in the United States, and Netflix’s global broadcast will reach more than 200 countries. “When viewers see Melbourne on their screens, they book flights and plan their next holiday here,” Carbines said. World.title: May the choice be with you: The next great Star Wars story might be a game
World.content:
TechnologyVideo games May the choice be with you: The next great Star Wars story might be a game Tim Biggs August 12, 2026 — 12:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Pinning down a squad of battle droids behind half-destroyed durasteel cover isn’t about fast reflexes or swinging a lightsaber; it’s about cold, hard calculations. And friends you can rely on. You pick out a line of sight, order your sniper to higher ground, set your flanker to overwatch and run the percentages, knowing that one wrong move could cost you a veteran soldier forever. Due to be released later this month, Star Wars: Zero Company is a game that trades fast-paced blockbuster action for the calculated tension of galactic chess. It’s the first time we’ve seen the galaxy far, far away represented as a turn-based tactics game (a fan-favourite genre that includes Fire Emblem, X-COM and Final Fantasy Tactics). But on top of that, the game is also angling to become a top-tier Star Wars story, albeit one that changes in the details from player to player. Nothing says Star Wars like a rag-tag group of misfits getting to know each other in the thick of it. Zero Company is set in the prequel era, during the war between the Republic’s clone army and the Separatist’s droids. Players take the role of Hawks – a former soldier now running a mercenary company – tapped by the galactic government to stop a shady cult called the Infinite Coil, which worships an infectious disease and has been invading planets to soften them up for Separatist control. But while the wider story is one of galactic intrigue and mysterious power, the game is also about more intimate narratives. Hawks is joined by many colleagues who could have been taken out of any Star Wars film or TV show – aliens, astromechs, clones, even a Mandalorian — who all have their own personalities and agendas, as well as their own abilities in battle.



Star Wars in live action has had success branching out to narratives beyond the Skywalkers and Palpatines, including with Rogue One and Andor. Animated series have delved into more mystical aspects of The Force, which seems to be where the Coil is headed. But in games, the franchise has recently been better recognised for its gameplay and spectacle than its story, as in Star Wars Jedi: Fallen Order. In Zero Company you can set a high difficulty for expert level hardcore, or a low one to relax and enjoy the story. Lucasfilm Games executive producer Orion Kellogg, who supervises external development of Star Wars games, said the brand didn’t set out to tell certain stories in certain ways. It looks to find creators with a distinct vision and match their story with the interactive medium that fits it best. “Our measuring stick here is our storyteller,” Kellog said. “Do they have something to say? Is there a reason why they’re poking into new territory?”



“We always want to tell the next great Star Wars story, and that could be a TV show, it could be a movie, it could be a comic, or it could be a game. And if we want to tell that story in the game space, we want to tell it in a way that makes for an awesome game.” Finding a sweet spot between hard-nosed strategy and broad-appeal storytelling requires a team that understands the genre inside out. Zero Company is developed by a new studio called Bit Reactor, composed of many staff formerly of Firaxis Games, which is known for its tactical expertise. Characters are all customisable in one way or another, but some have authored stories while others are recruits you mould from scratch. Game director Greg Foertsch worked on X-COM 2, Civilization IV, Marvel’s Midnight Suns and many other tactics games before founding Bit Reactor. He said Zero Company was designed to bring out the best of tactics and of Star Wars by having the two elements lean on each other. Unlike Midnight Suns, which some players criticised for lacking the risk of permanent death found in X-COM, the new game strikes a balance between character-building and peril. That’s why you won’t spend your time playing as Yoda or Obi-Wan.



“Choice and consequence is very important to us, and I think in order for your decisions to have weight, the characters do need to be new,” Foertsch said. “They need to be characters that you could lose. If you’re playing with only characters that are iconic, and have a storyline after the game, it takes the teeth out of everything.” So instead of playing as iconic characters, you get iconic Star Wars elements constantly orbiting original authored characters, recruits you design yourself, and a complex tactical game with a constellation of interlocking systems. As you progress, the characters grow, specialise in the areas of combat you chose, reveal more about themselves and develop relationships with each other. Which also strengthens them on the field, and raises the stakes. Skirmishes take place from a top-down perspective, with the player managing what each unit does with their pool of action points each turn. In my testing of an early version of the game, my Hawks was a sniper (the character is fully customisable in appearance and skills) with a special ability to take a shot that never misses, so I would generally put him up high to support as others rushed in. But a pistol-focused Hawks might have an ability that refunds ability points when you defeat an enemy, so you’d want them to brazenly rush into danger so they can take out many units consecutively without missing.



It’s a blast taking on familiar droids and ruffians, but acolytes of the Coil add an extra wrinkle as they tend to strengthen or mutate their teammates when they die. Players are basically omniscient, though, in their ability to see exactly what will happen in response to each action they take (or, in some cases, a percentage chance), and you can take all the time you want to get it right. X-COM fans will click with the cover system right away and start calculating the best order of operations for their team, but there’s a bonding system that also extends the strategic play into the narrative. As two characters work together, they not only grow to like each other more, but they unlock upgrades that make each one more capable. Lead designer James Brawley, who also worked on X-COM 2, said he referred to the bonding system as the sewing needle of the game. It brings players who are here for the tactics, and players who are here for the Star Wars story, onto the same thread. “[For a tactics player], as you maximise one of your favourite operators, you get kind of invested in their fate and their relationships with everyone else,” Brawley said. “But if you’re approaching this from the narrative side, you really like Tel’s story, you really like Luco’s story, you want to use those characters. And as you do, then they get stronger.”



Hawks can also build bonds in the game’s hub area, where missions are planned. Players can talk to other characters, help solve their problems, and even unlock missions and stories to resolve. Occasionally, a dilemma occurs during an operation and the player has to decide which way to go. Each solution will show how in favour or opposed each squad member is, and the decision will affect their relationship. If an authored character dies, their specific missions and the potential outcomes of their relationships will be locked off. On the battlefield, synergy between teammates is always vital in these kinds of games. If, for example, you put an operator in overwatch (meaning they will fire on an enemy that crosses their path), you could use another to blast or lure a bad guy into danger. The bonding makes for an additional incentive, which also feeds into the story. In my game I noticed characters who had a better bond were more likely to shout out during combat, to congratulate their friend on a smart play. According to narrative director Aaron Contreras, these dynamic relationships were designed to reflect organic military banter directly onto the battlefield, ensuring the story evolves naturally through gameplay rather than just cutscenes. Each player will get different story beats, different dialogue at different times, depending on who gets along with whom, and which characters stay alive.



Editor's pick Review

Video games James Bond’s battle with AI is his most human story yet “When operators really dislike each other or really like each other, you’ll unlock different reactions. You’ll see nicknames forming, or they’re really mean to each other … when somebody misses an easy shot,” he said. “The fantasy here is one of leadership and management. Whether you’re in a mission or in the hub, we want to make that an immersive world where narrative and tactics are constantly bouncing off each other.” For Star Wars fans who have never touched a turn-based grid in their lives, the jump into tactical strategy might sound daunting. But the team insists the game has been designed with an easy ramp-up, offering a dedicated story difficulty mode that gives players massive margins for error so they can enjoy the narrative without high-pressure stress. Having only played the opening few hours, I don’t have a full idea of where the story will go or how the semi-randomised permutations will mesh with my choices in a satisfying way. But there are heaps of potential in both the tactical gameplay and the relationship system, which could become one of the most engrossing Star Wars narratives in recent years if it delivers. World.title: Coalition wants to bring migration down to lowest level since Global Financial Crisis
World.content:
PoliticsFederalImmigration Coalition wants to bring migration down to lowest level since Global Financial Crisis Natassia Chrysanthos August 12, 2026 — 12:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Coalition wants to bring migration down to its lowest level since the Global Financial Crisis, and is preparing to argue that visas for students, graduates and backpackers must be cut so that housing construction can keep pace with inflows of new arrivals. Opposition housing spokesman Senator Andrew Bragg will on Wednesday reveal the Coalition will seek to take net overseas migration levels under 180,000 people per year on average – a target that is 45,000 lower than Labor’s short-term forecasts, and 120,000 below last year’s intake. Housing spokesman Andrew Bragg. Alex Ellinghausen The new detail on the heated question of net overseas migration, also known as NOM, will inject fresh energy into the debate over optimum migration levels and how to achieve them amid public concern that immigration has been too high since the pandemic. “Lifting migration standards, and analysing them carefully each year, is crucial to ensure integrity and public trust in our migration settings,” Bragg will tell the National Press Club on Wednesday.





Cabinet sources said the plan was not revisited at this week’s Monday cabinet meeting, and the government was still working through the social and economic trade-offs. The migration system has been largely demand-driven for the last two decades. Sources on both sides of politics privately concede that net migration won’t get any lower without more drastic changes. Some parts of the migration system will remain outside the government’s control, such as the soaring number of New Zealanders and British backpackers, because they moved to Australia under free trade agreements that stipulate numbers cannot be capped. But that creates impetus for tighter controls in other parts of the visa system – such as working backpackers, international students, graduate visas, refugees and skilled visas. Bragg will argue that it is possible to find deep cuts in a short time. “A NOM reduction on this scale is manageable and in line with reductions we have managed in recent history,” he will say.



“For example, in 2009-10 when NOM declined from 300,000 to 175,000 in around 18 months.” That surge and fall, however, came after the Global Financial Crisis, as Australians living abroad rushed home and the government cut tens of thousands of skilled migrant places to save local jobs in the economic downturn. Related Article Exclusive

Immigration Multicultural grants brawl: Coalition accuses Labor of funding ‘ghettoisation’ Australia last averaged net migration levels between 180,000 and 200,000 between 2014 and 2016. Before that, net migration levels were last consistently below 180,000 under the Howard government. Labor has sought to discredit the Coalition on migration by pointing out the opposition has not been willing to name which parts of the migration system it wanted to cut.



In a sign the debate has shifted, Bragg will name family visas, international students, working holidaymakers and post-study work visas as areas for “modest reductions”. At the same time, he wants to bring in a higher share of skilled migrant workers linked to jobs that meet Australian industry needs, such as construction. The NSW senator, who is a moderate, said last year that the Coalition’s chances were damaged at the 2025 election when the public thought the opposition blamed migrants for the housing crisis. To explain the target, Bragg will say that Australia’s population increased by 1.8 million people since mid-2022, 1.5 million of whom came through net overseas migration. However, dwelling stock in that time increased by 550,000 – under census assumptions that each dwelling hosts 2.6 people, this leaves a shortfall of 130,000 dwellings for about 340,000 people.



“If we win, each year the connection between migration and housing will be reported on to ensure that housing stock and related completions can support the annual migration intake,” Bragg will say. “The specific shortfall relating to housing created under Labor can be closed over the Budget forward estimates period by averaging a NOM of under 180,000.” Bragg will also explain plans for cutting back the National Construction Code to speed up housing supply. With Paul Sakkal

World.title: Coalition demands AFP probe of diplomatic cables over PM’s melon gaffe
World.content:
PoliticsFederalPolitical leadership Coalition demands AFP probe of diplomatic cables over PM’s melon gaffe James Massola August 11, 2026 — 10:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The federal opposition is demanding a police investigation into the apparent leaking of a diplomatic note sent by the Japanese government to its counterparts in Canberra, after details of the note were published in media outlets. The diplomatic note, dated July 13 and sent by the government in Tokyo, addressed Prime Minister Anthony Albanese’s appearance on the Bush Deep podcast with Nikki Osborne on July 3, during which the comedian made a joke to the prime minister about Japanese prime minister Sanae Takaichi smuggling in crown melons under her shirt “like Pamela Anderson” to present as a gift to Albanese. Loading The prime minister gestured with both hands in front of his chest as he told Osborne his Japanese counterpart had given him a couple of melons as a gift. While the comment mostly escaped scrutiny when the podcast was first published, a piece in the English-language Japanese Times in late July lamented the comment. This week, former Japanese ambassador to Australia Shingo Yamagami wrote a critical opinion piece in The Australian that labelled Albanese’s gesture “insulting” and ignorant.



Several media outlets have since published extracts of the diplomatic note sent to Canberra from Tokyo, which noted “sensationalised reporting in the Australian media” about the podcast interview and which undertook that “no action” would be taken over the incident. The note also stressed that the melons were not smuggled but bought locally. The sharing of this letter prompted the opposition’s defence spokesman James Paterson and foreign affairs spokesman Ted O’Brien to write to Australian Federal Police commissioner Krissy Barrett and ask for an investigation into the leak. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese arrives for question time on Tuesday. Alex Ellinghausen “We write to refer the possibly unlawful disclosure of confidential and sensitive correspondence from the Government of Japan to the Department of Prime Minister and Cabinet,” the pair wrote.



“We are concerned that a diplomatic note with a critical bilateral partner has potentially been provided to the media without authorisation. Given that communications between governments can be classified, it is possible that this disclosure is a criminal offence under Division 122 of the Commonwealth Criminal Code. “It is critically important that Australia’s bilateral partners believe that their confidential correspondence will be handled appropriately by the Australian government. It would be gravely damaging to our national interest if they formed the view the Australian government does not take unauthorised disclosure seriously by promptly investigating it.” The Coalition pursued Albanese over the matter in question time on Tuesday, with backbench MP Mary Aldred twice asking the prime minister if he would apologise to Takaichi to repair relations between the two countries. Related Article Analysis

Political leadership Albanese’s attempts to talk to everyone bear bitter fruit when he goes off script Albanese did not accept the premise of the question and talked up both his friendship with Takaichi, and the growing strength of the strategic relationship between the two countries - before sitting down and cutting his answer short.



In the Senate, Paterson pressed Foreign Affairs Minister Penny Wong over the matter, suggesting the decision to share Japan’s letter was a “desperate attempt to clean up the prime minister’s self-inflicted melon mess” that risked a critical bilateral relationship. Wong accused the opposition of “confecting a diplomatic issue”. Senior government ministers including Tanya Plibersek, Katy Gallagher and Murray Watt have all defended the prime minister on Monday and Tuesday this week. “I completed the census (C8) but don’t understand why there wasn’t a question about ‘fur babies’,” writes Natasha Lee of Alexandria. “Many of us consider our pets to be an important part of the family. The presence of pets paints a more detailed picture of our households, so why are they excluded?”

Here’s hoping Alan Phillips of Mosman doesn’t commit a capital offence: “My wife and I had planned to be in Canberra this week for some walking, cycling and galleries. Checking the weather predictions — freezing temperatures and rain — made us decide to postpone. But shock horror! We’d already filled in our census online which said we would be there. We were now stuck with it or risk possible arrest and imprisonment for lying to the Commonwealth.”

Sticking with the statistics, George Manojlovic of Mangerton says, “Obviously Jack Dikian finds crunching the numbers enlightening. He must have woken Tuesday morning and thought, ‘At last! I’ve finally come to my census!’”

“I believe the Wests Tigers approached the Pope (C8) to play five-eighth next year,” reports Peter Miniutti of Ashbury. “He respectfully declined the offer giving the excuse that not even God could save them.”

Regarding Nola Tucker’s opera (C8) commentary, John Boddington of Dalton reckons “there is really only one plot in opera. According to the comedian Ed Gardner: ‘Opera is when a guy gets stabbed in the back and, instead of bleeding, he sings’.”

World.title: Educators on the line in proposed Zoos Victoria job cuts
World.content:
PoliticsVictoriaAnimals Educators on the line in proposed Zoos Victoria job cuts Kieran Rooney August 11, 2026 — 7:51pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

More than a third of educator positions could be cut from Zoos Victoria under proposed redundancies, prompting fears the visits by 150,000 students each year will be cut and the standard of teaching affected. The Age revealed in June that Zoos Victoria was preparing a restructure that would cut up to 70 full-time roles from its 950-strong workforce – a figure the organisation has pushed back on as it consults staff about the changes. Among the most contentious proposals is a 38 per cent reduction in education staff at Melbourne Zoo – from roughly 6.2 full-time staff to 3.8 – who assist in teaching students and other groups about wildlife and conservation. A baby giraffe at Melbourne Zoo. Jo Howell The Community and Public Sector Union and United Workers Union said on Monday that about 600 staff – almost two-thirds of the organisation’s workforce – had responded to the proposed changes, which would be finalised later this month.



CPSU state secretary Jiselle Hanna said any cuts to education staff would devastate the 150,000 students who visited Melbourne Zoo, Werribee Zoo, Healesville Sanctuary and Kyabram Fauna Park every year. Related Article Animals Bailout backing was offered to Zoos Victoria a year before job cuts “Staff are telling us that they will not be able to maintain the volume of visits or the standard of education for young learners if these cuts go ahead,” Hanna said. “If this restructure is genuinely being driven by financial pressures, then why would cuts be made to an entity that brings in millions of dollars annually through school visits? “The impacted staff are highly skilled workers with decades of experience. They keep visitors educated, entertained and, most importantly, safe.”



The CPSU and the United Workers Union have urgently demanded Zoos Victoria wind back the scale of the cuts, arguing it will have flow-on effects across all parts of the organisation as staff are asked to handle new responsibilities. “This restructure process has demonstrated how out of touch the executive team is with the realities of the zoo and the work that zoo staff undertake,” Hanna said. A Zoos Victoria spokesperson said frontline services would not be impacted, as official consultation continued before a final decision was announced on August 25. “Our employees have provided valuable feedback through this consultation process, and we are considering this feedback carefully,” the spokesperson said. “Zoos Victoria will remain a world-class wildlife destination, and our commitment to fighting wildlife extinction remains.”



The Age has previously reported staff concerns that the restructure could also affect wildlife and conservation roles across the organisation, however, Zoos Victoria says frontline and animal care roles will not be directly affected. Related Article Animals Zoos Victoria to cut up to 70 jobs, including in conservation and wildlife Animal Justice Party MP Georgie Purcell said Zoos Victoria should be upfront about what the cuts would mean for conservation programs. “With bird flu ravaging our state and our volunteer wildlife carers under enormous strain, we simply can’t afford to lose any of the dedicated Zoos Victoria teams whose job it is to respond to injured wildlife and protect threatened species,” she said. “It’s simply not good enough to say there won’t be cuts to frontline services without being clear about what happens to the conservation and wildlife rescue work that sits behind them.”

World.title: Why a five-hour, 10.35am weekday game with no parking is the hottest ticket in town
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCity life Why a five-hour, 10.35am weekday game with no parking is the hottest ticket in town Cara Waters August 12, 2026 — 12:05am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

If Melbourne employers note an increase in sickies on a Friday morning in September, American football might well be to blame. The MCG will host Australia’s first in-season NFL game on September 11, and demand for a piece of the action is high, with tickets for the game selling out in the first half hour of release. Former NFL star Todd Gurley at Marriott Bonvoy’s W Hotel. Gurley played for the Los Angeles Rams, who will take on the San Francisco 49ers at the MCG in September. Jason South Pubs and hotels across Melbourne are preparing for an influx of NFL fans from overseas and interstate to watch the Los Angeles Rams and the San Francisco 49ers. Todd Gurley, a former Rams player, is in Melbourne as a Marriott Bonvoy ambassador ahead of the event, which is expected to attract a crowd of 100,000.



“I’ve talked to a lot of people; they’re just super-excited about it,” he said from the penthouse suite of the W Hotel. “I mean playing at the G is just legendary ... I know everybody’s pumped.” Related Article Exclusive

City life The art of the deal: Victoria to pay millions more than host cities overseas to bring NFL to Melbourne Gurley said the game was “a little bit early”, starting at 10.35am, a time aimed squarely at a US television audience, but said fans could expect a good contest in what would be the first NFL game of the season. “The NFL did think highly of Melbourne to give them two good teams instead of sending two trash teams over here,” he said. “I would say that they got two winners.” Gurley said Australian fans watching the game should be prepared for a long game that would last a minimum of four hours.



“It will be a lot of TV timeouts,” he said. “There will be hydration breaks out there, we call it, but it will give the fans more time to go grab a beverage.” Gurley and fellow Marriott ambassador Dylan Alcott said they expected Australians to get into the spirit early, inspired by the tailgate parties at NFL games in the United States out of cars and trucks parked around the ground. Fans tailgate in the car park before a Dallas Cowboys game in Arlington, Texas. Getty Images “I can safely say Australians and Melburnians don’t mind tailgating at 6am,” Alcott said. “They will find a way.” There will be no public parking, and therefore no tailgating at the MCG car parks, but an NFL Kickoff Festival will be held at Melbourne Park with NFL exhibits, flag football clinics, watch parties and an American food village. The Glasshouse in Olympic Park will host Australia’s Best Tailgate.



Marmont restaurant at Crown will be a base for the Los Angeles Rams during the event, and owner Grant Smillie said the venue would show the game and then host an after-party for Rams fans. Related Article Updated

American Football Tickets to Australia’s first NFL game went on sale. 26 minutes later, they were nearly all gone “With the novelty of an early morning start, by 2pm there will be a lot of people looking for sustenance after having breakfast beers,” Smillie said. “I think it is going to be an unofficial public holiday.” Over at the Waterside Hotel, manager Tommy Ellison said the pub was serving a special American-inspired menu of Buffalo chicken wings with blue cheese ranch, mozzarella sticks, spicy fried chicken burgers, glazed barbecue pork ribs and buckets of Budweiser beer. “It used to be a bit of a niche sport for Australians to follow,” he said. “But people are really getting into it.”



This masthead revealed that the multi-year contract secured by the Victorian government is likely to cost taxpayers between $10 million and $15 million per game, but Ellison said he thought the price was worth it. “The timing’s a bit weird,” he said. “It is very early on a Friday, so that does mean that people aren’t going to drink as they would on a Friday or Saturday night. From what we’re seeing here at least, I do believe it will be a really, really big weekend for Melbourne and for the economy.” Todd Gurley in his playing days for the Los Angeles Rams. Getty Images Data released by the state government shows fans from more than 35 countries have already bought tickets to the game, and almost 50 per cent of spectators at the MCG are expected to be from interstate or overseas. Hotel occupancy in the Melbourne CBD is up 39 per cent for the night of the game compared to the same day last year.



Minister for Major Events Anthony Carbines said events such as the NFL game were “economic powerhouses”, filling hotels, supporting jobs and putting Victoria on the world stage. The game will be screened as a standalone Thursday night football fixture in the United States, and Netflix’s global broadcast will reach more than 200 countries. “When viewers see Melbourne on their screens, they book flights and plan their next holiday here,” Carbines said. World.title: May the choice be with you: The next great Star Wars story might be a game
World.content:
TechnologyVideo games May the choice be with you: The next great Star Wars story might be a game Tim Biggs August 12, 2026 — 12:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Pinning down a squad of battle droids behind half-destroyed durasteel cover isn’t about fast reflexes or swinging a lightsaber; it’s about cold, hard calculations. And friends you can rely on. You pick out a line of sight, order your sniper to higher ground, set your flanker to overwatch and run the percentages, knowing that one wrong move could cost you a veteran soldier forever. Due to be released later this month, Star Wars: Zero Company is a game that trades fast-paced blockbuster action for the calculated tension of galactic chess. It’s the first time we’ve seen the galaxy far, far away represented as a turn-based tactics game (a fan-favourite genre that includes Fire Emblem, X-COM and Final Fantasy Tactics). But on top of that, the game is also angling to become a top-tier Star Wars story, albeit one that changes in the details from player to player. Nothing says Star Wars like a rag-tag group of misfits getting to know each other in the thick of it. Zero Company is set in the prequel era, during the war between the Republic’s clone army and the Separatist’s droids. Players take the role of Hawks – a former soldier now running a mercenary company – tapped by the galactic government to stop a shady cult called the Infinite Coil, which worships an infectious disease and has been invading planets to soften them up for Separatist control. But while the wider story is one of galactic intrigue and mysterious power, the game is also about more intimate narratives. Hawks is joined by many colleagues who could have been taken out of any Star Wars film or TV show – aliens, astromechs, clones, even a Mandalorian — who all have their own personalities and agendas, as well as their own abilities in battle.



Star Wars in live action has had success branching out to narratives beyond the Skywalkers and Palpatines, including with Rogue One and Andor. Animated series have delved into more mystical aspects of The Force, which seems to be where the Coil is headed. But in games, the franchise has recently been better recognised for its gameplay and spectacle than its story, as in Star Wars Jedi: Fallen Order. In Zero Company you can set a high difficulty for expert level hardcore, or a low one to relax and enjoy the story. Lucasfilm Games executive producer Orion Kellogg, who supervises external development of Star Wars games, said the brand didn’t set out to tell certain stories in certain ways. It looks to find creators with a distinct vision and match their story with the interactive medium that fits it best. “Our measuring stick here is our storyteller,” Kellog said. “Do they have something to say? Is there a reason why they’re poking into new territory?”



“We always want to tell the next great Star Wars story, and that could be a TV show, it could be a movie, it could be a comic, or it could be a game. And if we want to tell that story in the game space, we want to tell it in a way that makes for an awesome game.” Finding a sweet spot between hard-nosed strategy and broad-appeal storytelling requires a team that understands the genre inside out. Zero Company is developed by a new studio called Bit Reactor, composed of many staff formerly of Firaxis Games, which is known for its tactical expertise. Characters are all customisable in one way or another, but some have authored stories while others are recruits you mould from scratch. Game director Greg Foertsch worked on X-COM 2, Civilization IV, Marvel’s Midnight Suns and many other tactics games before founding Bit Reactor. He said Zero Company was designed to bring out the best of tactics and of Star Wars by having the two elements lean on each other. Unlike Midnight Suns, which some players criticised for lacking the risk of permanent death found in X-COM, the new game strikes a balance between character-building and peril. That’s why you won’t spend your time playing as Yoda or Obi-Wan.



“Choice and consequence is very important to us, and I think in order for your decisions to have weight, the characters do need to be new,” Foertsch said. “They need to be characters that you could lose. If you’re playing with only characters that are iconic, and have a storyline after the game, it takes the teeth out of everything.” So instead of playing as iconic characters, you get iconic Star Wars elements constantly orbiting original authored characters, recruits you design yourself, and a complex tactical game with a constellation of interlocking systems. As you progress, the characters grow, specialise in the areas of combat you chose, reveal more about themselves and develop relationships with each other. Which also strengthens them on the field, and raises the stakes. Skirmishes take place from a top-down perspective, with the player managing what each unit does with their pool of action points each turn. In my testing of an early version of the game, my Hawks was a sniper (the character is fully customisable in appearance and skills) with a special ability to take a shot that never misses, so I would generally put him up high to support as others rushed in. But a pistol-focused Hawks might have an ability that refunds ability points when you defeat an enemy, so you’d want them to brazenly rush into danger so they can take out many units consecutively without missing.



It’s a blast taking on familiar droids and ruffians, but acolytes of the Coil add an extra wrinkle as they tend to strengthen or mutate their teammates when they die. Players are basically omniscient, though, in their ability to see exactly what will happen in response to each action they take (or, in some cases, a percentage chance), and you can take all the time you want to get it right. X-COM fans will click with the cover system right away and start calculating the best order of operations for their team, but there’s a bonding system that also extends the strategic play into the narrative. As two characters work together, they not only grow to like each other more, but they unlock upgrades that make each one more capable. Lead designer James Brawley, who also worked on X-COM 2, said he referred to the bonding system as the sewing needle of the game. It brings players who are here for the tactics, and players who are here for the Star Wars story, onto the same thread. “[For a tactics player], as you maximise one of your favourite operators, you get kind of invested in their fate and their relationships with everyone else,” Brawley said. “But if you’re approaching this from the narrative side, you really like Tel’s story, you really like Luco’s story, you want to use those characters. And as you do, then they get stronger.”



Hawks can also build bonds in the game’s hub area, where missions are planned. Players can talk to other characters, help solve their problems, and even unlock missions and stories to resolve. Occasionally, a dilemma occurs during an operation and the player has to decide which way to go. Each solution will show how in favour or opposed each squad member is, and the decision will affect their relationship. If an authored character dies, their specific missions and the potential outcomes of their relationships will be locked off. On the battlefield, synergy between teammates is always vital in these kinds of games. If, for example, you put an operator in overwatch (meaning they will fire on an enemy that crosses their path), you could use another to blast or lure a bad guy into danger. The bonding makes for an additional incentive, which also feeds into the story. In my game I noticed characters who had a better bond were more likely to shout out during combat, to congratulate their friend on a smart play. According to narrative director Aaron Contreras, these dynamic relationships were designed to reflect organic military banter directly onto the battlefield, ensuring the story evolves naturally through gameplay rather than just cutscenes. Each player will get different story beats, different dialogue at different times, depending on who gets along with whom, and which characters stay alive.



Editor's pick Review

Video games James Bond’s battle with AI is his most human story yet “When operators really dislike each other or really like each other, you’ll unlock different reactions. You’ll see nicknames forming, or they’re really mean to each other … when somebody misses an easy shot,” he said. “The fantasy here is one of leadership and management. Whether you’re in a mission or in the hub, we want to make that an immersive world where narrative and tactics are constantly bouncing off each other.” For Star Wars fans who have never touched a turn-based grid in their lives, the jump into tactical strategy might sound daunting. But the team insists the game has been designed with an easy ramp-up, offering a dedicated story difficulty mode that gives players massive margins for error so they can enjoy the narrative without high-pressure stress. Having only played the opening few hours, I don’t have a full idea of where the story will go or how the semi-randomised permutations will mesh with my choices in a satisfying way. But there are heaps of potential in both the tactical gameplay and the relationship system, which could become one of the most engrossing Star Wars narratives in recent years if it delivers.
