World.title: Coalition wants to bring migration down to lowest level since Global Financial Crisis
World.content:
PoliticsFederalImmigration Coalition wants to bring migration down to lowest level since Global Financial Crisis Natassia Chrysanthos August 12, 2026 — 12:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Coalition wants to bring migration down to its lowest level since the Global Financial Crisis, and is preparing to argue that visas for students, graduates and backpackers must be cut so that housing construction can keep pace with inflows of new arrivals. Opposition housing spokesman Senator Andrew Bragg will on Wednesday reveal the Coalition will seek to take net overseas migration levels under 180,000 people per year on average – a target that is 45,000 lower than Labor’s short-term forecasts, and 120,000 below last year’s intake. Housing spokesman Andrew Bragg. Alex Ellinghausen The new detail on the heated question of net overseas migration, also known as NOM, will inject fresh energy into the debate over optimum migration levels and how to achieve them amid public concern that immigration has been too high since the pandemic. “Lifting migration standards, and analysing them carefully each year, is crucial to ensure integrity and public trust in our migration settings,” Bragg will tell the National Press Club on Wednesday.





Cabinet sources said the plan was not revisited at this week’s Monday cabinet meeting, and the government was still working through the social and economic trade-offs. The migration system has been largely demand-driven for the last two decades. Sources on both sides of politics privately concede that net migration won’t get any lower without more drastic changes. Some parts of the migration system will remain outside the government’s control, such as the soaring number of New Zealanders and British backpackers, because they moved to Australia under free trade agreements that stipulate numbers cannot be capped. But that creates impetus for tighter controls in other parts of the visa system – such as working backpackers, international students, graduate visas, refugees and skilled visas. Bragg will argue that it is possible to find deep cuts in a short time. “A NOM reduction on this scale is manageable and in line with reductions we have managed in recent history,” he will say.



“For example, in 2009-10 when NOM declined from 300,000 to 175,000 in around 18 months.” That surge and fall, however, came after the Global Financial Crisis, as Australians living abroad rushed home and the government cut tens of thousands of skilled migrant places to save local jobs in the economic downturn. Related Article Exclusive

Immigration Multicultural grants brawl: Coalition accuses Labor of funding ‘ghettoisation’ Australia last averaged net migration levels between 180,000 and 200,000 between 2014 and 2016. Before that, net migration levels were last consistently below 180,000 under the Howard government. Labor has sought to discredit the Coalition on migration by pointing out the opposition has not been willing to name which parts of the migration system it wanted to cut.



In a sign the debate has shifted, Bragg will name family visas, international students, working holidaymakers and post-study work visas as areas for “modest reductions”. At the same time, he wants to bring in a higher share of skilled migrant workers linked to jobs that meet Australian industry needs, such as construction. The NSW senator, who is a moderate, said last year that the Coalition’s chances were damaged at the 2025 election when the public thought the opposition blamed migrants for the housing crisis. To explain the target, Bragg will say that Australia’s population increased by 1.8 million people since mid-2022, 1.5 million of whom came through net overseas migration. However, dwelling stock in that time increased by 550,000 – under census assumptions that each dwelling hosts 2.6 people, this leaves a shortfall of 130,000 dwellings for about 340,000 people.



“If we win, each year the connection between migration and housing will be reported on to ensure that housing stock and related completions can support the annual migration intake,” Bragg will say. “The specific shortfall relating to housing created under Labor can be closed over the Budget forward estimates period by averaging a NOM of under 180,000.” Bragg will also explain plans for cutting back the National Construction Code to speed up housing supply. With Paul Sakkal

Welcome to the new-look Superquiz! Easier to play on your mobile, the new quiz features a fresh design and more interactive features. Click here to tell us what you think of the new format. Got questions or want to know more? Scroll past the quiz to see our FAQs. By Harry Hollinsworth



The question and answer to #9 has been corrected. Why has the quiz changed? Our new quiz format is faster, smoother and easier to play on your mobile. We’ve also introduced several new features. For the first time, you’ll see how other players scored in real time and be able to share your result with friends and family on Facebook, X and WhatsApp. We have more exciting updates on the horizon too. Tell us what you think about the new experience here. We’re keen to hear from you.



Although it has a new look, this is the same Superquiz you know and love. Our regular quizmaster is excited to put your general knowledge to the test with a new set of 15 crafty questions every day. Can I see the number of questions in the quiz? Yes, the total number of questions is displayed next to the progress bar at the top of the quiz. The number of your current question is also shown (e.g. 3/15). Want to keep track of your score? You can find a running tally in green at the top right of the quiz. Can I see all the quiz questions at a glance?



No, we challenge players to complete the quiz one question at a time. When I answer a question, there’s a percentage next to the correct and incorrect answers. Why? Thanks for noticing! This is a new addition to the quiz. It lets you track how your score compares to other readers by showing the percentage of players who chose that particular answer. It will also help you gauge the difficulty of each question after you’ve answered. Can I reset the quiz for other players on my device? Yes, click or tap ‘Play Again’ at the end of the results screen to reset the quiz.

World.title: Coalition demands AFP probe of diplomatic cables over PM’s melon gaffe
World.content:
PoliticsFederalPolitical leadership Coalition demands AFP probe of diplomatic cables over PM’s melon gaffe James Massola August 11, 2026 — 10:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The federal opposition is demanding a police investigation into the apparent leaking of a diplomatic note sent by the Japanese government to its counterparts in Canberra, after details of the note were published in media outlets. The diplomatic note, dated July 13 and sent by the government in Tokyo, addressed Prime Minister Anthony Albanese’s appearance on the Bush Deep podcast with Nikki Osborne on July 3, during which the comedian made a joke to the prime minister about Japanese prime minister Sanae Takaichi smuggling in crown melons under her shirt “like Pamela Anderson” to present as a gift to Albanese. Loading The prime minister gestured with both hands in front of his chest as he told Osborne his Japanese counterpart had given him a couple of melons as a gift. While the comment mostly escaped scrutiny when the podcast was first published, a piece in the English-language Japanese Times in late July lamented the comment. This week, former Japanese ambassador to Australia Shingo Yamagami wrote a critical opinion piece in The Australian that labelled Albanese’s gesture “insulting” and ignorant.



Several media outlets have since published extracts of the diplomatic note sent to Canberra from Tokyo, which noted “sensationalised reporting in the Australian media” about the podcast interview and which undertook that “no action” would be taken over the incident. The note also stressed that the melons were not smuggled but bought locally. The sharing of this letter prompted the opposition’s defence spokesman James Paterson and foreign affairs spokesman Ted O’Brien to write to Australian Federal Police commissioner Krissy Barrett and ask for an investigation into the leak. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese arrives for question time on Tuesday. Alex Ellinghausen “We write to refer the possibly unlawful disclosure of confidential and sensitive correspondence from the Government of Japan to the Department of Prime Minister and Cabinet,” the pair wrote.



“We are concerned that a diplomatic note with a critical bilateral partner has potentially been provided to the media without authorisation. Given that communications between governments can be classified, it is possible that this disclosure is a criminal offence under Division 122 of the Commonwealth Criminal Code. “It is critically important that Australia’s bilateral partners believe that their confidential correspondence will be handled appropriately by the Australian government. It would be gravely damaging to our national interest if they formed the view the Australian government does not take unauthorised disclosure seriously by promptly investigating it.” The Coalition pursued Albanese over the matter in question time on Tuesday, with backbench MP Mary Aldred twice asking the prime minister if he would apologise to Takaichi to repair relations between the two countries. Related Article Analysis

Political leadership Albanese’s attempts to talk to everyone bear bitter fruit when he goes off script Albanese did not accept the premise of the question and talked up both his friendship with Takaichi, and the growing strength of the strategic relationship between the two countries - before sitting down and cutting his answer short.



In the Senate, Paterson pressed Foreign Affairs Minister Penny Wong over the matter, suggesting the decision to share Japan’s letter was a “desperate attempt to clean up the prime minister’s self-inflicted melon mess” that risked a critical bilateral relationship. Wong accused the opposition of “confecting a diplomatic issue”. Senior government ministers including Tanya Plibersek, Katy Gallagher and Murray Watt have all defended the prime minister on Monday and Tuesday this week. World.title: Scratching the stats
World.content:
“I completed the census (C8) but don’t understand why there wasn’t a question about ‘fur babies’,” writes Natasha Lee of Alexandria. “Many of us consider our pets to be an important part of the family. The presence of pets paints a more detailed picture of our households, so why are they excluded?”

Here’s hoping Alan Phillips of Mosman doesn’t commit a capital offence: “My wife and I had planned to be in Canberra this week for some walking, cycling and galleries. Checking the weather predictions — freezing temperatures and rain — made us decide to postpone. But shock horror! We’d already filled in our census online which said we would be there. We were now stuck with it or risk possible arrest and imprisonment for lying to the Commonwealth.”

Sticking with the statistics, George Manojlovic of Mangerton says, “Obviously Jack Dikian finds crunching the numbers enlightening. He must have woken Tuesday morning and thought, ‘At last! I’ve finally come to my census!’”

“I believe the Wests Tigers approached the Pope (C8) to play five-eighth next year,” reports Peter Miniutti of Ashbury. “He respectfully declined the offer giving the excuse that not even God could save them.”

Regarding Nola Tucker’s opera (C8) commentary, John Boddington of Dalton reckons “there is really only one plot in opera. According to the comedian Ed Gardner: ‘Opera is when a guy gets stabbed in the back and, instead of bleeding, he sings’.”

World.title: Victoria - you’ve let yourself go
World.content:
Letters NationalVictoriaLetters Victoria - you’ve let yourself go August 11, 2026 — 8:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Matt Golding To submit a letter to The Age, email letters@theage.com.au. Please include your home address and telephone number below your letter. No attachments. See here for our rules and tips on getting your letter published. INFRASTRUCTURE It would be overkill to list the grievances or problems Victorians have had to deal with during the last decade or so of Labor government. It hurts to say this, but Victorians have had to put up with a government that is increasingly revealed to have been a closed shop of factional power.

While COVID was difficult to manage, Daniel Andrews got the state through it but had to give up the Commonwealth Games at great cost. Under Jacinta Allan, it appeared only those who wore high vis garments to work were sure of work while criminal factions allegedly took their cut of taxpayers’ money aided by one thuggish union in particular.

Meanwhile, state coffers were plundered of funds that should have gone to state schools, hospitals, teachers and nurses, and roads throughout the state crumbled.

The pothole state, or the state of potholes, is the final straw (″⁣Drivers stranded as potholes wreak carnage in wild weather″⁣, 11/8).

Unless these holes are fixed properly for the long term, road traffic throughout Victoria will slow to a crawl and the economy, dependent on trucking, will suffer as a result. And so will we.

John Whelen, Box Hill Sth When vital services fail, who is accountable?

Yet another day of significant delays and non-arrivals for passengers on V-line services. Passengers were delayed by up to three hours. This is not a minor inconvenience. The loss in productivity and the emotional turmoil is significant and to hear more hapless apologies is wearing thin.

There are two questions.

Firstly, is the government doing anything about the apparent lack of technical expertise that leads to these catastrophic maintenance failures?

The Telstra outage and the debacle of August 10 when a vital piece of infrastructure failed are maintenance failures. Is anyone held to account? Both the minister for transport and the minister for transport infrastructure remain silent, and for all we know so far, indifferent to these disruptions. What actions are being taken?

Secondly, given the inevitability of major disruptions on V-line services, there is no management plan to mitigate disruptions. In the latest maintenance failure, the fault happened at 6.30am of a working day.

Passengers should have been alerted and given the choice to either work from home or find alternative transport.

The government needs to address these problems urgently and explain to the public why these disruptions keep occurring and what they are doing about it.

Anne Bourke, Ocean Grove



Excessive bureaucracy before best-practice services

I totally agree with Professor Pat McGorry’s major concerns about the standards of care and safety for both patients and staff working in Victoria’s public mental health services (″⁣FIFO boss leads Victoria’s flagship youth mental health service amid reports of patient deaths and violence″⁣, 11/8).

I have not worked in the system for several years but have a partner and a number of close friends who recently worked or continue to work in this system.

These are experienced clinicians who have the skills, commitment and fortitude to provide the best care and humanity to people (at all stages of life) who are experiencing extremely distressing and debilitating mental health conditions.

Yet, so many of these clinicians are being hounded out of the services by management that appears more focused on maintaining an image of excellence through corporate awards, arbitrary KPIs, and excessive bureaucracy than on delivering genuine best-practice services.

Another royal commission bites the dust.

Jenny Hutchens, Greensborough Sustainable goals

For many years now, we have been seeing increasing pressure on our systems. Existing infrastructure is being run down, suburban and rural roads are increasingly potholed and damaging vehicles, governments face workforce and funding constraints, schools and hospitals all seem on the never-never road to funding, while proposed developments such as data centres will create enormous additional demands for electricity, water and other infrastructure and cost.

At the same time, our natural environment is being depleted at an ever-increasing rate. Climate change adds another layer to the problem. More extreme heat, flooding, storms, bushfires and pressure on water supplies will require additional investment simply to maintain the resilience of existing communities and infrastructure.

This needs to be factored into decisions about what new development we can realistically afford and sustain. Simply adding more projects to the pipeline does not make us sustainable.

If we do not have the workers, money, energy, water or infrastructure capacity to maintain what we already have, we need to ask whether continually expanding development is economically or socially sustainable, let alone environmentally sustainable.

Paul Caine, Glen Huntly From zoom to doom

I have a friend who claims he’s an expert on potholes. I call him the Roads Scholar (RS for short). He says our number plates should say “Victoria - The Holey State” or “Victoria - State of Holeiness”.

RS says that repairs are too superficial and don’t go deep enough. He says that one day, a distant car ahead suddenly disappeared. When he got there, he said he looked into a gigantic pothole to see the car, which would have been more severely damaged if it hadn’t landed on a B-double!

RS does tend to exaggerate. He says the Hume Highway has gone from zoom to doom. Thank God, RS doesn’t write to The Age, or it could be a very tedious run-up to the November election.

Kevan Porter, Alphington Pothole detector

Cars nowadays are fitted with all sorts of safety technology, such as autonomous emergency braking, lane-keeping assist and adaptive radar cruise control. The car company that develops a system that detects and warns the driver of any upcoming potholes will be an absolute winner in Victoria.

Graeme Daniels, Balwyn North Cars must adapt

The recent wild weather (″⁣Tyres completely shredded: Motorists stranded for hours after falling victim to massive potholes″⁣, 10/8) is only part of the equation in the ″⁣carnage″⁣ reported on country roads across the past few days and makes meaningless any claims of technological progress represented by the cars being sold nowadays.

It’s time consumers stood up against vehicles that aren’t even equipped with spare tyres, instead boasting expensive oversized wheels and fragile low-profile tyres, for little purpose beyond fashion. In addition, the hefty weight of electric cars in particular means that when they encounter potholes, they hit hard. As with extreme climatic conditions, these are predictable variables that need to be addressed by savvy consumers seeing through superficial showroom sheen.

Marish Mackowiak, Ormond



Spending our money

Whose bright idea was it to spend an enormous amount of money on bringing an NFL team to Melbourne, estimated to cost

$10.7 to $15 million? Surely, this event would appeal to a very niche market at most.

New South Wales was smart enough to reject the proposal as too expensive. Victoria could spend that money on far more essential things such as addressing the appalling state of the mental health system.

Or even, dare I say it, the truly horrendous condition of Victoria’s roads. Victoria was once ″⁣the Garden State″⁣; it is now ″⁣the Pothole State″⁣. What happened to common sense?

Oriana Collins, Hawthorn THE FORUM SRL will benefit us

Your correspondent (Letters, 11/8) comments on the two Suburban Rail Loop tunnels, saying they will require energy, and create pollution and transport disruption during construction.

If these are not constructed, just think of all the additional energy, diesel and petrol needed along with the pollution and transport chaos caused by the transport of the growing population.

I think the savings in terms of energy, fuel, pollution and disruption from the use of the SRL will outweigh its construction.

Laurens Meyer, Richmond Densified already

The Age reports (5/8) that urban planning expert Carlos Moreno says Melbourne needs to become a more densely settled city. If we do, he says, this will promote liveability.

The problem with his claim is that census data shows that between 2006 and 2021, Melbourne did “densify” (especially in the inner municipalities – “Tram Track Melbourne”). Yet, at the same time, according to Mercer and The Economist Intelligence Unit, liveability fell.

A further significant problem with densification is that such construction is relatively complex and has shown to be subject to rorting.

The future of housing Australians is actually in the regions, and in DIY construction such as what Robin Boyd facilitated with the Small Homes Service, and Tasmanian architect Jiri Lev is promoting now.

Alun Breward, Malvern East Deaf political class

Ehsan Noroozinejad’s article, “Why Australia’s megaproject boom may deepen the housing crisis” (11/8), is well written and to the point about infrastructure and planning in Australia, but the political elite doesn’t listen to common sense.

Gaye Bryant Burwood



Albanese’s punt

The deal is done. The major parties have sorted out their gambling problem. Aussies can still “have a punt” as the prime minister likes to say. That is a big red herring: gambling is legal and no one was calling for a ban.

So now, against the advice of the Murphy report that the major parties led, gambling ads stay and regulation remains weak.

The gambling lobby will be happy, they can still have confidence to send complaints to the regulator as it remains under-resourced and out of sight in the Northern Territory.

The major parties have bet that gambling reform is not the top issue for ordinary people as we manage cost of living. Sadly, for too many people, the cost of living with gambling is just too high.

When the major parties fail us, do we need more courage and clear thinking of independents like David Pocock to hold the powerful lobby groups and big donors to account?

Jenny Kashyap, Bentleigh Twiggy’s data centre

Andrew Forrest, sometime champion of salmon farmers and giant green energy projects, is planning a super-sized data centre in Australia’s arid Pilbara region.

He may have the clean energy to run his behemoth, but so far, has failed to say which water source will nurture his data centre. The daily water usage of a large data centre is equivalent to that used by a town of up to 50,000 people.

The health of rivers is reliant on ground-water. Maltreating and misusing the waters above or below the earth affects the lot.

Nature is reality. We must protect it. Without water, we living things die.

Yvonne Parker, Portarlington Awash with stupidity

Having seen the awkward snippet of our prime minister with some influencer referring to those melons, it wasn’t Albanese who was making offensive comments or gestures. The real issue here is politicians lowering their standards of communication efforts to engage with influencers on social media.

Looks like we’ll either have to raise the voting age to 40, or ban social media altogether.

Enough with this unaccountable drivel as entertainment for young people who’ve never been taught how to think for themselves.

No wonder we are awash with so much stupidity these days.

Bernadette George, Mildura Netanyahu’s agenda

Of course, Benjamin Netanyahu has rejected the latest US-brokered plan for Gaza (″⁣Netanyahu rejects plan for Hamas″⁣, 11/8). It involves Israel gradually withdrawing from Palestinian land. That is not on the agenda for Netanyahu nor his right-wing allies.

The demands for complete disarmament of Hamas are not genuine negotiating tactics; they are simply a way to prolong Israeli occupation of large swaths of Gaza. The “yellow line″⁣ is moving inexorably forward, squeezing Gazans into a smaller and smaller portion of their own country. The “yellow line’ is moving inexorably forward, squeezing Gazans into a smaller and smaller portion of their own country.

Lorel Thomas, Blackburn South Smart phone problems

Smart phones are radically different to pinball machines, colour television or video games (“″⁣Not snowflakes’: Severe mental disorders surge among young people,” 11/8). Smart phones are carried 24 hours a day, potentially exposing their users to parasocial media and preventing or reducing rsocial contact with friends and family .

The young are particularly susceptible having grown up with smart phones while their brains are developing.

There’s nothing intrinsically wrong with smart phones; they’re great for making phone calls, receiving texts - it’s many of the parasocial apps and games that cause the harm.

Wayne Robinson, Kingsley, WA



AND ANOTHER THING Matt Golding Anthony Albanese

Anthony Albanese needs to stop going on podcasts. He has neither the wit nor dexterity required. In his attempts to appeal to increase his reach and popularity, he only reveals his limitations.

Russell Kidd, Carnegie Anthony Albanese can dismiss his tasteless comments about Japanese melons as much as he likes but his body language was explicit.

Robyn Williams, Sale When it comes to real gambling reform, Anthony Albanese is a complete melon.

Geoff Allen, Parkdale



A great cartoon from Cathy Wilcox (10/8) on the PM and gambling! He prefers to see it as a harmless punt and ignores its potential to destroy lives and families,

Phil Lipshut, Elsternwick John Howard served his time years ago. If I were Albanese or Taylor (or should I say if I were in the shoes of either of them), I’d ignore him too.

Brandon Mack, Deepdene Furthermore

Barnaby Joyce says why can’t Australians pick strawberries and not migrants? Off you go then Barnaby.

Ross Hosking, Blackwood, SA The government can no longer be in any doubt. The state of potholes in our roads is a big issue in the upcoming election.

Matthew Hamilton, Kew Gridiron comes to Melbourne – do the helmets protect their heads one wonders? At what cost?

Greg Curtin, Nunawading



Could I remind your correspondent (Letters ″⁣Global and local″⁣, 11/8) the reason for expending all the energy on building the Suburban Rail Loop tunnels is ultimately to remove vehicles from the road, thus reducing greenhouse gases.

Suzanne Palmer-Holton, Seaford Is Trump trying to avenge the humiliating hostage crisis of 1979, when Iran imprisoned 52 Americans in the American embassy in Tehran for 444 days? I think he’s just opened the door to more humiliation.

Tim Durbridge, Brunswick The opinion newsletter is a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own. Sign up here.

World.title: Educators on the line in proposed Zoos Victoria job cuts
World.content:
PoliticsVictoriaAnimals Educators on the line in proposed Zoos Victoria job cuts Kieran Rooney August 11, 2026 — 7:51pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

More than a third of educator positions could be cut from Zoos Victoria under proposed redundancies, prompting fears the visits by 150,000 students each year will be cut and the standard of teaching affected. The Age revealed in June that Zoos Victoria was preparing a restructure that would cut up to 70 full-time roles from its 950-strong workforce – a figure the organisation has pushed back on as it consults staff about the changes. Among the most contentious proposals is a 38 per cent reduction in education staff at Melbourne Zoo – from roughly 6.2 full-time staff to 3.8 – who assist in teaching students and other groups about wildlife and conservation. A baby giraffe at Melbourne Zoo. Jo Howell The Community and Public Sector Union and United Workers Union said on Monday that about 600 staff – almost two-thirds of the organisation’s workforce – had responded to the proposed changes, which would be finalised later this month.



CPSU state secretary Jiselle Hanna said any cuts to education staff would devastate the 150,000 students who visited Melbourne Zoo, Werribee Zoo, Healesville Sanctuary and Kyabram Fauna Park every year. Related Article Animals Bailout backing was offered to Zoos Victoria a year before job cuts “Staff are telling us that they will not be able to maintain the volume of visits or the standard of education for young learners if these cuts go ahead,” Hanna said. “If this restructure is genuinely being driven by financial pressures, then why would cuts be made to an entity that brings in millions of dollars annually through school visits? “The impacted staff are highly skilled workers with decades of experience. They keep visitors educated, entertained and, most importantly, safe.”



The CPSU and the United Workers Union have urgently demanded Zoos Victoria wind back the scale of the cuts, arguing it will have flow-on effects across all parts of the organisation as staff are asked to handle new responsibilities. “This restructure process has demonstrated how out of touch the executive team is with the realities of the zoo and the work that zoo staff undertake,” Hanna said. A Zoos Victoria spokesperson said frontline services would not be impacted, as official consultation continued before a final decision was announced on August 25. “Our employees have provided valuable feedback through this consultation process, and we are considering this feedback carefully,” the spokesperson said. “Zoos Victoria will remain a world-class wildlife destination, and our commitment to fighting wildlife extinction remains.”



The Age has previously reported staff concerns that the restructure could also affect wildlife and conservation roles across the organisation, however, Zoos Victoria says frontline and animal care roles will not be directly affected. Related Article Animals Zoos Victoria to cut up to 70 jobs, including in conservation and wildlife Animal Justice Party MP Georgie Purcell said Zoos Victoria should be upfront about what the cuts would mean for conservation programs. “With bird flu ravaging our state and our volunteer wildlife carers under enormous strain, we simply can’t afford to lose any of the dedicated Zoos Victoria teams whose job it is to respond to injured wildlife and protect threatened species,” she said. “It’s simply not good enough to say there won’t be cuts to frontline services without being clear about what happens to the conservation and wildlife rescue work that sits behind them.”

World.title: Live: Christopher Luxon calls urgent caucus meeting amid leadership speculation
World.content:
National Party MPs have been summoned for an "urgent in-person" caucus meeting in Wellington.

It comes amid renewed pressure on Christopher Luxon's leadership.

Luxon wrote on social media on Tuesday, after postponing various prior arrangements, that it was "clear from various media reports and conversations there is increased speculation about my leadership".

"It is my firm belief that division and disunity are a major distraction only 90 days out from the election.

"I also believe this distraction is unfair to the New Zealand people, and dedicated National Party candidates, supporters and volunteers, when there is so much at stake."

For those reasons, he wrote, the issue "needs to be resolved quickly".

"I am calling an urgent in-person Caucus meeting tomorrow at 9:30am in Wellington to resolve the issue."

World.title: Kiwi firefighters head to US to help tackle unprecedented wildfires
World.content:
New Zealand firefighters have answered a call for help from the United States.

A convoy of 57 firefighters, chainsaw crews and forestry experts depart this week to help their counterparts fight wildfires in America's north-west.

It's senior firefighter Cameron Grylls' first deployment overseas.

"It's going to be pretty different for us given the scale and the size of what they're dealing with over there," Grylls said.

"It's just that next level so we're expecting some long hot days and a lot of strenuous exercise, but we're going to to help our teammates out over there and do our best."

He's Fire and Emergency's assistant district commander for Waikato and would be leading a crew of boots on the ground - they could be deployed to any of the neighbouring states of Oregon, Washington State or Idaho.

They would spend 28 days firefighting.

The team is made up of 43 personnel from Fire and Emergency, four from the Department of Conservation (DOC), five from the Defence Force and five from the forestry industry.

They would be taking on multiple roles, ranging from firefighters and fire engine crews to chainsaw specialists, and including incident management roles such as helibase managers, logistics and liaison officers.

"They could be blacking out, that's extinguishing, dampening down where fires have gone through so that they don't reignite, could be clearing access for other crews, cutting down trees," Grylls said.

"We go over with a fairly open mind and know that we're going over to help them in whatever task they might need doing. So we're pretty flexible."

Cameron Grylls. RNZ / Amy Williams

The scale of wildfires in America's north-west and Canada is unprecedented.

In western Canada, over 20,000 people were forced to flee communities in British Columbia over the weekend and in the US, crews in Washington have been fighting three wildfires that began burning in the Spokane area.

The New Zealand firefighters are experienced working in arduous conditions, including steep terrain and high temperatures, and living in fire camps in remote areas.

It's not just the scale of the wildfires that would be challenging for the Kiwi crews - they've been told to keep an eye out for local wildlife.

"Bears, scorpions, rattlesnakes any of those sorts of things that we typically don't have over here that are out to hurt us. It's a different environment for us...we just have to keep our wits about us."

Blair Calder is a DOC ranger in Dunedin and his team is likely to be focused on making fire breaks.

"There'll be a lot of walking onto the fire ground then there'll be a lot of using hand tools and not a lot of water, possibly, where we're going. We've got chainsaw operators with us," Calder said.

"It's crucial and it can be very time consuming and physically demanding."

This was his sixth deployment overseas, he'd been to Canada and Australia to join firefighting efforts.

"I really enjoy the challenge. I enjoy working with other people from around New Zealand who you don't always get to work with.

"When you get over there, the upskilling you get from 28 days of firefighting is pretty intense and it's a really good way to learn."

The Bald Range wildfire near Summerland in Canada's western British Columbia province on August 7, 2026. Handout / BC Wildfire Service / AFP

Forestry-trained firefighters have worked with Fire and Emergency in overseas deployments for decades, bringing specialised chainsaw skills and expertise.

Forestry worker Jarron McInnes is going to the US as a leader for a chainsaw crew and had previously fought wildfires in Canada and Australia.

"It's their chainsaw skills where they really shine - tree felling, cutting fire breaks and fire lines," he said.

Defence force Staff Sergeant Matthew Anker is a Fire Master based in Waiouru and he said it was the type of deployment soldiers train for.

"They are experienced in wildfire response and accustomed to operating in demanding environments as part of a coordinated multi-agency team," he said.

"It is an opportunity for them to apply those skills in support of our international partners, while gaining further experience that will strengthen our response capability at home."

Cameron Grylls said they would come back home to New Zealand with news skills to tackle an expected dry spring and summer...something crews were already preparing for.

"Some brigades are looking at going out and starting up training around working with helicopters and all of that rural aspect that we do...our crews are very much aware of that and looking to start building that into their training now as we move forward into that season."

Some of the fire fighters departed for the US on Tuesday and the remainder leave Wednesday.

World.title: What happens to your KiwiSaver if you die?
World.content:
What happens to your KiwiSaver money if you die?

Australians might be being warned to make sure they've organised who will get their superannuation savings when they die - but New Zealanders don't have as much to worry about.

ABC reported this week that 15.5 million Australians might not have made a binding death nomination for their superannuation accounts, to direct their fund on who to pay the money to.

In Australia, superannuation does not automatically become part of a person's estate if they die.

In New Zealand, the situation was quite different - and simpler.

Why have Ooshies taken over my house? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 11m

KiwiSaver formed part of a person's estate when they died and became another asset that was dealt with by their will if they had one.

"New Zealanders don't generally need the equivalent of Australia's binding death benefit nomination to make sure their KiwiSaver follows their estate wishes," Pie Funds chief executive Ana-Marie Lockyer said.

"There are still good reasons to have an up-to-date will and make things easy for your executor, but there isn't the same additional layer of superannuation estate planning that Australians face."

If they did not have a will, there were rules that determined how the estate was distributed.

If they had a spouse or partner and children, the spouse or partner would get all personal possessions, $155,000 and a third of anything remaining. The other two-thirds would be divided among the children.

Kernel founder Dean Anderson said the main thing for New Zealanders to be aware of was that the limit at which probate was required had increased.

It was now the case that most estates under $40,000 could be handled without the need to apply to the court.

It was increased from $15,000 because many KiwiSaver balances had grown past that level.

World.title: 'Bonkers' to fund climate disaster recovery but not prevention - local government leader
World.content:
It's "bonkers" that the government contributes to disaster recovery but not to climate adaptation to prevent damage in the first place, a local government leader says.

The Climate Change Commission on Tuesday published a progress report on how well the country is adapting to climate change, finding that delays were leaving communities exposed to future damage and costs.

It made six urgent recommendations to the government, including setting out how adaptation would be paid for.

The government should decide what it was willing to pay for itself, and then work with local councils and the private sector to find ways to fund and finance the remaining costs.

Successive governments have avoided making decisions on how to pay for adaptation, with the current government saying it would not address the issue of cost-sharing until after the election.

Local Government New Zealand deputy chair Deon Swiggs said he largely agreed with the report's recommendations.

"It really does correctly identify that adaptation can't be delivered by local government alone."

There were already precedents out there for how adaptation costs could be shared.

"The Crown co-funds 60 percent of eligible costs after a disaster, but there's no equivalent co-funding to prevent that damage in the first place," he said.

"That's just bonkers - we should be talking about, how do we fund this stuff before it happens?

"We all know that it's cheaper to fund resilience or projects that prevent things from happening in the first place."

The National Land Transport Fund was another model that could be adapted, he said.

"That dedicates revenue, that councils apply contributions of scale to the risk, and then the rating base picks up the contribution so that you can start delivery."

The Climate Change Commission has previously pointed out that, of the $64 billion the government has spent on natural hazards since 2010, only three percent has gone to proactive measures to limit risk and damage.

A proposed law change - which the government has said is unlikely to pass before the election - would require councils to develop adaptation plans for high-risk areas at least 30 years into the future.

Councils would comply if that came into effect, but Swiggs said many of them already knew which communities were at risk.

"The reality is we can't afford to defer these conversations any further," he said.

"We've got all of this information, we've got these reports, we've got bills in [Parliament]. I think we need to work at the same time to make sure that we are talking funding."

Without that, communities would be trapped in a cycle or recovering and rebuilding.

The commission's report also recommended that the government establish funding mechanisms for iwi and Māori to adapt to climate change.

Bioeconomy Science Institute research leader Shaun Awatere. Supplied / Bioeconomy Science Institute

Bioeconomy Science Institute research leader Shaun Awatere (Ngāti Porou) said efforts to support Māori adaptation initiatives had been uneven to date.

Supporting Māori adaptation was an equity issue, but also a chance to strengthen the entire country's resilience, he said.

"During significant weather events, marae have often served as hubs for shelter, welfare support, and community coordination," he said.

Māori-led environmental initiatives were contributing to the protection and restoration of coastal areas, freshwater systems, and other resources, but were often small scale and under-resourced, Awatere said.

World.title: Surging EV sales in 2026 not just temporary - market analyst
World.content:
One in three new cars sold in NZ now an EV, according to new research.

ChargeNet calls for NZ to copy Australia's payroll-lease scheme to help families into EVs.

2026 is shaping up as a standout year for sales of electric vehicles and plug-in hybrid electric vehicles in New Zealand.

In a new research note, global market analyst BMI - which is a part of the Fitch Group - forecasts New Zealand sales of passenger EVs will jump from about 11,726 units in 2025 to more than 37,445 in 2026.

That would amount to growth of nearly 220 percent year-on-year.

BMI said that would lift EV market penetration in New Zealand to 35.2 percent.

Based on its forecast for overall passenger vehicle sales of 106,378 units, EVs would then account for roughly one in three new cars sold in New Zealand.

The recent surge in petrol prices as a result of the Iran war is believed to have sparked more interest in EVs this year.

However BMI said the big jump reflected a structural improvement in accessibility rather than a temporary demand spike.

It said more affordable models, especially Chinese brands such as BYD, MG and Zeekr, were entering the market at prices that were broadening the buyer base.

Local EV infrastructure company ChargeNet's chief executive, Danusia Wypych, said it was also forecasting strong growth in sales.

ChargeNet's chief executive, Danusia Wypych. Supplied / ChargeNet

"In the middle of last year, we were looking at 15 percent EV growth and now we're sort of seeing 20 percent year-on-year EV growth, and I'm sure it will go higher than that in the coming months," Wypych said.

ChargeNet is one of the leading providers of fast charging sites around the country.

Wypych was confident ChargeNet would be ready to meet the growing demand for EVs.

"If you think about the sites that we were putting in back in the day when we started in the 2010s, we'd put in one charging unit. Now a base install for a site host will be three or five charging units, and those units will be able to deliver a lot more energy. So, we're confident that if we continue to invest, we'll be able to continue to meet the demand."

Politicians urged to help low- and middle-income families access EVs

Wypych said she would like to see more done to help lower-income New Zealanders into EVs, particularly families struggling with the upfront costs.

She is calling for politicians to adopt a government-backed EV scheme used in Australia, which incentivises families to lease EVs with the option to buy.

"In Australia, middle income earners get to own or get to drive around new cars because they lease them. "And at the end of the lease, they can decide whether or not they want to own them.

"So I think that would be a real benefit to everyday families in New Zealand if they could be driving electric, saving money every week while things are tight, and then long term, they can make a decision about whether or not they keep the car."

The scheme, known as a novated lease, sees an employer take money out of an employee's gross, or before-tax, salary in order to pay a finance company for the car lease and running costs.

That lowers the employee's taxable income and avoids the need for a large upfront payment.

The lease scheme has been credited with helping drive an increase in EV sales in Australia.

Most New Zealand families were already buying second-hand cars on finance, Wypych said.

"So, we reckon EV leasing costs would sort of be in the ballpark of $130 to $200 a week, and that compares very favourably to having to buy a car on finance," Wypych said.

The scheme would need government backing and minor law changes, and Wypych said it would be important to include parameters and safeguards.

She hoped all political parties would be open to the idea as they headed into the election.

World.title: Arthur's Pass tramper died of hypothermia after losing marked track
World.content:
A woman died of hypothermia while hiking in Arthur's Pass National Park after she became lost and could not find the marked track, a coroner has found.

Rebecca Woolley, 37, was an experienced tramper who set out out in fine weather on a day walk on Mount Aicken Track from the Devil's Punchbowl Track car park with a friend on 30 October 2021.

Her friend turned back early and Woolley continued alone but was reported missing that night. A search team found her body the next day, about 700m off the track.

In findings released on Wednesday, coroner Alexandra Cunninghame urged trampers to carry appropriate navigation tools before heading into unmarked terrain.

Cunninghame found Woolley died of hypothermia resulting from prolonged exposure to cold and wet weather, with a contributing spinal fracture likely caused by a tumbling fall or multiple falls.

Rebecca Woolley. Supplied / Brett Woolley

In a statement provided to RNZ, Woolley's father Brett Woolley thanked the coroner for her inquiry and said he hoped the findings would prevent a similar tragedy happening to another family.

"Rebecca (Bex) was an incredible person who lived life to its fullest. She is very much missed by all that knew her," he said.

The coroner described Woolley as an "adventurous, curious, loving person" by her friends and family. She enjoyed outdoor activities and was experienced with day walks and multi-day tramps.

Woolley and her friend had planned to walk up the Cons Track, but when they could not find the start decided to walk Mount Aicken Track instead. Neither had been on the track before.

Mount Aicken Track branches off the Devil's Punchbowl Track near Arthur's Pass Village. The Department of Conservation (DOC) classifies it as an advanced tramping track, climbing about 540 vertical metres through steep, rugged terrain to the bush line.

The top of Mount Aicken Supplied / DOC

DOC said the track ended at bush line and terrain beyond there was challenging and mostly unmarked. There were three strategically placed markers at key decision points.

Neither Woolley nor her friend had a map, compass, GPS device or a personal locator beacon.

At about 3pm the pair reached the bush line and shortly after started up the unmarked route into alpine terrain.

At this point, Woolley's friend decided to turn back and wait at the bush line because of a sore leg, while Woolley planned to continue for 30 minutes.

At about 3.40pm, Woolley sent a text message saying she had taken a wrong turn, but could see the road and would make her way back to the car park.

When Woolley had not returned by 7.35pm, her friend called the police. By that time the weather had deteriorated with rain and a significant drop in temperature.

"Police walked the Devils Punchbowl area calling out for Rebecca, to no avail. It was agreed that a full search and rescue operation would start the next day, once it was light," the coroner said.

Woolley's body was found at 1pm the following day in difficult terrain about 700m to the south of the track near Graham Stream.

Rebecca Woolley. Supplied / Brett Woolley

Cunninghame said two scenarios explaining Woolley's death were possible.

"Either she fell, injuring her spine and was unable to move herself to a place of shelter before succumbing to hypothermia, or she had become hypothermic before falling," she said.

NZ Mountain Safety Council (MSC) chief executive Mike Daisley said the coroner's findings highlighted the importance of being fully prepared for all outdoor trips, including taking navigation tools, even for day walks.

Coroner Cunninghame said people who became lost should stop and seek help early while communication options remained available.

She also recommended DOC review the timing of its annual marker inspection on Mount Aicken Track, with a view to scheduling inspections for October when conditions allowed staff to complete them safely.

Since Woolley's death, DOC had updated its track webpage, highlighting the risks of venturing above the bush line, she said.

DOC visitor safety and standards manager Andy Roberts said markers on Mount Aicken were in place and in good condition at the time.

The top of Mount Aicken. Supplied / DOC

He said DOC staff were planning to check markers in early October if snow conditions allowed as per the coroner's recommendation.

"Following a tragedy in the same area in 2006, we installed more markers where it seemed trampers were taking a wrong turn and updated the information on our website highlighting the risks with this route and the difficult, steep terrain," he said.

Roberts said people becoming lost on unmarked routes was an increasing problem.

"What we have seen over recent years is people going off tracks or routes and not necessarily having the equipment or the skills to deal with the conditions," he said.

"It's a tragedy when people lose their lives in the mountains and we do as much as we can to prevent this, providing safety information on our website and at our visitors centres. Our tracks and structures are maintained for people to use, but on unmarked difficult routes even while doing a day walk, you can get into challenging alpine terrain pretty quickly and you need to be very careful, take precautions by having the right gear, maps and communication devices.

"If in doubt, ask experts and seek advice on whether the trip is right for you and your experience and always check the weather forecast."

At the time of her death, Woolley was living in Christchurch and studying for a nursing degree. She had moved to the city from Marlborough where she had volunteered with St John and Civil Defence.

World.title: Christopher Luxon's leadership on the line as he fronts do-or-die caucus meeting
World.content:
Christopher Luxon's leadership is on the line as he prepares to front a do-or-die meeting with his National Party caucus in Wellington on Wednesday morning.

Luxon called the urgent in-person meeting as speculation swirled he was losing his grip on the leadership.

It followed reporting by the New Zealand Herald on Monday night that National MPs had spent the day on the phones, with one confirming they had fielded "several" calls about a potential leadership change.

"There's going to be change in the top job. It's just a question of who is going to be it", the Herald reported the MP to have said.

The three most likely contenders are deputy Nicola Willis, third-ranked Chris Bishop, and senior MP Erica Stanford - while Simeon Brown and Mark Mitchell could be considered for the deputy role.

Willis and Bishop publicly supported Luxon on Tuesday, but when Stanford arrived at Wellington Airport she did not say a word to reporters - even when they directly asked her whether she backed her leader.

Erica Stanford arriving at Wellington Airport on Tuesday before the National Party caucus meeting. Screengrab

Luxon seeks to silence agitators - again

Luxon did not take long to respond to murmurings of caucus disunity.

On Tuesday morning Bishop confirmed an online caucus meeting had been set for Tuesday evening, but stressed it was not unusual for that to happen during a recess week at Parliament. That meeting was later cancelled.

By early afternoon, Luxon posted on social media that he was calling his caucus to Wellington during a recess week at Parliament for a 9.30am Wednesday meeting, saying there was clearly increased speculation about his leadership.

"It is my firm belief that division and disunity are a major distraction only 90 days out from the election," he wrote.

"I also believe this distraction is unfair to the New Zealand people, and dedicated National Party candidates, supporters and volunteers, when there is so much at stake."

The issue needed to be resolved quickly, he said.

Stepping off the plane in Wellington later in the day, Luxon refused to talk to reporters, only saying "talk to you tomorrow ... take care team".

It is unclear whether Luxon will call a confidence vote on Wednesday, as he did just four months ago - the last time his leadership was under pressure with some of his caucus telling the media of flagging support.

He ultimately survived that vote and drew a line under it, blaming a "media soap opera" for causing a stir.

The ballot was secret, with only the scrutineers - junior whip Suze Redmayne and party president Sylvia Wood - privy to the votes.

An unconfirmed margin of 27-22 has since circulated, fuelling questions about whether he would have the numbers to survive this time around.

On Tuesday morning Chris Bishop confirmed an online caucus meeting had been set for that evening, but it was later cancelled. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

A shocker week

Fresh rumblings about rolling Luxon followed a week of poor headlines for the National leader - and a far longer stretch of dismal polling.

Luxon on Monday apologised to Rotorua Business Chamber leaders after he criticised them at an event on Friday for having a "parent-child mentality" and relying on government too much.

He also faced scrutiny about his unwillingness to reprimand his Foreign Minister Winston Peters, who had in Parliament told a Chinese-born MP Lawrence Xu-Nan to go back to his own country.

The Prime Minister then had to justify using a Defence Force plane flying him home from a National Party fundraising dinner, the same day unemployment hit a record 11-year high.

On Thursday, speaking on Newstalk ZB, he made an out of the blue captain's call to hold a referendum on MMP if he's re-elected, which blindsided his own caucus.

A slight bump in the Taxpayers' Union Curia poll on Friday seems not to have won Luxon much repreive.

The poll had National up 0.5 points to 31 percent and would return the coalition to power by a slim margin.

It followed multiple polls this year which had National bouncing around the high 20s to low 30s, unable to make ground.

Just last month the party was down 2.1 points in the RNZ-Reid Research poll to 28.7 percent.

On Saturday Luxon released National's list for the upcoming election with little upset, keeping senior MPs and new talent happy with high enough spots to make it back to Parliament.

During that press conference he declared he had the full backing of his caucus.

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon at Wellington Airport on Tuesday. SCREENSHOT / RNZ

Most MPs pledge support for Luxon, Stanford stays silent

Most MPs arriving in the capital on Tuesday night were quick to throw their support behind Luxon.

But notably, Stanford did not say a word to gathered reporters.

Asked whether she had confidence in Luxon, Stanford did not reply.

World.title: Veteran Manly prop Nathan Brown outlines NRL exit plan
World.content:
Manly prop Nathan Brown has revealed he decided at the start of the season this would be his last in the NRL, as the veteran forward eyes a move to the Super League.

Off contract at the end of 2026, Brown has confirmed he will finish up at Manly this year as the Sea Eagles begin a changing of the guard in the forward pack.

Brown's final month at Manly will take on even more importance on Friday night, after he was called in to start for the first time in two years against the Dolphins amid the Sea Eagles' forwards shortage.

The 33-year-old is still hoping to exit the NRL in a finals series, with Manly likely needing to win their last four games to return to the top eight.

Munster free to play Melbourne Storm five-eighth Cameron Munster avoids suspension after the NRL match review committee downgrades his dangerous contact charge from Saturday's win over Manly.

"I just knew it was my time to call it quits in the NRL … I made my debut in 2013, so it's my 14th year. When your time's up, your time is up," Brown told AAP.

"The last thing I wanted to do was sit on the fence with whether I want to stay or go overseas.

"It's just made everything a lot easier to go all in this year and enjoy every moment, every training session and every game."

Brown was regarded as one of the most aggressive forwards in the game when he debuted at Wests Tigers in 2013, as well as during a two-year stint at South Sydney.

Nathan Brown played six seasons at the Eels, making his Origin debut while at the club. (Getty Images: Anthony Au-Yeung)

He came into his own at Parramatta, playing two State of Origins for NSW in 2020 and the 2022 grand final for the Eels before reviving his career with a train-and-trial deal at Manly in 2024.

"I find it funny [looking back at old footage)]" said Brown, who is on track to reach 200 games this month.

"When I started, I was a lot bigger. I wasn't really that fit. I was a bit overweight for my size and my position. And I had a different attitude back then.

"But at the same time, you learn a lot from it. You feel grateful that you had to go through those things."

Brown's NRL retirement comes with fellow veteran Manly prop Siua Taukeiaho off contract after breaking his leg in two places in May.

The Sea Eagles have signed props Davvy Moale and Toni Mataele for next year, while Kayliss Fatialofa will arrive as a highly-heralded second rower.

Teenage prop Simi Laiafi has also shown promise starting this year alongside Taniela Paseka, and looms as a long-term prospect.

Brown said he was proud of the impact he was able to have off the bench this year, still hitting the line with gusto.

"You don't want to be finishing by just clutching at the straws and hanging on by a thread," he said.

"I feel like I can probably still physically play another year in the NRL. But in the mental side of things, I'm just ready."

Manly expect to be without prop Paseka for at least a fortnight after he injured his knee against Melbourne last week, in a seismic blow to their finals chances.

Ethan Bullemor (concussion) remains sidelined, while Kobe Hetherington (biceps) last week joined Taukeiaho in being out for the season.

Second-rower Ben Trbojevic (concussion) is also still out, while his superstar brother Tom has been kept on ice for another week in his return from a hamstring injury.

World.title: Slater still firing at 54 at Tahiti Pro, eliminating Medina
World.content:
Kelly Slater has advanced to the third round of the Tahiti Pro after the 54-year-old American overcame Brazil's Gabriel Medina and ​some heavy wipeouts at the 2024 Paris Olympics venue of Teahupo'o.

Slater's emotional Margaret River exit Surfing legend Kelly Slater holds back tears as his career effectively ends at Western Australia's Margaret River Pro, although the 11-time world champion is hoping for one last wildcard in Fiji.

Slater, who recently underwent hip surgery, retired from full-time competition in 2024 and welcomed a third child earlier this year ​but showed he had ‌lost none of his competitive edge against three-times world champion Medina.

In dangerous, challenging waves, Slater got smashed on his first attempt and was hit even harder on ‌his second wave, breaking his board in two.

But the Floridian recovered ⁠and threaded a long, deep tube that scored a 9.73 ‌out of 10 to take ​the lead.

He ‌then backed it up with another excellent score to advance over Medina, who beat Slater in an epic final at the same venue in 2014.

"I don't know if I'll ever have another heat with him, and ​he ‌got me last time," said Slater, who dominated the first day of competition.

He said he had been motivated by criticism of the ⁠decision to award him a wildcard ‌to compete.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"You see those comments, ‌a lot of people doubting me or saying [the opportunity] should have gone to ‌a local wildcard," he said. "Even after all this time, I have something to prove."

Slater finished with an excellent two-wave ‌total ​of 19.06 out of ⁠20 to set up a third-round meeting with reigning champion Jack Robinson of Australia, who was pushed hard by countryman Callum Robson in round two.

California's Griffin Colapinto, who was born six years after ⁠Slater won the first of his 11 world titles, was the only man to better Slater's ‌performance in ‌the second round, racking up a perfect 10-point ride ​on his way to a season-high heat total of 19.6 out of 20.

World.title: Vine time: Matildas hero seals A-League Women return
World.content:
Cortnee Vine has returned to A-League Women with champions Melbourne City in a move that could help the Matildas' penalty shootout hero push for a second Women's World Cup berth.

Elsewhere, Matildas great and Brisbane captain Tameka Yallop has joined Wellington in a huge recruiting coup for the grand finalists.

Vine, 28, starred for Sydney FC as an explosive and tricky winger, winning three premierships and two championships.

Vine catapulted to stardom when she scored the winning spot-kick in the Matildas' famous penalty shootout against France that secured a maiden Women's World Cup semi-final berth in 2023.

The winger joined North Carolina Courage in 2024 but made just 23 appearances in two years, scoring twice, while also taking time away from football to prioritise her mental health.

With golden boot winner Holly McNamara leaving City for Super League club Everton, Vine is instantly the club's biggest name.

"I'm really excited to be coming home and joining Melbourne City," Vine said in a statement.

"I've watched what City has achieved over the last few seasons and the standards this group continues to set, so the opportunity to come into that environment and be part of a team competing for trophies was really exciting to me.

"My time in the NWSL has helped me grow both as a player and a person, and I'm looking forward to bringing those experiences back to Australia."

Vine will have the opportunity to impress and push for three trophies across the ALW and the Women's Asian Champions League.

Tameka Yallop has left Brisbane Roar after 158 games and 66 goals in various stints since 2008. (Getty Images: Chris Hyde)

Attacking midfielder Yallop looms as the missing piece for Bev Priestman's Phoenix.

Yallop's wife Kirsty Yallop is a former New Zealand international and the move allows the couple and their two young daughters to be closer to family.

The 35-year-old, who missed this year's Asian Cup through injury, can also press her Women's World Cup case with the ambitious Phoenix.

Bev Priestman took Wellington Phoenix to the grand final in her first season at the helm. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

"I'm chasing that trophy and so is Wellington, so we're aligned," Yallop said.

"Getting the opportunity to work under Bev was a massive drawcard, not to mention the facilities at NZCIS. They're second to none.

"It's a high performance environment in Wellington and that's something that I love being a part of.

"And the Phoenix have shown they're dedicated to their women's program. That was a major pull for me too."

Loading Instagram content

Brisbane is retiring the former Julie Dolan Medallist's number 13 jersey — the first time the club has done so for a men's or women's player.

Yallop, who has attended four World Cups and three Olympics and played overseas in several top leagues, spent the majority of her decorated A-League Women career at the Roar, bar a one-season stint at City in 2018-19.

An inaugural Queensland Roar player at the age of 17 in 2008, Yallop won three premierships at Brisbane and scored in two grand final wins.

Yallop scored 66 goals in 158 games in three separate stints at the Roar.

The new season is due to start on Friday October 16.

AAP

World.title: 'Never forgotten where he's from': Outback community pride for Crows legend
World.content:
Taylor Walker will go down in history as an AFL legend but when all is said and done, the boy from the bush wants to return home and attempt to win a premiership in the town that made him.

Walker announced his retirement from the Adelaide Crows Football Club on Monday after 19 seasons playing for the AFL club.

The 36-year-old's playing career started in the outback New South Wales community of Broken Hill, located just over the South Australian border.

"I've said to my two best mates that are still playing back in Broken Hill that I want to go and try and win a premiership back there, so we'll try and do that next year," he said in his retirement announcement speech.

Jayden Kelly is one of those mates and says he is holding Walker to that promise.

Jayden Kelly played junior footy with Walker, and is hopeful he'll come back to Broken Hill and play. (ABC News: Bill Ormonde)

"He has mentioned it once or twice that he would love to [come back]. So there's myself and a couple of his close mates that are just hanging on and still playing local footy back here," he said.

Walker is no stranger to a winning a flag with the North Broken Hill Football Club.

As a self-proclaimed "skinny kid from Broken Hill", the then 17-year-old helped the Bulldogs to premiership glory in 2007.

Taylor Walker (left) was instrumental in the 2007 grand final, when the North Broken Hill Bulldogs won. (Supplied: Gavin Schmidt)

Broken Hill inspiration

But while Taylor Walker will undoubtably be remembered for his on-field contributions for the Crows, the legacy he leaves in Broken Hill is just as significant.

Kelly said Walker's career had shown young people in the town what could be possible.

"He's really put us on the map," he said.

"He's shown young kids in Broken Hill, if they put their mind to it and by working hard, what they can achieve."

Kelly, who played junior football alongside Walker, said he remembered feeling it was "unreal" to see a boy from Broken Hill picked when he was drafted .

"Being able to go and live out a childhood dream; he supported the crows growing up and had all the Tony Modra posters all over his wall," he said.

"He loved everything Crows and when he got the phone call that they were interested ... he was over the moon."

Taylor Walker plays alongside fellow Crow and Broken Hill export Isaac Cumming. (Supplied: AFC Media)

Wayne Walker is Taylor Walker's dad who proudly remains living in the outback town.



He said he had most admired his son's relationship with his family, the Adelaide Crows and club supporters.

"He's always never forgotten where he come from. His mates are so dear to him, it's not funny, they keep him grounded," he said.

"That's probably one thing he has been, he's been very grounded during the whole 19 years."

Walker's friends and family say he's never forgotten where he came from. (Supplied: Gavin Schmidt)

It is a sentiment Walker's friend, Jayden Kelly agreed with.

"He's had so many ups and downs, the resilience he has shown, and he's never forgotten where he's come from," he said.

"He's so loyal to the people around him, to his family, and to the town that he grew up in.

World.title: Aussie open water swim queen Johnson triumphs at Pan Pacs
World.content:
Australia's world champion Moesha Johnson has continued her season of complete dominance in open water swimming, winning the Pan Pacific Championships 10-kilometre title off Long Beach, California.

Racing on the same waterfront expected to be used for the 2028 Olympics, 28-year-old Johnson grabbed the lead on the second of six laps and won comfortably in one hour 55 minutes and 33 seconds on Tuesday (AEST).

She finished more than 26 seconds clear of silver medallist Airi Ebina of Japan, with Ichika Kajimoto (Japan) third and fellow Australian Jacqueline Davison-McGovern fifth in the 23-strong field.

"I really wanted to win going into the race today, and it's a strong group of girls, they're really fit and everyone's in really good shape," Johnson said after the race.
